verification_test: The author tries to sign as checker -> blocked. A Draft MBR cannot issue a batch. A batch size not in the approved list -> issuance blocked. Version history shows who prepared, checked and approved each version and when.
notes: Clause and paraphrase correct. The binding basis for accepting e-signatures here is 11.1(c) in the uploaded Part 11 text; the DI Q&A is supporting guidance. Implication on batch-size ranges tightened because 211.186(a) requires a master record for each batch size. | DI Q&A portion faithful to Q11 (line gave no Q number). The 211.186(a) wording matches the local CFR text. Added Q11's expectation to document signer-identification controls and the Q3/Q6 links relevant to the MBR lifecycle.

requirement: The master record must contain: the product name, strength and dosage-form description; each active ingredient's name and quantity, expressed per dosage unit or per weight/volume unit of product, and the total weight or measure of one dosage unit; a complete component list using names or codes specific enough to show any special quality characteristic; an accurate amount for each component, all expressed in one weight system (metric, avoirdupois or apothecary), with reasonable variations allowed only if justified in the record; a statement of any calculated excess of a component; theoretical weight or measure at appropriate processing phases; theoretical yield together with the upper and lower percentage limits that trigger a 211.192 investigation; a description of containers, closures and packaging materials, plus a sample or copy of every label and other labeling piece bearing the approver's signature and date; and full manufacturing and control instructions together with the sampling and test procedures, specifications, and any special notes and precautions.
system_implications: The MBR data model has mandatory structured fields for all nine elements. Validation rules block approval if any element is missing: one weight system (e.g., metric) used consistently across all components of the record, with unit prefixes (mg, g, kg) allowed within it; overage fields with justification text; yield limits mandatory at each yield checkpoint; label specimens linked to approved artwork with approver signatures; instructions as structured steps with parameters and limits, IPC/sampling plans and specification references; hazard/precaution notations. Component codes must reference material master records carrying quality grade (e.g., 'WFI', 'low-endotoxin', 'micronized'). Scope note: enforcing structured fields is a design choice; the rule requires the content, not its format.
verification_test: Try to approve an MBR missing yield limits, a label specimen or an overage justification -> approval blocked with a list of missing elements. Mixed units for one component -> blocked.
notes: Clause and paraphrase correct (the meta-comment about verbatim confirmation was dropped). Implication corrected: 211.186(b)(4) requires the same weight system across the components, not a single unit per component.

source: 21 CFR Part 211 (with FDA DI Q&A on control of blank forms)
clause: FDA DI Q&A Q6 (blank-form control, reconciliation, keeping spoiled forms); binding basis 211.188(a); document controls per 211.100, 211.160(a), 211.186; retention of replaced forms per 211.192, 211.194 (as cited in Q6)
requirement: Binding (211.188(a), checked against the local CFR text): every batch has a production and control record with complete information on its production and control, starting with an accurate reproduction of the applicable master record that has been checked for accuracy, dated and signed. DI Q&A Q6: document controls must exist; blank forms, if used (Q6 names electronic worksheets, lab notebooks and MPCRs), should fall under quality-unit control or some other document-control method; where appropriate, numbered sets may be issued and should be reconciled once all issued forms are completed; incomplete or erroneous forms should remain in the permanent record with a written reason for their replacement.
system_implications: Keep: issue only from the Effective MBR with version ID/hash stored; issuance signature; instructions frozen after issue with controlled amendments; unique numbering; issued/executed/voided reconciliation; voided or reissued instances retained with reason and approver. Clarify: Q6 presents numbered issuance as one option; the expectation is QU (or equivalent) document control, reconciliation and retention of replaced instances with written justification. Generating the batch record from the MBR is itself a workflow to validate (Q3).
verification_test: Change the MBR after issuance -> the issued instance is unchanged, and the hash still matches the version it was issued from. Issuing from a Draft -> blocked. Voiding an instance keeps it visible with a reason. The issuance reconciliation report has no gaps.
notes: Clause and paraphrase correct; the blank-form statement is guidance (outside the uploaded texts) and is labelled as such. Implications correct. | Faithful to Q6 (line gave no Q number). Precision added: numbered issuance is an example, and control may be by the QU or another document-control method.

requirement: The batch record must document that each significant step of manufacture, processing, packing or holding was accomplished, covering: the dates; which individual major equipment and lines were used; specific identification of each component or in-process material batch used; component weights and measures used during processing; in-process and laboratory control results; checks of the packaging/labeling area both before and after it is used; actual yield and percentage of theoretical yield at appropriate phases; complete labeling control records with specimens or copies of all labeling used; a description of containers and closures; any sampling performed; who performed each significant step and who directly supervised or checked it (or, for a step done by automated equipment under 211.68, who checked the equipment's work); any 211.192 investigation; and the results of the 211.134 label examinations.
system_implications: Steps are flagged as 'significant' in the MBR, and each flagged step requires a performer signature plus a verifier/supervisor signature from a different user (or automated execution plus one checker). The batch report must render all 13 data categories. A completeness engine blocks 'Production complete' if any category is missing: sampling events with sample IDs linked to LIMS, label specimens (image of the first printed label or scan), container/closure descriptions from master data, and investigations linked. Dates and times come from server timestamps. Clarifications: the completeness engine must test only the categories applicable to the step type (e.g., packaging-area inspections only for packaging), and specimens must cover all labeling used (labels, cartons, inserts), not only the first printed label. Scope note: a second person on every significant step matches (b)(11) ('directly supervising or checking'); for automated steps one checker suffices per 211.68(c).
verification_test: Execute a full test batch. The completeness report shows all 13 elements. A significant step signed by only one person -> cannot complete. Removing a label specimen -> 'Production complete' blocked.
notes: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct; small clarifications on applicability and labeling specimens.

requirement: Before a batch is released or distributed, the QCU must review and approve all its production and control records, packaging and labeling records included, to establish compliance with all established, approved written procedures. Any unexplained discrepancy (including a percentage of theoretical yield outside the master-record limits), or any failure of a batch or its components to meet specifications, requires a thorough investigation, even if the batch has already shipped, and that investigation must extend to other batches of the same product and to other products that may be associated with the failure or discrepancy. A written investigation record with conclusions and follow-up is required.
system_implications: A QA review workbench does review-by-exception. It lists every deviation, out-of-limit value, late entry, correction of critical data (from the audit trail, per the DI Q&A), manual fallback/override, alarm, timer breach and open item. Each exception must be individually acknowledged or dispositioned before release. The full record stays viewable, because review-by-exception supplements full-record access and does not replace it. The investigation module (or QMS link) has a mandatory impact-assessment step. The system supplies impact queries: other batches sharing component lots, intermediate lots, equipment (and the previous/next product), rooms, personnel, utilities, time windows, APS or EM excursions, and other products made on the same equipment. Investigations require conclusion and follow-up/CAPA fields. Post-distribution investigations can be linked to distributed lots and their consignees. Scope notes: routine review of critical-data audit trails before release and per-exception acknowledgment come from FDA data-integrity guidance and design choices, not 211.192 text; CAPA fields are good practice (the rule requires conclusions and follow-up). Review-by-exception is acceptable only because the QCU still approves the complete record, so the release e-signature meaning should state that the full record was reviewed.
verification_test: Seed a batch with one exception of each type -> all appear and release is blocked until each is dispositioned. The impact query for a component lot or equipment returns the correct set of batches, verified against an independent query. An investigation cannot close without conclusion and follow-up.
notes: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct; guidance-derived elements labelled.

requirement: Laboratory records must contain complete data from every test needed to assure compliance with specifications and standards, including: a description of each sample with its source (where it was taken), quantity, lot number or other distinctive code, date sampled and date received for testing; a statement of each test method used, with the location of data showing the method is accurate and reliable for the product (a citation suffices for unmodified compendial, AOAC, other recognized or approved-application methods), plus verification that every method is suitable under actual conditions of use; the sample weight or measure used for each test where appropriate; a complete record of all raw data, including instrument graphs, charts and spectra, each identified to the specific material and lot tested; all calculations with units, conversion and equivalency factors; the results and how they compare with the standards; the tester's initials or signature and the test dates; and a second person's initials or signature confirming the original records were checked for accuracy, completeness and compliance.
system_implications: For IPCs executed in the eBMR (weights, hardness, pH, fill volume), the system stores raw instrument output (files or strings) linked to instrument ID, sample ID and the step, the calculation with formula version, the result vs limits, and performer and date. A second-person review of IPC data is required where the SOP classifies the test as a laboratory test. Result-only entry is not allowed when the instrument can transmit raw data. Invalidated or repeated measurements are retained with justification (US-DI-10). Corrections (falls short): IPC records must also capture the test method reference and version (with the location of its validation/suitability data), the sample quantity used where relevant, units and conversion factors in calculations, and a link from the raw data to the specific material and lot tested (not only to the instrument). Whether shop-floor IPCs count as laboratory records is a firm decision that must be justified; if they do, the second-person review in (a)(8) is mandatory, and in any case 211.188(b)(11) requires a checker for significant steps. Scope notes: 'no result-only entry' is a design choice; US-DI-10 is not part of this set.
verification_test: A pH IPC stores the meter's raw record and calibration reference. Deleting a replicate is impossible; invalidating one requires a reason and QA visibility.
notes: Corrected: (a)(4) requires the data (graphs, charts, spectra) to be identified to the material and lot tested; the paraphrase shifted this to 'properly identified instrumentation'. Also restored the omitted date received for testing, the method-validation location/citation rule and the suitability-under-actual-use requirement of (a)(2), and units/factors in (a)(5).

requirement: Written, followed procedures must govern handling of all written and oral complaints about a drug product, including QCU review of any complaint about a possible failure to meet specifications, a decision on whether a 211.192 investigation is needed, and a review of whether the complaint is a serious and unexpected adverse drug experience that must be reported under 21 CFR 310.305 or 514.80. Each complaint is recorded in a designated complaint file kept at the establishment that made, processed or packed the product, or elsewhere if the records are readily available for inspection there. Where known, the record gives product name and strength, lot number, complainant name, nature of the complaint and the reply. If investigated, the record includes findings and follow-up (the investigation record itself stays where the investigation was done, per 211.180(c)); if not, it gives the reason and names the person who decided no investigation was needed. Complaint records are kept for the later of 1 year after the product's expiry or 1 year after receipt of the complaint; for OTC products exempt from expiry dating, 3 years after distribution.
system_implications: A complaint lot lookup must immediately retrieve the full BPR, genealogy, deviations and distribution for the lot, and the eBMR exposes an API for the QMS complaint module. Complaint-to-lot links feed APR (211.180(e)) and extend batch-record retention if the complaint's retention end is later. Correction (goes beyond): 211.198(b) sets the retention of the complaint record itself; it does not require extending batch-record retention, so auto-extension is a design choice (useful where the complaint file relies on the batch record). Scope note: the complaint workflow normally sits in the QMS; the eBMR's regulatory role is fast lot lookup and links for investigations and the annual review.
verification_test: From a complaint referencing a lot, open the BPR, genealogy and shipments within the defined SLA. Retention recalculates when a late complaint is linked.
notes: Clause and paraphrase correct; retention wording now verified against the uploaded text. Added the omitted adverse-drug-experience reportability review in (a) and the file-location rules. Implication on extending batch-record retention flagged as beyond the rule.

requirement: Part 11 sets the criteria for FDA to regard electronic records, electronic signatures, and handwritten signatures applied to electronic records as reliable, trustworthy and broadly equivalent to paper records with handwritten signatures. It covers any record kept in electronic form (created, modified, maintained, archived, retrieved or transmitted) under an FDA records requirement, but not paper records that have merely been sent electronically. Computer systems (hardware and software), controls and associated documentation kept under Part 11 must be open to FDA inspection and readily available to inspectors. For records kept but not submitted to FDA, electronic records and signatures may replace paper and handwritten signatures in whole or in part if Part 11 is met (11.2(a)). Definitions: in a closed system, access is controlled by the people responsible for the records' content; in an open system it is not. Other defined terms include electronic record, electronic signature (symbols an individual executes, adopts or authorizes as the legally binding equivalent of a handwritten signature), digital signature (cryptographic, allowing signer identity and data integrity to be verified), biometrics, and handwritten signature (which also covers a scripted name or legal mark applied with a stylus to a capturing device).
system_implications: Every 211 record held in the eBMR is a Part 11 record. Validation documentation, configuration specifications, SOPs and supplier documentation must be inspection-ready at each site (11.1(e)). Classify the deployment as a closed system: for vendor-hosted or multi-tenant SaaS, access control, identity provisioning and privileged access must stay under the regulated company's control (contractually and technically), with vendor/admin access logged and approved. If that cannot be demonstrated, apply 11.30: the applicable 11.10 controls plus additional measures such as document encryption and digital signature standards as needed for the circumstances (11.30 gives these as examples, not a fixed pair).
verification_test: Documentation review: system classification rationale (closed/open), access-control ownership and a privileged-access log demonstrating that the regulated company controls access. An inspection-readiness drill produces validation and configuration documents on request.
notes: Clause and paraphrase correct; filled in what the cited 11.2 and 11.3(b) definitions actually say (the original listed them without content) and the 11.1(b) carve-out for paper records sent electronically. Implication corrected: 11.30 requires the 11.10 controls plus extra measures as needed, with encryption and digital signatures given only as examples.

requirement: Closed systems must be validated to show that they are accurate and reliable, perform consistently as intended, and can detect records that are invalid or have been altered.
system_implications: Risk-based validation (see US-CSA-01) with traceability from the URS (this requirement set) to test evidence. Technical means to discern altered records: cryptographic content hashes on each record version and signature, a hash-chained append-only audit trail, and a scheduled integrity-verification job that recomputes chains and alarms on mismatch. Site-specific configuration baselines are compared against the validated baseline to detect configuration drift. Scope notes: cryptographic hashing, hash chains and integrity jobs are design choices that serve the ability to detect altered records; the rule does not prescribe them. Risk-based/CSA validation (US-CSA-01, not in this set) is FDA guidance.
verification_test: In a test environment, tamper directly with a database row, bypassing the application -> the integrity job detects it and raises a critical alert naming the record. The traceability matrix covers 100% of the high-risk requirements.
notes: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

requirement: The system must be able to output full, accurate copies of its records, both as human-readable renderings and in electronic form, suitable for FDA to inspect, review and copy; firms should contact FDA with any questions about the agency's ability to review and copy the records.
system_implications: One-click export of the complete batch record: human-readable (PDF/A including all data, signature manifestations, deviations, attachments and the audit trail) and electronic (structured JSON/XML/CSV with metadata, plus native attachments). Exports are themselves logged (who, when, what). For dynamic data (process trends, chromatograms, lyophilizer cycle data), provide the data plus a viewer and the static rendering. Supports FDA records requests under FD&C Act 704(a)(4) and remote regulatory assessments. Scope note: logging of exports and support for FD&C Act 704(a)(4) requests and remote assessments are good practice or other-statute drivers outside the uploaded texts.
verification_test: Export a batch and compare it field by field with the database. Confirm signatures show name, date/time and meaning, and that the audit trail is included and complete. Export time for a large batch meets the SLA.
notes: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

requirement: Records must be protected so they can be retrieved accurately and readily for the whole retention period.
system_implications: Immutable storage for finalized records (object lock/WORM), geo-redundant backups, periodic restore tests, and format-longevity policy (open formats such as PDF/A and JSON with schema versions). Periodic readability tests of the oldest archived records. Documented and validated data migrations with before/after hash reconciliation. Retention is tied to US-211-180.
verification_test: Annual retrieval test of records older than N years. The restore test proves the recovery point and recovery time objectives. Migration reconciliation report shows zero mismatches.
notes: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct; the named storage technologies are design choices.

requirement: Access to the system must be limited to authorized individuals.
system_implications: Unique named accounts only, with no generic or shared accounts (see US-DI-04). Identity provider/SSO integration with MFA is acceptable. Joiner/mover/leaver provisioning tied to HR, with immediate disablement on termination. Periodic access recertification by area owners. Session inactivity timeout and auto-lock on shop-floor terminals. Break-glass accounts are sealed, alarmed and reviewed. Scope note: HR-driven provisioning, access recertification and inactivity locks are good-practice ways of meeting this; inactivity locks also matter for defining a continuous period of controlled access under 11.200(a)(1). US-DI-04 is not part of this set.
verification_test: A terminated user in HR is disabled in the eBMR within the defined time. An inactive session locks after the configured period. An access-review report is produced and signed.
notes: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

requirement: The system must use secure, computer-generated, time-stamped audit trails that capture on their own the date and time of each operator entry or action that creates, changes or deletes an electronic record. A change must leave the previously recorded information visible. Audit trail documentation is kept at least as long as the underlying electronic records and is available to FDA for review and copying.
system_implications: The audit trail is generated server-side, independent of the application UI, and is append-only. Each entry captures: who (unique user ID plus printed name at the time), what (record, field, old value, new value), when (UTC server timestamp plus site time zone), why (reason for change, mandatory for any modification of GMP data after initial commit, chosen from a controlled list plus free text), and where (terminal/device ID). Nobody, including administrators, can edit, delete or disable audit trails on GMP objects; audit configuration changes are themselves audited and alarmed. Corrections create new record versions and the original value stays visible. GMP records are never physically deleted in normal operation; they are voided or invalidated with a reason. Audit trail retention equals record retention. The audit trail is searchable, filterable by batch, step, user and critical data, and exportable. Hash chaining provides tamper evidence. Record-level and system-level events (logins, failed logins, permission changes, configuration changes) are captured too, per the DI Q&A definition. Scope notes (beyond 11.10(e)): a mandatory reason for change comes from FDA guidance and EU Annex 11, not from 11.10(e); device ID capture is good practice (related to 11.10(h)); login and failed-login logging supports 11.300(d) rather than 11.10(e). A ban on physical deletion is a design choice (11.10(e) assumes deletions can occur but must be audit-trailed without obscuring prior data). Hash chaining is a design choice.
verification_test: Modify a value -> the audit shows old and new values, user, timestamp, reason and device. An administrator tries to disable or purge the audit trail -> not possible, or the attempt is alarmed and audited. A database-level tamper is detected by the hash-chain check. The audit trail of an archived batch is still retrievable.
notes: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct; flagged implication items that come from guidance or other clauses.

requirement: Where appropriate, operational system checks must enforce the permitted order of steps and events.
system_implications: An MBR execution state machine enforces step order (with MBR-declared parallel branches) and prerequisites: line clearance, equipment status, material status, IPC due, timer states, QA gates. The batch lifecycle (Issued -> In Execution -> Production Complete -> Under QA Review -> Released/Rejected, with Hold and Cancelled) has guarded transitions. Out-of-sequence execution is only possible via a deviation path with QA approval, and is recorded. Scope note: the QA-approved deviation path for out-of-sequence execution is a design choice; the rule only requires sequencing checks where appropriate.
verification_test: Attempt step N+1 before step N -> blocked. Attempt release before review -> blocked. The deviation path for out-of-sequence execution requires QA e-signature and appears in the review list.
notes: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

requirement: Authority checks must confirm that a person is authorized before letting them use the system, sign a record electronically, reach the operation or the system's input/output devices, change a record, or carry out the operation in question.
system_implications: Fine-grained, least-privilege permissions per action (execute, verify, supervise, QA review, approve MBR, change master data, configure, administer), scoped by legal entity, site, area, product and line. Signature meanings are bound to roles (a user without QA role cannot sign 'Approved for release'). Segregation-of-duties rules: performer is not verifier; author is not checker; executor is not QA approver for the same batch; administrator is not a GMP data user on the same system unless an approved exception with a second reviewer applies (per the DI Q&A). Cross-site data isolation is enforced by default. Scope note: the segregation-of-duties rules 'executor is not QA approver' and 'administrator is not a GMP data user' are good practice from FDA data-integrity guidance; 11.10(g) itself requires authority checks, while 'performer is not verifier' and 'author is not checker' come from the Part 211 second-person rules (211.101, 211.103, 211.186(a), 211.188(b)(11)).
verification_test: A permission-matrix test suite runs positive and negative tests per role and action, including cross-site isolation and signature-meaning binding.
notes: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct; sources of the segregation-of-duties rules clarified.

requirement: Where appropriate, device (e.g., terminal) checks must confirm that the source of data input or operational instructions is valid.
system_implications: Registered devices only: terminals, tablets, scales, instruments and PLC/SCADA connectors carry device identities (certificates or IDs) and are assigned to a room or line. Data is accepted only from a device registered to the location of the executing step. Each value stores its source device ID. Operational instructions sent to equipment (recipe download) go only to the registered equipment for that step. Scope note: binding every device to a location is one way to meet the 'as appropriate' device checks; the rule does not require it for all devices.
verification_test: Data from an unregistered or relocated scale -> rejected with an alert. A terminal registered to room A cannot execute steps assigned to room B (if configured).
notes: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

requirement: (i) It must be established that the people who develop, maintain or use the electronic record/signature system have the education, training and experience for their assigned tasks. (j) Written policies, established and followed, must make individuals accountable and responsible for actions taken under their electronic signatures, so that record and signature falsification is deterred. (k) Systems documentation must be appropriately controlled: its distribution, access and use for system operation and maintenance must be controlled, and revision and change control procedures must keep an audit trail showing, in time order, how that documentation was developed and modified.
system_implications: (i) Training records cover end users, key users, administrators and vendor developers (supplier qualification). (j) Before first signing, each user electronically acknowledges the e-signature accountability statement, and the acknowledgment is recorded and a prerequisite for signing; it is refreshed periodically. (k) System documentation (URS, configuration specifications, SOPs, admin manuals) lives in a controlled document system. Configuration changes are versioned with diffs and linked to change records, and the system's own configuration audit trail is retained. Scope note: an electronic acknowledgment before first signing and its periodic refresh are good-practice ways to show adherence to the 11.10(j) policy; the text does not require them.
verification_test: A new user cannot sign before acknowledging the accountability statement. A configuration change without a change record ID -> blocked (where enforced). Configuration diff history is available for any date.
notes: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

requirement: Anyone using an open system to create, modify, maintain or transmit electronic records must apply procedures and controls that protect the records' authenticity, integrity and, where appropriate, confidentiality from creation until receipt. These include the 11.10 controls as appropriate plus additional measures, such as document encryption and suitable digital signature standards, as needed in the circumstances.
system_implications: Apply to any record flow crossing organizational boundaries or the public internet outside the company's access control: CMO/CDMO data exchange, DSCSA EPCIS exchange with trading partners, remote vendor support, FDA submissions. Use TLS 1.2+ in transit, encryption at rest, message-level signing (e.g., signed payloads or digital signatures) for data exchanged with third parties, and certificate management. Clarification: whether a system is open or closed depends on who controls access, not on the network used; 11.30 also requires the applicable 11.10 controls, not only encryption and signing. DSCSA EPCIS exchange is a DSCSA driver outside the uploaded texts.
verification_test: Interface security tests: unsigned or tampered messages from a partner are rejected. Encryption is verified in transit and at rest.
notes: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

requirement: Signed electronic records must show, with each signing, the signer's printed name, the date and time of signing, and what the signature means (e.g., review, approval, responsibility or authorship). These three items are controlled in the same way as the electronic records themselves and must appear in every human-readable form of the record, such as a screen display or printout.
system_implications: Every signature is displayed and printed with: full printed name (not just the user ID), date and time including time zone (store UTC; show site-local with offset), and a meaning from a controlled list bound to the step ('Performed by', 'Verified by', 'Supervised/Checked by', 'Reviewed by QA', 'Approved for release', 'Rejected', 'Prepared', 'Checked', 'Approved'). The manifestation is stored immutably with the signature at signing time, not re-derived from the mutable user table, so later name changes do not alter historic signatures. Manifestations appear on every screen and report view of the signed data.
verification_test: Sign a step and view it on screen, in the batch report PDF and in the export -> all three elements appear. Rename the user -> historic signatures still show the original printed name. Signatures across time zones show the correct local time and offset.
notes: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

requirement: Electronic signatures, and handwritten signatures applied to electronic records, must be linked to their records so that nobody can, by ordinary means, remove, copy or transfer a signature to falsify an electronic record.
system_implications: Each signature record binds the signer identity, meaning, timestamp and a cryptographic hash of the exact signed content (the record version). A later permitted correction of signed data automatically marks the signature 'superseded by change' and requires re-signing (the performer's or verifier's as applicable), with the audit trail kept. Signatures cannot be moved or copied between records, and the integrity job detects any such tampering. Hybrid wet-ink signatures on printouts are avoided. If unavoidable, the scanned signed page is indexed to the record ID and content hash and the hybrid process is covered by an SOP. Scope note: cryptographic content hashes and automatic re-signing after a correction exceed the 'ordinary means' standard of 11.70; they are sound design choices, not requirements.
verification_test: Correct a signed value -> the signature status becomes superseded and re-sign is required. Copying a signature row to another record in the test database -> the integrity check fails. Hash verification succeeds for untouched records.
notes: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

source: 21 CFR Part 11 (11.100(c)(1) as amended by the technical amendment of March 2, 2023)
requirement: (a) Each electronic signature belongs to exactly one individual and is never reused by or reassigned to anyone else. (b) The organization verifies a person's identity before it establishes, assigns, certifies or otherwise sanctions that person's electronic signature or any element of it. (c) Before or when they first use them, persons using electronic signatures certify to FDA that the signatures in their system (used on or after 20 August 1997) are meant to be legally binding like traditional handwritten signatures; the certification carries a traditional handwritten signature and is sent electronically or on paper, with submission details on FDA's Letters of Non-Repudiation Agreement web page. On request, they give FDA additional certification or testimony that a particular e-signature legally binds the signer as a handwritten one would.
system_implications: User IDs are never reused or reassigned, even after deactivation; enforced by a permanent uniqueness registry across all sites and tenants. Account activation requires a recorded identity-verification step (who verified, method, date). A go-live checklist per legal entity records the non-repudiation letter submission (date, scope: company-wide or individual). Signature credentials are personal: no proxy signing or delegated signing on behalf of another person. Scope note: 11.100(c) is an organizational submission, not a system function; tracking it in a go-live checklist is good practice.
verification_test: Create a new account with the ID of a deactivated user -> blocked. Activate an account without an identity-verification record -> blocked. Configuration shows NRL status per legal entity.
notes: Clause and paraphrase correct, including the 2023 amendment to (c)(1) as shown in the uploaded text.

requirement: Electronic signatures not based on biometrics must use at least two distinct identification components (such as an ID code and a password). Within one continuous period of controlled system access, the first signing uses all components and later signings use at least one component that only the individual can execute and that is meant for that individual's use alone; signings made outside such a continuous period each use all components. Non-biometric signatures may be used only by their genuine owners and must be administered and executed so that any attempt by someone else to use them would need two or more people to collude. Biometric signatures must be designed so that nobody other than their genuine owner can use them.
system_implications: The signing dialog re-authenticates at the moment of signing (user ID + password, or an SSO step-up with a second factor). The 'continuous period of controlled access' is defined strictly: any lock, timeout, logout or terminal switch ends it. Recommendation: require both components for all critical signatures (verification, QA review, release, MBR approval), because shop-floor terminals are shared. A verifier signs in the same dialog with their own full credentials; the performer's session can never supply the verifier's signature. No 'remember password'. Administrators cannot see passwords, and admin-set passwords force a change at first use (so misuse needs collusion). Biometric options, such as badge plus fingerprint in cleanrooms where typing is impractical, need liveness and anti-spoofing evidence.
verification_test: Sign twice in one session -> the second signing requires at least the password. After timeout or lock -> both components required. Try to record a verifier signature using the performer's session -> requires the verifier's own ID and password. An admin-reset password cannot be used to sign before it is changed.
notes: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct; the rule to require both components for all critical signatures is correctly labelled as a recommendation.

requirement: Where e-signatures rely on ID codes combined with passwords, controls must protect their security and integrity, including: keeping every ID-code/password combination unique to one person; periodically checking, recalling or revising issued codes and passwords (e.g., password aging); procedures for managing losses, so that tokens, cards or other devices that hold or generate codes/passwords and are lost, stolen, missing or possibly compromised are electronically deauthorized, with temporary or permanent replacements issued under rigorous controls; transaction safeguards that prevent unauthorized use of passwords or ID codes and that detect any attempted misuse and report it immediately and urgently to the system security unit and, where appropriate, to management; and initial and periodic testing of such tokens or cards to confirm they work and have not been altered without authorization.
system_implications: Password policy: complexity, history, and aging or a documented risk-based equivalent (e.g., NIST SP 800-63B with compromised-password screening), with the rationale recorded. Account lockout after N failed login or signature attempts. Real-time security alerting (SIEM) on repeated failures, signature attempts on locked accounts, and anomalous access, routed to the security unit with acknowledgment tracking and escalation to management. Immediate revocation of lost badges or tokens, with replacement issued only after identity verification. Periodic badge and token functional tests. Clarification: if password aging is replaced by a NIST-style risk-based policy, 11.300(b) still requires periodic checking of issued credentials (e.g., access recertification and compromised-credential screening); document how that is met.
verification_test: N failed signature attempts -> the account locks and an alert reaches the security unit within the defined minutes. A revoked badge cannot authenticate. Token test records exist.
notes: Clause, paraphrase and implications correct.

source: FDA Guidance 'Part 11, Electronic Records; Electronic Signatures - Scope and Application' (August 2003)
clause: Sections III.A-III.C (narrow interpretation of scope; enforcement discretion; predicate rules)
requirement: FDA interprets Part 11's scope narrowly. Part 11 applies to predicate-rule records kept electronically in place of paper; to records kept electronically in addition to paper and relied on for regulated activities (business practice decides); to records submitted electronically; and to e-signatures intended as handwritten equivalents. FDA exercises enforcement discretion on the validation, audit trail, record retention and record copying requirements, but predicate rules (e.g., 211.68, 211.180) still apply. Audit trails are particularly appropriate where users are expected to create, modify or delete regulated records during normal operation. FDA intends to enforce all other provisions, including access limits, operational, authority and device checks, training, accountability policies, documentation controls, open-system controls, and all e-signature requirements (11.50, 11.70, 11.100, 11.200, 11.300). Enforcement discretion also applies to legacy systems operational before August 20, 1997, under certain circumstances.
system_implications: Enforcement discretion is not a design basis. The eBMR is the primary record for regulated activity and users routinely create and modify GMP data, so implement every 11.10 control, including validation and full audit trails; the DI Q&A (2018) and 211.68 independently expect them. Document in an SOP or system specification that the electronic record is the official record, and treat printouts as copies. Avoid hybrid paper and electronic processes, or define them explicitly with linking controls (11.70).
verification_test: Documentation check: a record-type inventory stating the official record per data type. A risk assessment justifies any control not implemented (none expected for GMP batch data).

source: FDA Guidance 'Data Integrity and Compliance With Drug CGMP: Questions and Answers' (December 2018)
clause: FDA DI Q&A Q1a-Q1f (definitions) and footnote 5; binding basis: ALCOA letters mapped to 211.101(d), 211.122, 211.186, 211.188(b)(11) (attributable), 211.180(e) (legible), 211.100(b), 211.160(a) (contemporaneous), 211.180, 211.194(a) (original/true copy), 211.22(a), 211.68, 211.188 (accurate); metadata retention 211.188, 211.194; backup 211.68(b), 211.180; systems 211.68
requirement: Q1a: data integrity means data are complete, consistent and accurate, and such data should show the ALCOA traits (Attributable; Legible; Contemporaneously recorded; Original or true copy; Accurate); the letters are listed, not individually defined. Integrity matters from first capture through use, storage and transfer to disposal after retention, and system design and controls should make errors, omissions and aberrant results easy to spot. Q1b: metadata is the context needed to make sense of a value (e.g., units, timestamps, who acquired it, which instrument, material identity/status, and audit trails); data should be retained for the full retention period with the metadata needed to reconstruct the activity, and the data-metadata link kept secure and traceable. Q1c: an audit trail is a secured, time-stamped electronic record generated by the computer itself, from which the creation, change or deletion of an electronic record can be reconstructed; it covers data-level changes and record/system-level actions such as access attempts or renaming/deleting files, and reprocessing should be documented with its justification. Q1d: static = fixed (paper, image); dynamic = the user can interact with the content (e.g., re-integrate a chromatogram, alter spreadsheet formulas that compute results or a calculated yield). Q1e: the 211.68(b) backup is a true copy of the original kept securely for the retention period, holding data plus metadata in the original or a compatible format; FDA equates it with an archive; temporary copies kept against crashes or interruptions do not meet 211.68(b). Q1f: 'computer or related systems' reach beyond software and servers to attached devices, networks, cloud hosting, the people who run them and their documentation (manuals, SOPs).
system_implications: Keep: each value stored with its metadata; dynamic data (historian trends, cycle data, spectra) kept natively with a viewer; the ALCOA-to-control mapping. Add: (1) audit trail entries are part of each value's metadata and must go with it into backup, archive, export and migration; (2) dispensing/charging metadata includes material identity and status; (3) in-system yield and other calculations are dynamic content - version-lock formulas and keep inputs, formula version and result (DI-NEW-03); (4) the 211.68(b) backup is a true copy with metadata and audit trails, in original or compatible format, kept for the full retention period; short-lived crash-recovery snapshots do not qualify, and a replica that mirrors deletions or corruption is not secure from alteration or loss; (5) hosting/cloud, network, peripherals, users and SOPs are within the 211.68 system (DI-NEW-04); (6) build detection of errors, omissions and aberrant results into the design (DI-NEW-01).
verification_test: For sample records, confirm the metadata is complete and the native dynamic data can be re-rendered. Confirm the backup contains metadata and audit trails.
notes: Stated points are accurate, but the line under-covered its own clause: Q1f (systems include cloud infrastructure, personnel, SOPs) was named but not paraphrased; audit trails being listed as metadata, the life-cycle and error-detection design expectation, and the backup = archive equivalence were missing. 'Must be kept with it' softened to 'should', with the binding hooks in 211.188/211.194.

clause: FDA DI Q&A Q3; binding basis 211.63, 211.68(b), 211.110(a); MPCR-review analogy 211.100, 211.186
requirement: Yes: each CGMP workflow run on a computer system (FDA's example is building an electronic MPCR) is an intended use that should be checked through validation, with validation effort proportionate to the risk of the automated system. Qualifying a platform such as an MES shows it meets its own requirements but not that a particular MPCR it generates calculates correctly; validating the workflow shows the MPCR's steps, requirements and calculations work as intended - comparable to reviewing a paper MPCR and its supporting procedures before production use. If one system serves both CGMP and non-CGMP purposes, the firm should assess, and mitigate as appropriate, the chance that the non-CGMP features influence CGMP operations. Controls should cover software, hardware, personnel and documentation.
system_implications: Keep: validation of configured workflows, site configurations, interfaces and GMP-decision reports; every MBR version verified (steps, requirements, calculations) before it becomes Effective. Correct: a built-in MBR simulation/dry-run mode is a design choice, not an FDA expectation; if offered, it is a non-CGMP function inside a CGMP system and needs a documented assessment showing it cannot alter, leak into or be mistaken for real batch records (segregated data, visible marking, no real lot IDs, never used with actual product samples - cf. Q13). Scale validation depth to risk; validate review-by-exception rules because Q8 expects review reliability to be demonstrable; include hardware, personnel (roles, training) and documentation in scope.
verification_test: An MBR cannot become Effective without a linked verification record from dry-run execution. Validation evidence exists for each GMP report and review-by-exception rule.
notes: Faithful to Q3 (now checked against the primary text, so the 'secondary summaries' caveat can be dropped). Added the risk-proportionate extent, the CGMP/non-CGMP coexistence point and the four control elements; system implications trimmed where a product feature was presented as required.

clause: FDA DI Q&A Q4; binding basis 211.68(b) (changes only by authorized personnel)
requirement: Must (211.68(b)): controls ensuring only authorized personnel can change computerized MPCRs or other CGMP records or enter laboratory data into computerized records; Q4 extends the restricted-control expectation to records from automated visual inspection, electronic materials management and automated dispensing/weighing systems. Should: technically limit, where feasible, who can change specifications, process parameters, data, or manufacturing and testing methods (e.g., through permissions over settings and data); give the system administrator role, including rights over files and settings, to people independent of those responsible for record content; establish a documented record of each CGMP system's authorized users and their privileges (e.g., a maintained list).
system_implications: Keep: IT/configuration administration segregated from GMP data roles; specifications, process parameters and MBR content editable only via the MBR/master-data change workflow; privileged activity logged and periodically reviewed. Add: weighing/dispensing, materials-management and visual-inspection data are explicitly in scope; restriction covers data generally, not only process-parameter data; current and historical user/role/privilege listing per system (DI-NEW-06). Correct: FDA gives no small-site fallback - a one-person admin-plus-QA exception with secondary review is a firm-defined compensating control needing its own justification, not an FDA recommendation.
verification_test: Try to grant admin and QA/production roles to one account at the same site -> blocked, or requires exception approval. Change a specification limit through the admin console -> impossible. The privileged-activity review report is produced.
notes: Q number supplied (Q4). Removed 'where that is not possible, secondary review is recommended': no such fallback exists in the final Dec 2018 text, and the line's 'FDA suggests' wording differs from the final 'should' (likely draft-era or other-guidance wording); similar compensating-control language exists in other DI guidance (e.g., PIC/S PI 041, MHRA GXP DI) - confirm there before citing. Fixed 'process parameter data' (Q4 lists process parameters and data separately). Added Q4's record examples and the documented access-privilege list.

clause: FDA DI Q&A Q5; binding basis 211.100, 211.68(b), 211.188(b)(11), 211.194(a)(7)-(8) (actions attributable to a specific individual)
requirement: With shared login credentials the login cannot identify a unique individual, so the system would not meet the part 211/212 CGMP requirements; system and documentation controls must be designed to assure product quality (211.100), and actions such as changing records or entering data must be traceable to one specific person (211.68(b), 211.188(b)(11), 211.194(a)(7)-(8)). Read-only accounts shared among users, which cannot alter data or settings, may be used just to look at data, but not for actions such as second-person review, which must be attributable to one individual.
system_implications: Keep: no shared or generic accounts for any GMP action, including line logins; fast individual re-authentication on shared terminals; individual authentication per GMP entry in kiosk mode; interface/service accounts non-interactive, unable to sign, attributed to the device or interface. Add: a shared read-only view (e.g., line status display) is acceptable only if it technically cannot create, change, sign, verify or acknowledge anything; every review or verification action requires individual authentication.
verification_test: Scan the user directory for generic accounts -> none with GMP permissions. A service account attempting a signature -> blocked. On a shared terminal, each entry is attributed to the individual who authenticated.
notes: Q number supplied (Q5). The sentence that audit trails cannot be relied on with shared logins is a reasonable inference but is not stated in Q5, so it is no longer presented as FDA text. Added the read-only shared-account allowance and the binding clauses FDA cites.

clause: FDA DI Q&A Q6; binding basis 211.100, 211.160(a), 211.186 (document controls required); 211.192, 211.194 (retaining replaced forms)
requirement: Must: document controls that assure product quality are in place. Should: blank forms, if used - Q6 explicitly names electronic worksheets, laboratory notebooks and MPCRs - be controlled by the quality unit or another document-control method (bound, paginated, officially stamped notebooks are cited as good practice because unofficial books and missing pages stand out); where appropriate, issue numbered sets and reconcile them once all issued forms are completed; retain spoiled or incomplete forms in the permanent record together with a written reason they were replaced; keep all data needed to recreate the CGMP activity in the complete record.
system_implications: Keep: controlled issuance of batch record instances, logbooks and ad-hoc forms from approved template versions; unique numbering; issued/completed/voided reconciliation; voided instances retained and retrievable with reason. Adjust: QA approval of every void is a firm choice - Q6 asks for a written justification under QU or other document control, not QA sign-off per void. Spreadsheets or electronic worksheets used to produce CGMP data are controlled forms (Q6 names electronic worksheets); uncontrolled attachments may be kept only as clearly labelled supporting information and never as the source of a CGMP result.
verification_test: The reconciliation report shows every issued instance accounted for. Voiding requires a reason and QA approval and the voided instance remains retrievable.
notes: Faithful to Q6 (Q number supplied). Added that 'electronic worksheets' are named explicitly - important for an eBMR - and the complete-record sentence.

clause: FDA DI Q&A Q7 (who) and Q8 (how often), footnote 13; binding basis 211.192 (QU reviews and approves all production and control records, audit trails included, before release), 211.22, 211.188(b) (each significant step); also 211.101(c)-(d), 211.103, 211.182, 211.186(a), 211.194(a)(8) as cited in Q7
requirement: Q7: audit trail review is comparable to examining cross-outs on paper; whoever is responsible for reviewing a CGMP record should review the audit trails of changes to that record's data during the same review; the quality unit must review and approve every production and control record, audit trails being part of those records (211.192); some review may be done by the person directly supervising or checking a step (211.188); FDA advises overseeing and reviewing CGMP records through a quality-system approach. Q8: where CGMP regulations fix a review frequency for the data, use the same frequency for its audit trail - for batch records, review after each significant step (211.188(b)) and before batch release (211.22); otherwise set the frequency from process knowledge and a risk assessment of data criticality, control mechanisms and product-quality impact; the approach must satisfy CGMP and its reliability should be proven. Footnote 13 names risks such as unauthorized or undetected deletion, amendment or exclusion, and offers logs of instrument status and communications, and alerts, as candidates for risk-based review.
system_implications: Keep: mandatory QA release-review section listing post-entry changes (old/new value, who, when, reason) with release blocked until reviewed; step verifiers see changes to the data they verify; drill-down to the full audit trail; periodic recorded system-level review. Correct: (1) step and release reviews cover changes to all data in the batch record, not only fields the MBR designer flags as critical - criticality may prioritise or highlight, not exclude; (2) the frequency for system and interface logs (logins, permissions, configuration, equipment communication, alarms) comes from a documented risk assessment of criticality, controls and product impact, not 'system complexity'; (3) validate the review-by-exception filters so review reliability can be shown (DI-NEW-08); (4) show changes inline like paper cross-outs, old value visible beside the new.
verification_test: Change a critical value after initial entry -> it appears in the QA release review section and release is blocked until acknowledged. The periodic system audit-trail review record exists with reviewer and findings.
notes: Split into Q7 and Q8. The phrases 'critical data reviewed with each record and before final approval' and 'schedule based on system complexity and intended use' are not in the final Dec 2018 text (likely carried over from the 2016 draft); the final ties audit trail review frequency to the regulatory review frequency of the underlying data (each significant step and before release, for batch records) or to a documented risk assessment.

clause: FDA DI Q&A Q12 and footnote 14; binding basis 211.100(b), 211.160(a) (documented at the time of performance), 211.180(d)
requirement: Any data created to meet a CGMP requirement is a CGMP record and must be documented or saved when the activity is performed (211.100(b), 211.160(a)). FDA expects processes designed so that required data cannot be changed unless the change itself is recorded (its lab example: write to durable media as each step or injection finishes, including incomplete or aborted ones, rather than at the end of a set; audit-trail changes and investigate aborted runs). Jotting data on scrap paper for later transcription is not acceptable, and neither is any electronic storage that lets records be manipulated before a permanent record exists. Technical and procedural controls may be combined - e.g., an EBR or LIMS that commits automatically after every entry (the electronic counterpart of indelible, contemporaneous entries on a paper batch record) plus a procedure requiring data to be entered as soon as generated. Footnote 14: FDA also reviews records not intended for CGMP that contain CGMP information.
system_implications: Keep: durable server-side commit with audit trail at each entry; no silent draft state for GMP observations; post-commit edits are audit-trailed changes with reason; offline clients use a tamper-evident append-only journal that syncs with original timestamps (engineering choice). Add: an SOP requiring immediate entry at the point of work (Q12 pairs technical and procedural controls); no free-text scratch fields later transcribed into GMP fields; outages handled with controlled, pre-issued contingency forms (DI-NEW-12), never ad-hoc notes; aborted or interrupted operations captured and justified (DI-NEW-13). Automatic instrument capture is good practice, not an explicit Q12 requirement.
verification_test: Enter a value, then kill the browser or network before completing the step -> the value is persisted and visible with its timestamp. Change it afterwards -> the audit trail shows the original. Offline mode: entries survive device reboot and sync with the original timestamps, and local tampering is detected.
notes: The 'temporary memory' sentences are not in the final Dec 2018 text (likely draft-era wording). The final states a broader rule - no storage method may allow manipulation before a permanent record exists - and adds that required data must not be changeable without a record of the change, plus the scrap-paper prohibition. Q number supplied.

clause: FDA DI Q&A Q9 (true copies) and Q10 (printouts vs dynamic originals); binding basis 211.180(d) (original records or true copies; suitable reader available), 211.68(b), 211.188, 211.194, 211.194(a)(8)
requirement: Q9: yes, electronic copies may serve as true copies of records originally on paper or in electronic form if they keep the original's content and meaning - all metadata needed to reconstruct the activity and the original's static or dynamic nature; true copies of dynamic records may be kept in the original format or another format that preserves content and meaning, provided suitable reader and copying equipment (software, hardware, media readers) remains readily available. Q10: a printout or static record can meet retention requirements when it is itself the original or a true copy - e.g., balances and pH meters that print at acquisition, in which case the printout or a true copy must be kept (211.180); for instruments whose records are dynamic (e.g., a reprocessable FT-IR spectral file), a printout or static record does not satisfy 211.180(d), and a partial spectrum display could hide contaminants. Original lab records, paper or electronic, must receive second-person review (211.194(a)(8)).
system_implications: Keep: native archival and export of dynamic data (historian series, cycle data, images, spectra) with metadata; interactive re-rendering test. Add: keep a validated viewer for the full retention period or migrate to a format that keeps content and meaning (DI-NEW-09); where a balance or similar device prints a ticket that is the original, retain it (or a true copy) linked to the eBMR entry, or capture the value electronically so the electronic record is the original (DI-NEW-10). Correct: a verifier signature for scanned true copies and conditions for destroying paper originals are reasonable firm controls but are not described in the DI Q&A.
verification_test: Restore an archived batch and re-render its trend data interactively. A scanned-document workflow requires a true-copy verification signature.
notes: Faithful (Q9 + Q10; Q numbers supplied). Added that a static printout can be the original for simple devices such as balances and pH meters - directly relevant to eBMR weighing - and the reader-availability condition.

clause: FDA DI Q&A Q11; binding basis 211.186(a); 21 CFR 11.2(a), with Part 11 signature controls 11.50, 11.70, 11.100, 11.200, 11.300
requirement: Yes: electronic signatures with appropriate controls may stand in for handwritten signatures or initials in any record CGMP requires; for the handwritten full-signature wording of 211.186(a), an electronic signature with controls that securely link it to its record meets the requirement (11.2(a)); Part 11 sets the criteria for legal equivalence. Firms should document the controls that let them identify the specific person who signed. PET MPCRs (part 212) have no handwritten-signature requirement.
system_implications: Keep: paperless MPCR preparation/check/approval, execution and release once Part 11 signature controls are met; initials fields use the same mechanism. Add: the validation file documents the signer-identification controls (unique IDs, identity verification before credential issue, signature manifestation, signature-record linking).
verification_test: MBR approval and batch release are completed end to end with e-signatures, and all signature controls pass their tests.
notes: Faithful to Q11 (Q number supplied). Added the expectation to document signer-identification controls.

clause: FDA DI Q&A Q2 (with Q13 on retaining all data and testing into compliance); binding basis 211.22, 211.180 (QU evaluation, retention), 211.160(b), 211.188, 211.192 (scientifically sound justification and investigation)
requirement: The quality unit must assess all data generated within a CGMP record when deciding on release, and those data are retained for CGMP purposes; electronic data include the metadata needed to reconstruct the activity. Excluding test results from QU decisions on conformance to a specification needs a valid, documented, scientifically sound justification (see the OOS guidance). Even after legitimate invalidation based on a scientifically sound investigation, the complete batch record handed to the QU still carries the invalidated original data plus the investigation report. Retention and review requirements are the same for paper and electronic records. Q13 adds that every result - obvious errors, failing, passing and suspect - must be retained and reviewed, and invalidation needs an investigation.
system_implications: Keep: invalidation never deletes; the value is marked invalid with justification, user and timestamp and stays visible in the record and exception list. Correct: invalidating a genuine measurement must link to a documented investigation (deviation/OOS-type record) whose report is part of the QU release package - the QU sees invalidated data and the report at release (Q2), not only 'QA concurrence where the SOP says so'; distinguish correcting an entry error (audit-trailed change with reason, still retained per Q13) from invalidating a real result (investigation). Repeat-until-pass flagging is supported by Q13 (DI-NEW-14); a fixed 'three repeats' threshold is a design choice.
verification_test: Invalidate a value -> it stays visible and marked with the justification, and appears in the QA review list. Three repeats of the same IPC -> an automatic flag.
notes: Q number supplied (Q2). Added the investigation-report element and QU evaluation of all CGMP data at release; 'cannot be deleted or selectively reported' is a fair synthesis of Q2 and Q13 rather than Q2 wording. Q2 speaks of test results versus specifications; applying it to IPC/production data is a reasonable extension.

source: FDA DI Q&A (Dec 2018); FDA Guidance 'Conducting Remote Regulatory Assessments - Questions and Answers' (final, June 2025)
clause: FDA DI Q&A Q17 (and footnote 14 to Q12); binding basis 211.180(c) (records available for authorized inspection and copying), FD&C Act 704
requirement: Every record required under CGMP is open to FDA inspection, including records created and kept on computerized systems and electronic communications that support CGMP activities (FDA's example: an email authorizing batch release is a CGMP record). Firms must permit authorized inspection and review, and copying of records including electronic data (211.180(c)). Footnote 14: FDA routinely asks for records not intended to meet a CGMP requirement that still contain CGMP information (e.g., shipping records used to reconstruct an activity). Metadata and audit trails are covered because Q1b and Q7 treat them as part of the record.
system_implications: Keep: ability to provide read-only, audited, time-limited viewing access and to generate complete export packages (data, metadata, audit trails) quickly. Add: exports usable as electronic copies (native/structured, not only PDF) so electronic data can be copied; keep release and other GMP approvals inside the eBMR with e-signatures so informal channels are not the approval record, and retain any that are used (DI-NEW-18). Correct: a dedicated inspector account is a design option, not an FDA expectation (firm staff often operate the system; Q5 allows shared read-only viewing, though individual accounts are preferable); SLA targets and remote-assessment support come from other sources.
verification_test: Create an inspector account -> it can view but not change anything and is auto-disabled at expiry. A records-request package for five batches is generated within the SLA and includes audit trails.
notes: Q number supplied (Q17). The DI Q&A does not mention 704(a)(4) record requests, remote regulatory assessments or the 2025 RRA guidance; these cannot be verified from the local files and must be cited to their own sources. Added the duty to allow copying of electronic data and the electronic-communications point.

source: FDA Guidance 'Computer Software Assurance for Production and Quality (Management) System Software' - final Sept 24, 2025; revised final Feb 3, 2026 (aligned to QMSR)
clause: Risk-based assurance framework: intended use; process-risk determination (high vs not high); assurance activities (scripted, unscripted: ad hoc, error-guessing, exploratory; vendor evidence; monitoring); assurance record
requirement: FDA recommends a risk-based approach to establish confidence that automation used in production or the quality system performs as intended. Identify intended use; determine whether a feature is high process risk (failure could compromise product quality/safety) or not; choose proportionate assurance activities (scripted testing for high-risk features; unscripted or exploratory testing, leveraging vendor activities, etc., for lower risk); and keep a record of intended use, risk determination, assurance activities, issues and their disposition, conclusion, date and responsible person. The guidance was issued by CDRH and CBER for medical device production/quality system software. It supersedes Section 6 of 'General Principles of Software Validation'. The Feb 2026 revision aligns it with the QMSR (effective Feb 2, 2026) and reportedly adds explicit consideration of revalidation when software is updated (from a secondary source).
system_implications: For a drug eBMR, CSA is not binding under 21 CFR 211 (it is a CDRH/CBER device guidance), but it is a recognized risk-based model FDA endorses and can support the 211.68 and 11.10(a) validation approach. Classify eBMR features by process risk. High-risk features (scripted testing plus independent review): material status hard stops; weighing and dispense calculations (potency adjustment); dual-verification enforcement; yield and reconciliation calculations and limits; label and variable-data verification; release gate; e-signature controls; audit trail; timers; interfaces that carry GMP data; data integrity and hashing; retention and purge prevention. Not-high-risk features (unscripted/exploratory, with objective evidence): UI layout, non-GMP dashboards, help text. Automate regression suites for multi-site configurations and for every vendor release. Keep the CSA-style assurance record per release.
verification_test: The validation plan contains a risk classification of all URS items. Each high-risk item has scripted test evidence. Each vendor release has a documented assurance record (intended use, risk, activities, issues, conclusion, date, name).

source: FDA Guidance 'Sterile Drug Products Produced by Aseptic Processing - CGMP' (September 2004)
clause: Time limits for aseptic processing phases (Section on time limitations/validation)
requirement: Time limits should be established for each phase of aseptic processing. These include the period between the start of bulk product compounding and its sterilization, filtration processes, product exposure on the processing line, and storage of sterilized equipment, containers and closures. Total filtration time should be limited to an established maximum to prevent microorganisms from penetrating the filter. Time limits should be supported by data, and bioburden and endotoxin load should be assessed when setting them (e.g., for the formulation stage).
system_implications: The injectables MBR must require timers for at least: compounding start -> sterilizing filtration start; total filtration duration; sterilized equipment/components/closures expiry (from end of sterilization to use); product exposure on the line (e.g., fill start -> end, open-vial exposure); and stoppered -> capped. Timer limits reference validation study IDs. A breach auto-creates a deviation (US-211-111) and blocks release until dispositioned.
verification_test: An injectables MBR without the mandatory timer set -> approval blocked. Exceed the filtration time limit -> deviation created and batch flagged.

source: FDA Guidance 'Sterile Drug Products Produced by Aseptic Processing' (Sept 2004)
clause: Section IX.A - Process simulations (media fills): frequency, interventions, acceptance criteria
requirement: Aseptic processes are validated by process simulations. The guidance sets initial qualification with multiple (three) successful runs and semi-annual requalification per line and shift. Simulations should include activities and interventions representative of each shift and shift changeover. Acceptance: when filling fewer than 5,000 units, no contaminated units should be detected, and one contaminated unit is cause for revalidation after investigation. For 5,000-10,000 units, one contaminated unit should result in an investigation including consideration of a repeat media fill, and two are cause for revalidation after investigation. For more than 10,000 units, one contaminated unit should result in an investigation, and two are cause for revalidation after investigation.
system_implications: Support an 'Aseptic Process Simulation' batch type in the injectables edition with its own MBR: media and its growth promotion, units filled, incubation, inspection, contaminated-unit identification. Record every intervention performed, with type, time, operator and count. Keep a line/operator APS qualification status driven by results (US-211-113). Interventions during commercial batches are recorded in the BPR with type, time and personnel, so they can be checked against those qualified in the APS; an intervention type not qualified in the APS is flagged as a deviation.
verification_test: A failed APS (e.g., 2 positives in 12,000 units) -> the line status becomes Not Qualified and commercial filling is blocked. A commercial batch intervention type not in the APS-qualified list -> deviation.

source: FDA Guidance 'Sterile Drug Products Produced by Aseptic Processing' (Sept 2004)
clause: Section IV / Table 1 (air classifications) and Section X.A (environmental monitoring program: alert/action levels, trending, investigations)
requirement: The critical zone should meet ISO 5 (3,520 particles >= 0.5 micron per cubic meter, in operation). The area adjacent to the aseptic line should be at least ISO 7, with ISO 8 for less critical activities. Table 1 gives microbiological action levels. From recollection of the guidance, not re-verified: ISO 5 active air 1 cfu/m3 and settling plates (90 mm, 4 h) 1 cfu; ISO 6 7 and 3; ISO 7 10 and 5; ISO 8 100 and 50. The EM program should include alert/action levels, trending, investigation of excursions, and evaluation of their impact on batches.
system_implications: An EM data model links each sample (location, grade, type, time, operator for personnel samples) to the batch and time window. Limits are configured per grade from site SOPs, which may be stricter (e.g., EU Annex 1 'no growth' in Grade A). An action-level excursion in Grade A/ISO 5 during the batch window auto-creates an event requiring an investigation and batch impact assessment before release. Continuous particle monitoring alarms in the batch window are attached to the batch.
verification_test: Enter an ISO 5 viable result above the action level for a location and time inside the batch window -> an event is created and release is blocked until assessed. Adverse trends generate alerts.

source: FDA Guidance 'Sterile Drug Products Produced by Aseptic Processing' (Sept 2004)
clause: Section XII - Batch Record Review: Process Control Documentation
requirement: The guidance has a dedicated section on batch record review for aseptic processing (confirmed section title). From recollection of the text, not re-verified because the document could not be fetched: before batch release, the QCU review should cover all in-process and laboratory control results together with process-control documentation for the aseptic operation. That documentation includes environmental and personnel monitoring data, interventions and deviations during filling, sterilization and depyrogenation records for equipment, containers and closures, filter integrity results, and adherence to time limits. Discrepancies and excursions should be investigated and their impact on the batch assessed.
system_implications: The injectables release gate (US-211-160-167) includes an 'Aseptic process control review' checklist that is generated automatically from linked data: EM and personnel monitoring results complete and within limits or investigated; interventions reviewed; all sterilization/depyrogenation cycles for items used passed; filter integrity passed; all timers within limits; APS status valid on the fill date; particle monitoring alarms reviewed. QA must acknowledge each section.
verification_test: A batch with one pending EM result -> the aseptic review section is incomplete and release is blocked. All sections complete -> QA can proceed.

source: FDA Guidance 'Sterile Drug Products Produced by Aseptic Processing' (Sept 2004)
clause: Sections on filtration efficacy and sterilization of equipment, containers and closures (integrity testing; qualification/validation of cycles)
requirement: From recollection of the guidance, not re-verified: sterilizing-grade filter integrity testing can be done before processing and should be done routinely after use to detect filter leaks or perforations during processing. Sterilization and depyrogenation cycles for equipment, containers and closures should be validated and each run's physical parameters recorded and reviewed.
system_implications: Integrity tester integration captures test type (bubble point, diffusion/forward flow, pressure hold), limits, result, filter lot and instrument ID. Post-use integrity is mandatory in the MBR for sterilizing filters. Sterilizer/tunnel cycle data (time, temperature, pressure, F0, load pattern ID, validated recipe version) is linked to each load and the items it released. A failed or missing record blocks item use or batch release.
verification_test: Missing post-use integrity result -> release blocked. Cycle data outside validated parameters -> the load's items are blocked.

source: FDA Guidance 'Submission of Documentation in Applications for Parametric Release of Human and Veterinary Drug Products Terminally Sterilized by Moist Heat Processes' (Feb 2010); CPG Sec. 490.200
clause: Parametric release data and monitoring positions; 211.167(a) sterility testing otherwise required
requirement: FDA has accepted parametric release for moist-heat terminally sterilized products since 1985, where approved in the application. Positions in the load should be identified so the load's exposure to the sterilization process is measured and recorded against defined criteria for parametric release, with the location and number of monitors described and justified in the application. A Class 5 chemical indicator is recommended for most applications. Without an approved parametric release, 211.167(a) requires sterility testing of each batch.
system_implications: The product master has a 'release mode' attribute: sterility test or approved parametric release (with the application reference). In parametric mode, the release gate requires: the validated cycle and load pattern used; all critical parameters (time at temperature, temperature, pressure, F0 at each specified monitoring position) within limits from the sterilizer's raw data; chemical indicator results; and pre-sterilization bioburden where required. Any failed parameter means the batch cannot be released parametrically, and sterility-test release is not an allowed substitute unless the application permits it. Terminal sterilization loads are linked to the units, trays and positions they contain.
verification_test: One probe below the F0 minimum -> the parametric release criterion fails and release is blocked. A product without approved parametric release -> the gate requires a sterility result.

source: FDA 'Guide to Inspections of Lyophilization of Parenterals' (July 1993); 21 CFR 211.137(c)
clause: FDA Guide to Inspections of Lyophilization of Parenterals (1993) - not in the uploaded texts; the 211.137(c) citation was verified
requirement: FDA's 1993 investigator guide on lyophilization of parenterals covers the freeze-drying cycle and its controls, cycle validation, and lyophilizer sterilization and design; cycle records are reviewed against the validated/filed cycle (details from recollection, not verified here). The one Part 211 citation, 211.137(c), is confirmed: products reconstituted at dispensing need labeled expiry information for both the reconstituted and the unreconstituted forms.
