system_implications: Integrate the lyophilizer SCADA/historian: recipe ID and version, and per-phase setpoints and actuals (shelf temperature, chamber pressure, condenser temperature, product thermocouple/wireless probe temperatures, pressure-rise or comparative pressure tests, phase durations). Record loading pattern and time, stoppering, and chamber sterilization/leak-test status before loading. Excursions against validated ranges auto-create deviations. Loading/unloading times feed time-limit timers. Store native cycle data as dynamic records (US-DI-08). Anchors in the uploaded Part 211 text for these controls: 211.113(b) (validated sterilization and aseptic processes, covering chamber sterilization), 211.68(a) (routine calibration/checks of the lyophilizer and its sensors), 211.111 (time limits such as loading and unloading), 211.188(b)(5) and (b)(11) (process results and the person checking automated steps). US-DI-08 is not part of this set.
verification_test: Replay a cycle file with a shelf-temperature excursion -> deviation created. A chamber with no valid SIP/leak test -> loading blocked.
notes: Guide is outside the uploaded texts and left as is (reworded only); the 211.137(c) reference was verified and in-text anchors added.

source: FDA draft guidance 'Inspection of Injectable Products for Visible Particulates' (Dec 2021; still draft as of 2026 per search)
clause: 100% visual inspection plus AQL sampling; lifecycle inspection program
requirement: FDA's draft recommends a holistic program in which every unit of an injectable is inspected (100% inspection, manual, semi-automated or automated), followed by statistical sampling (AQL) of accepted units to verify batch quality. Meeting a USP compendial standard alone is generally not sufficient for CGMP. USP <790> frames the 'essentially free' expectation with a sampling plan (AQL 0.65 cited in secondary sources). Defects should be classified, trended and investigated.
system_implications: The inspection step in the BPR records: units presented, units accepted, and rejects by defect category (critical, major, minor; particle type such as fiber, glass or metal; container/closure defects), inspector IDs and qualification status (manual inspection), and machine recipe and challenge-set results (automated). It then records the AQL sample size, acceptance and rejection numbers, and results. The system calculates the reject rate against alert/action limits. AQL failure -> reinspection only if allowed by SOP, with a deviation, and reinspection counts are recorded separately. Units accounted for: filled = accepted + rejected + samples + destroyed, within limits.
verification_test: Enter reject counts above the action limit -> deviation. AQL result exceeding the acceptance number -> batch hold. The unit accountability equation must balance.

source: FDA Guidance 'Process Validation: General Principles and Practices' (January 2011, Revision 1)
clause: Stage 2 (PPQ) and Stage 3 (Continued Process Verification) - data collection and trending
requirement: Stage 3 provides ongoing assurance in routine production that the process stays in a state of control. FDA recommends continued monitoring and sampling of process parameters and quality attributes at the level established during process qualification until enough data exist for significant variability estimates. It recommends that a statistician or person with adequate statistical training develop the data collection plan and analysis methods, that intra-batch and inter-batch variation be evaluated, and that variation be detected through timely assessment of defect complaints, OOS findings, process deviation reports, process yield variations, batch records, incoming raw material records and adverse event reports.
system_implications: The eBMR must capture CPPs and CQAs as structured, typed, time-stamped data with units and limits, not free text or scanned PDFs, so they can be trended: intra-batch (time series within a run, e.g., compression force, fill weights) and inter-batch (across batches and sites). The MBR supports a PPQ mode (enhanced sampling plans, protocol reference) and a routine mode with CPV sampling levels. CPV data exports and SPC charts (control limits, Nelson/Western Electric rules) are available with provenance. Material attributes from incoming lots are linked for multivariate analysis.
verification_test: A PPQ batch executes the enhanced sampling plan and data link to the protocol. A CPV dashboard shows correct control charts, recomputed independently for a sample dataset.

source: FD&C Act sec. 581(14), 582(a)(9), 582(b)(2) (DSCSA); FDA Guidance 'Product Identifiers Under the DSCSA: Questions and Answers' (final, June 2021)
clause: Product identifier definition; data carriers; manufacturer obligation to affix to each package and homogeneous case
requirement: The product identifier is a standardized graphic containing the standardized numerical identifier (NDC plus a unique alphanumeric serial number of up to 20 characters), lot number and expiration date, in both human-readable and machine-readable form. On packages it must be a 2-dimensional data matrix barcode; on homogeneous cases, a linear or 2D data matrix barcode (case carrier rule from the statute's text). Since Nov 27, 2017, manufacturers must affix or imprint a product identifier on each package and homogeneous case of product intended to be introduced in a transaction into commerce. The guidance allows human-readable elements to appear in different locations on the label if space requires.
system_implications: Applies to Rx finished dosage forms (tablets and injectables); OTC is generally outside DSCSA 'product'. The packaging BPR records the serialization order: the NDC/GTIN, the lot and expiry (from the BPR, not typed in), serial number range or list requested/allocated, commissioned, packed, rejected/decommissioned, sampled, and destroyed. Each printed/verified code is graded (ISO/IEC 15415 for 2D) by the line's vision system, and results are stored. Serial reconciliation equation per lot: commissioned = packed into saleable units + decommissioned (rejects, destroyed, samples, damaged), within zero tolerance for unexplained serials. Aggregation (unit -> bundle -> case -> pallet) parent-child records are stored if the company aggregates (US-DSCSA-03). The lot and expiry in the 2D code must equal the BPR values, with an automated consistency check before release.
verification_test: Print an intentionally wrong expiry on a test unit -> the vision system rejects it and the line stops. The serial reconciliation report for the test lot balances with zero unexplained serials. Release is blocked if reconciliation fails or commissioning events are missing.

clause: Transaction information/statement; verification of suspect/illegitimate product; response to verification requests; record retention
requirement: Manufacturers provide transaction information and statements to subsequent owners and keep them for at least 6 years. They must verify product at package level (including the standardized numerical identifier) when they determine product is suspect or when FDA requests it. They must respond to verification requests from authorized trading partners within 24 hours (secondary-source confirmation). Illegitimate product must be quarantined, investigated and notified (Form 3911 to FDA and trading partners within 24 hours per statute), and investigation records are kept at least 6 years. The 24-hour notification and 6-year retention for investigations are partly from statutory text knowledge.
system_implications: The packaging record and serialization repository must support a serial -> lot -> BPR lookup in seconds, to answer verification router requests (e.g., VRS) and to check whether a serial was commissioned, decommissioned or shipped. The retention engine must apply the 6-year DSCSA minimum in addition to 211.180 periods (retention = the longer of the two). Suspect-product investigations link to the lot's batch record and genealogy.
verification_test: Query a random commissioned serial -> the correct lot, expiry and status are returned within the SLA. A decommissioned serial returns 'not verified/decommissioned'. The retention calculation uses max(211.180, 6 years).

source: FD&C Act sec. 582(g)(1) enhanced drug distribution security; FDA Guidances 'Enhanced Drug Distribution Security at the Package Level Under the DSCSA' (final, Aug 2023) and 'DSCSA Standards for the Interoperable Exchange of Information for Tracing' (final, Sept 2023); FDA exemptions
clause: Package-level interoperable electronic tracing; EPCIS; exemptions timeline
requirement: Since Nov 27, 2023 (with a one-year stabilization period to Nov 27, 2024), transaction information must include the product identifier at package level and be exchanged securely, interoperably and electronically. FDA recommends the GS1 EPCIS standard. FDA's exemption for eligible manufacturers and repackagers ended May 27, 2025 (wholesale distributors Aug 27, 2025; dispensers with 26+ FTE Nov 27, 2025; small dispensers exempt to Nov 27, 2026). Manufacturers are therefore fully subject to the enhanced requirements as of Sept 2026. The package-level guidance discusses use of aggregation/inference by trading partners; statute does not explicitly mandate aggregation (interpretation; verify with regulatory counsel).
system_implications: The packaging eBMR (or the linked L3 line serialization system) must produce EPCIS-compatible commissioning, aggregation, decommissioning and shipping events tied to the batch. The parent-child aggregation hierarchy must be accurate: a vision-verified aggregation step, rework/unpack/repack events recorded, and aggregation errors treated as deviations. Batch release should include a serialization/aggregation completeness check so no unreconciled or unaggregated saleable units exist. The genealogy model must represent the aggregation hierarchy as containment edges (see US-GEN-01).
verification_test: Build a pallet, unpack a case, and repack -> the EPCIS event history is correct and the final hierarchy is consistent. Release is blocked if any saleable unit is not aggregated when the product is configured for aggregation.

requirement: The lot number on a drug's label should be capable of yielding the complete manufacturing history of the package. An incorrect lot number may be regarded as causing the article to be misbranded.
system_implications: The printed lot number is sourced only from the BPR lot master: no manual keying on label printers, and the printer receives lot data from the eBMR/L3 over a validated interface. Printed-lot verification is done by vision. Lot numbers resolve to full genealogy (US-210-01). Packaging lots split across multiple packaging orders or sites need explicit sub-lot or packaging-lot linkage so each package lot still yields the complete history.
verification_test: Try to override the lot number at the printer HMI -> not possible, or detected by the vision check against the BPR. A package lot lookup returns full history, including bulk and intermediate lots.

source: 21 CFR 201.25 (bar code label requirements) as revised by FDA final rule 'Revising the National Drug Code Format and Drug Label Barcode Requirements' (published March 5, 2026)
clause: 201.25(c) barcode content and symbology; NDC format (12-digit, 6-4-2) and transition
requirement: Drug products subject to the bar code rule must carry a barcode containing at least the NDC. Before the 2026 rule, only a linear barcode meeting EAN/UCC or HIBCC standards (or another approved standard) was allowed. The March 5, 2026 final rule standardizes all FDA-assigned NDCs to 12 digits (6-digit labeler, 4-digit product, 2-digit package), effective March 7, 2033. It adds a further transition to March 6, 2036 for labeling updates and depletion of old labels, after which drugs with 10-digit NDCs introduced into commerce may face action. It revises 201.25 to allow linear or nonlinear (e.g., 2D Data Matrix) barcodes that meet recognized standards.
system_implications: Product and packaging master data must support both 10-digit (current) and 12-digit NDC formats, the NDC-to-GTIN mapping for each, effective-dated NDC changes per SKU, and label artwork versions tied to NDC format. Label and serialization templates must support linear and 2D carriers and verify the encoded NDC equals the master data. Keep historical lots correct: a lot's recorded NDC must never be rewritten when the master NDC changes (effective-dated, immutable per batch).
verification_test: Change a SKU to a 12-digit NDC effective on a future date -> batches before it keep the old NDC and later batches pick up the new NDC, GTIN and artwork version. Vision verification decodes the NDC from the 2D code and matches master data.

source: 21 CFR Part 4 (CGMP for combination products), as amended to align with the QMSR (amendments effective Feb 2, 2026 per the medical gases rule summary)
clause: 4.4(b) streamlined approach for drug-led combination products (e.g., prefilled syringes, autoinjectors)
requirement: Drug-device combination products manufactured under Part 211 must also meet specified device QS/QMSR provisions (historically 820.20 management responsibility, 820.30 design controls, 820.50 purchasing controls, 820.100 CAPA, 820.170 installation, 820.200 servicing). The exact post-QMSR cross-references were not verified in this pass.
system_implications: The injectables edition must handle prefilled syringes and autoinjectors: device component genealogy (plunger rod, autoinjector subassembly lots), assembly and labeling steps, device functional IPCs (break-loose/glide force, activation) and design-output linkage. MBR change control must reference design control records where applicable. Confirm the current Part 4 wording after the QMSR alignment.
verification_test: A combination product MBR requires device component lots and functional test IPCs, and genealogy includes device subassembly lots.

source: Composite requirement (derived): 21 CFR 210.3 (lot number = complete history), 211.184(c), 211.188(b)(3), 211.130(c), 211.192 (extend investigation to associated batches/products), 211.150/211.196 (distribution for recall), 211.182 (equipment use sequence), 201.18, DSCSA 581/582 (serial -> lot; aggregation)
requirement: Within Part 211, traceability is required as follows. Backward: the lot or control number must allow the batch's manufacturing and control history to be determined (211.130(c)), and the batch record must identify the major equipment, the component and in-process lots used, and the people who performed and checked each significant step (211.188(b)(2), (b)(3), (b)(11); 211.105(b)). Forward: component, container and closure inventory records must identify every product lot that used them (211.184(c)); equipment logs must show each batch processed (211.182); and the distribution of each lot must be readily determinable for recall (211.150(b), 211.196). Investigations must reach other batches and products possibly associated with a failure or discrepancy (211.192). The wording 'complete history including distribution' belongs to the Part 210 lot-number definition (outside the uploaded texts), and serial-number/aggregation traceability comes from DSCSA (outside). Room-level and person-level forward tracing are not explicit requirements; they are useful for 211.192 impact assessments.
system_implications: This answers the user's question on graph-based data structures and databases; the recommendation below is engineering judgment, not regulatory text. Genealogy is inherently a directed, time-stamped multigraph. Nodes: material lots, sublots/containers, batches/steps, equipment units, rooms, persons, sterilizer loads, EM samples, serial numbers, cases, pallets, shipments, consignees, deviations. Edges: consumed-by, produced, split/merge, used-equipment, performed-by, sterilized-in, aggregated-into, shipped-in, relates-to-investigation. Queries are variable-depth (multi-stage API -> granulate -> tablets -> coated -> packaged; rework; blending of several intermediate lots; inter-site transfers), so graph modelling fits naturally. The same regulations also set outcomes that constrain the design, though they do not prescribe technologies: unreleased material must not be used and second-person checks must be enforced (211.84(a), 211.101); audit trails must be secure, computer-generated and time-stamped and must not obscure prior entries (11.10(e)); signatures must be linked so they cannot be excised, copied or transferred by ordinary means (11.70); backups must be exact, complete and secure (211.68(b)); records must stay retrievable and copyable for their retention period, which 211.180 sets at a minimum of 1 year after batch expiry (3 years after distribution for exempt OTC), so any 10+ year horizon is a business or other-regulation assumption; and the system must be validated (11.10(a), 211.68(b)). ACID transactions, append-only ledgers and cryptographic binding are engineering choices that meet these outcomes. Recommended pattern: (1) The system of record is an ACID store (relational, e.g., PostgreSQL, or equivalent) with an append-only, hash-chained event/transaction ledger. Genealogy edges are written in the same transaction as the business event (e.g., a consumption record), so the graph can never disagree with the batch record and there is no dual-write inconsistency. (2) Most genealogy queries run fine as recursive queries (SQL recursive CTEs, or SQL/PGQ property-graph queries where the RDBMS supports them) on indexed edge tables. DSCSA aggregation is shallow (unit -> bundle -> case -> pallet) but high-volume (millions of serials per batch), which relational parent-pointer tables handle well. (3) If scale or latency across many sites needs a dedicated graph database for investigation or recall analytics, make it a derived, read-only, rebuildable projection (CQRS) fed from the ledger via outbox/CDC. Add automated reconciliation (edge counts and hashes per lot) and treat it as GMP-relevant, validated software if its outputs drive GMP decisions such as investigation scope or recall lists. Never make it the sole store of signed records unless it provides equivalent Part 11 audit trail, immutability, point-in-time recovery and long-term export, which most graph databases do not offer natively. (4) Keep genealogy bitemporal (valid time and recording time), so the graph 'as known at release' can be reconstructed after later corrections. (5) Use globally unique IDs with site-scoped business lot numbers to support multi-site graphs, and partition operational data by site with a global genealogy index. 211.180(c) permits central electronic retrieval. (6) The MBR/recipe structure (ISA-88 procedure -> unit procedure -> operation -> phase, with parallel branches) is a DAG that can live as versioned structured documents inside the relational store; it does not require a graph database.
verification_test: (a) Backward and forward trace for seeded complex scenarios (split, merge, rework, inter-site transfer, repack) returns the exact expected node sets. (b) Reconciliation job: the graph projection (if used) equals ledger-derived edges for 100% of lots, and any drift raises an alert. (c) Impact query performance: forward trace from a high-usage excipient lot across 3 years and N sites completes within the SLA. (d) Point-in-time query reproduces the genealogy as of the release timestamp after a later correction. (e) Rebuild the projection from the ledger in a test environment and compare hashes.
notes: Corrected: anchors made precise; the implications claimed the regulations 'require' ACID transactions, cryptographic signature binding and 10+ year retention, which overstates them (these are design choices, and 211.180 sets a shorter minimum). Room/person traceability flagged as good practice. The architecture recommendation itself is engineering judgment and was left intact.

clause: Composite. DI Q&A support: Q1a (ALCOA), Q1b (audit trails are metadata kept for the retention period), Q1c (audit trail definition; data not lost or obscured), Q1e (backup), Q5 (attributable), Q11 (signature securely linked), Q12 (saved at time of performance; no change without a record); binding basis 11.10(e), 11.70, 211.68(b), 211.100(b), 211.180
requirement: The composite is consistent with the DI Q&A and the cited rules: records attributable and contemporaneous (211.100(b); Q1a, Q5, Q12); changes must not obscure earlier entries (11.10(e); Q1c, Q12); audit trails secure, computer-generated, time-stamped and retained at least as long as the records (11.10(e); Q1b); signatures linked so they cannot be removed, copied or moved to falsify a record (11.70; Q11); backups exact, complete and protected from alteration, erasure or loss (211.68(b); Q1e).
system_implications: The append-only/event-sourced store, hash chaining, trusted time source, UTC storage with local rendering, DST tests and DBA-tamper detection are engineering choices not found in the DI Q&A (it says nothing about clocks, time zones or hashing); keep them labelled as design decisions. DBA segregation is supported by Q4 (administrators independent of record content). Correct one risk: blocking data capture on clock drift must come with a controlled contingency (issued contingency forms, Q6; DI-NEW-12) so operators never fall back on scrap-paper notes, which Q12 rejects; log the drift event and the affected entries for review.
verification_test: Daylight-saving transition test: events around the change keep a correct order and correct displayed local times. Simulated NTP failure raises an alarm and stops capture on edge devices past the drift threshold. DBA-level update is detected by hash verification and database activity monitoring.
notes: Corrected: 'inseparably linked' overstated 11.70, which requires protection against excision, copying or transfer by ordinary means; anchors made explicit and guidance vocabulary labelled. | Requirement faithful to the Q&A and cited rules. System implications marked as beyond the guidance, and one conflict corrected: blocking capture without a controlled fallback would work against Q12's contemporaneous-recording expectation.

clause: Ch.4 4.17(a)-(d); the per-product and per-batch-size rule sits in the unnumbered lead-in to the Manufacturing Formula and Processing Instructions section
requirement: For every product and every batch size made, an approved written manufacturing formula and processing instructions must exist. The formula names the product with a product code tied to its specification; gives the dosage form, strength and batch size; lists each starting material and its amount, noting any substance that may be lost during processing; and states the expected final yield with its acceptable range, plus relevant intermediate yields where applicable.
system_implications: Master recipe entity keyed by product code + batch size (or an explicitly approved set of discrete sizes); no ad-hoc scaling at batch creation. Bill of materials with quantity per batch and a 'removed during processing' flag (tablets: granulation water/ethanol; injectables: WFI removed by lyophilisation, process gases such as nitrogen used for blanketing; an overage is not a lost substance - any registered overage is part of the stated quantity and must match the MA). Mandatory expected final yield with acceptable limits; expected yields at configured intermediate stages where applicable (limits on intermediate yields are good practice, not demanded by 4.17(d); significant yield deviations are handled under Ch.5 5.44). Only masters in Approved/Effective status can be instantiated. The per-product and per-batch-size rule covers the processing instructions too, so the processing master is keyed the same way.
verification_test: Try to create a batch for an unapproved batch size -> rejected. Try to approve a master lacking yield limits or spec-linked product code -> rejected. Flagged evaporating ingredient is listed in the BOM but excluded from theoretical output mass used in yield calculation.
notes: No substantive change. Clause refined: the 'each product and batch size' rule is in the lead-in paragraph before 4.17 and also applies to processing instructions. Implications: 'declared overages' removed as an example of a disappearing substance (an overage is part of the stated amount); limits are only demanded for the final yield, so intermediate-yield limits are relabelled good practice.

requirement: Processing instructions must state where processing takes place and the main equipment; give, or refer to, the methods for readying critical equipment (e.g., cleaning, assembly, calibration, sterilisation); require a pre-start check that equipment and workstation hold no earlier products and no documents or materials unneeded for this process, and that equipment is clean and fit for use; set out detailed ordered steps (material checks, pre-treatment, order of addition, critical parameters such as time and temperature); give in-process control instructions with limits; where needed, define bulk storage requirements (container, labelling, special conditions); and list any special precautions.
system_implications: Master step model must carry: room/area and equipment class; equipment-preparation prerequisites evaluated at run time (clean status and clean-hold expiry, calibration due date, assembly check, sterilisation status and sterile-hold expiry for injectables); a mandatory pre-start clearance step confirming removal of previous products, of documents and of materials not needed for this process, and that equipment is clean and fit for use; ordered steps with CPP set-points and ranges; IPC definitions with limits; bulk hold definitions (container type, label, storage condition, maximum hold time); precaution text shown and acknowledged at the step. Tablets: granulation end-point, drying temperature/LOD, compression force/hardness. Injectables: SIP/autoclave cycle, filter integrity, bulk solution hold time. Verifier: 4.18 requires the instructions to contain these elements; run-time enforcement of clean-hold/sterile-hold expiry and calibration due dates, maximum bulk hold times, and blocking masters whose CPPs lack a range go beyond 4.18 (supported by Ch.4 4.31 logbooks, Ch.5 and, for sterile products, Annex 1) - keep as design choices. Only the equipment-preparation methods may be incorporated by reference (4.18(b)).
verification_test: Master approval blocked if a CPP has no range or an IPC has no limit. At execution, selecting equipment whose clean or sterile status has expired, or whose calibration is overdue, blocks the step. Bulk hold exceeding maximum time raises an exception.
notes: No substantive change; paraphrase tightened: the clearance check also covers documents and materials not needed for the planned process (not only leftovers), and 'by reference' is allowed only for equipment-preparation methods (4.18(b)). Implications: run-time controls labelled as beyond the clause; clearance scope added.

requirement: Approved packaging instructions must exist for each product, pack size and pack type, containing or referencing: product name with bulk and finished batch numbers; dosage form, and strength where applicable; pack content by number, weight or volume; a complete packaging-material list with quantities, sizes, types and specification codes; where appropriate, specimens of printed materials showing where batch number and shelf-life are to be applied; line-clearance checks and a careful pre-start examination of area and equipment, plus other special precautions; a description of the packaging operation including significant ancillary operations and equipment; and in-process controls with sampling instructions and acceptance limits.
system_implications: Packaging master keyed by product + pack size + pack type, versioned and approved separately from the processing master. Component BOM with item codes linked to approved specifications and artwork versions; artwork specimen image stored with coding/expiry print zones; mandatory line-clearance checklist template; operation steps with equipment classes; IPC plans with sample size, frequency and limits. Batch record must hold both the bulk batch number consumed and the finished-goods batch number. Tablets: blister/bottle counts, desiccant, leaflet. Injectables: vial/ampoule labels, cartons. Safety features (unique identifier and anti-tampering device) apply to most prescription medicines - tablets and injectables alike - under Directive 2011/62/EU and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/161; they are not a Ch.4 requirement but belong in the packaging master where the product is in scope. Verifier: printed-material specimens are required only 'where appropriate' (4.19(e)), so allow a justified 'not applicable' rather than a hard block for every printed component.
verification_test: Approving a packaging master where a printed component has no linked artwork specimen or no coding zone is blocked. Starting a packaging order is blocked until the clearance checklist is complete. Packaging record shows bulk lot and finished lot linkage.
notes: No substantive change. Implications: serialisation/anti-tampering stem from the Falsified Medicines Directive and Delegated Reg. 2016/161 (both tablets and injectables if prescription-only), not Ch.4; printed specimens are 'where appropriate'.

requirement: A batch processing record must be kept for every batch processed, derived from the applicable sections of the formula and processing instructions currently approved. It captures: product name and batch number; start, key intermediate stage and completion dates and times; who carried out each significant step and, where appropriate, who checked it; for each starting material its batch and/or QC control number and the quantity actually weighed, plus the lot and quantity of any recovered or reprocessed material that was added; relevant processing operations or events and the main equipment used; in-process control results with the identity of whoever performed them; yields at relevant stages; notes on special problems with signed authorisation of any departure from the formula or instructions; and approval by the person responsible for processing.
system_implications: Batch record instance is generated only from the effective master version and stamps that version ID. Automatic server-time stamps at step start/stop and stage milestones. Per-step performer e-signature plus configurable second-person verification. Material consumption captured by lot scan and balance integration (actual weight, not keyed-in theoretical), with a distinct flag and source-batch reference for recovered/reprocessed material. Equipment ID captured per step. IPC results entered against limits with performer ID. Stage and final yields auto-calculated. Deviations linked to the step with authorised signature. Final 'production approval' signature role gates hand-over to QA/QP review. Verifier: also record the QC/analytical control number where that, rather than a batch number, identifies the material (4.20(d)). Scale/scanner capture is a design choice - Annex 11 §6 equally accepts a second-person check of manually entered critical data. Blocking production approval while steps are open or deviations unsigned is good practice beyond 4.20. Deviation authorisation should follow Ch.5 5.15 (competent person, QC involved where appropriate).
verification_test: Execute a test batch; confirm master version is recorded, every significant step shows performer and time, weighed lots and actual quantities are present, yields computed, and that production approval cannot be applied while any step is incomplete or any deviation unsigned.
notes: No substantive change; paraphrase reworded. Implications: beyond-clause controls labelled; analytical control number added.

requirement: Where a process has been validated and is subject to continuous monitoring and control, the batch reports the system generates automatically can be cut down to compliance summaries plus exception and out-of-specification reports.
system_implications: Support review-by-exception: a per-batch compliance summary and an exception report listing every out-of-range value, alarm, override, manual entry, correction, deviation and audit-trail change. Only steps configured (under change control, referencing the validation) as validated and continuously monitored may use summary-only reporting; full underlying data is still captured, retained and viewable on drill-down. Verifier: the Note is a permission (reports may be limited), not an obligation, and it does not relax 4.20 content for manually executed steps. Retaining the full underlying data is not stated in the Note itself; it follows from the raw-data definition in the Ch.4 preamble (see EUA-NEW-01) and 4.10/4.12. Listing manual entries, corrections and audit-trail events in the exception report goes beyond the Note (good practice, consistent with 4.27 and Annex 11 §8.2/§9).
verification_test: Run a batch with one injected out-of-limit reading and one manual correction; both must appear in the exception report; data for in-range steps is available on drill-down; attempt to enable summary-only reporting on a step without a validation reference is refused.
notes: No change to the requirement. Implications: clarified that raw-data retention comes from the Ch.4 preamble, and that the Note is optional and limited to validated, continuously monitored processes.

requirement: Every batch or part-batch that is packed needs its own batch packaging record, derived from the applicable parts of the packaging instructions. It holds: product name and batch number; dates and times of packaging; who performed each significant step and, where appropriate, who checked it; identity and conformity checks against the instructions, including in-process results; details of the operations with references to the equipment and lines used; where possible, samples of the printed components actually used, with specimens of the batch code, expiry date and any extra overprint; notes on special problems or unusual events with signed authorisation of departures from the instructions; the amounts and identity of every printed component and of the bulk that were issued, consumed, destroyed or sent back to stock, and the amount of finished product obtained, enough for reconciliation; and approval by the person responsible for packaging.
system_implications: Packaging record supports part-batch (sub-lot) records linked to one bulk lot. Captures line ID and equipment IDs, IPC results, and an attached specimen of printed material (scanned sample or vision-system image of the actual coded item). Reconciliation table per printed component and bulk: issued, used, destroyed, returned, plus finished units, samples and rejects. Final approval signature by packaging-responsible role. Verifier: an image is an interpretation of 'samples'; the literal expectation is a physical specimen whenever possible, which an eBMR can keep as a controlled physical attachment cross-referenced to the electronic record (hybrid control per 4.1) - support both. Investigating reconciliation discrepancies before release comes from Ch.5 5.61, not 4.21.
verification_test: Complete a packaging run; record contains line ID, IPCs, a specimen image of a coded label/carton, full reconciliation table, and approval; approval is blocked while reconciliation fields are empty (unless the documented electronic-control exemption in EU4-07 is active).
notes: No substantive change; paraphrase reworded. Implications: clarified physical versus image specimens and where discrepancy investigation comes from.

requirement: The reconciliation data described in 4.21(h) - identity and quantities of printed materials and bulk issued, used, destroyed or returned, and the product quantity obtained - may be left out of the packaging record only where robust electronic controls operate during packaging and the omission is justified.
system_implications: Reconciliation is ON by default for every packaging master. Turning it off for a component requires a controlled configuration change that names the electronic control relied on (e.g. 100% code/vision verification with verified reject, roll-fed labels with splice detection, serialization aggregation), references its validation, and is approved by QA. The record then shows the justification reference instead of counts. Serialized injectable/tablet packs: reconcile commissioned vs. decommissioned vs. shipped serial numbers as the electronic equivalent. Verifier: the serial-number reconciliation 'equivalent' is an interpretation (serialisation derives from Delegated Regulation (EU) 2016/161), not something Ch.4 states. The exemption only changes what must appear in the record: significant discrepancies must still be investigated before release (Ch.5 5.61) and unused batch-coded materials destroyed with a record (Ch.5 5.62).
verification_test: Attempt to disable reconciliation without a QA-approved justification record -> blocked. With an approved justification, packaging record displays the justification ID; audit trail records who enabled it and when.
notes: No change to the requirement. Implications: serialisation equivalence labelled as interpretation; added the Ch.5 limits on what the exemption relaxes.

requirement: Documentation may be paper, electronic or photographic and the same rules apply to every medium; the document types and media used must be defined in the QMS and followed. Complex systems must be understood, well documented, validated and adequately controlled. For hybrid and single-medium systems alike, the relationships and controls between masters, official copies, data processing and resulting records must be stated; electronic templates, forms and masters need appropriate controls; and record integrity must be assured for the whole retention period.
system_implications: eBMR must declare, per record type, which is the official (master) record: electronic record, printout, or combination. Hybrid points (e.g. printed labels, paper chart recorder output, instrument printouts, paper deviation forms) must be formally mapped with a documented linkage (scan attached as true copy, ID cross-reference). Templates/forms in the system are version-controlled, approved and locked. System is validated (Annex 11) and its configuration controlled. Verifier: 'true copy' is EMA data-integrity Q&A / PIC/S PI 041 terminology rather than Ch.4 wording; fine as a design means.
verification_test: Documentation review: a record-type register exists showing official medium per record type. Test that editing a released template is impossible without a new version and approval. Test that a paper attachment carries a unique ID, is linked to the batch and step, and is reviewed as part of the record.
notes: No change.

requirement: Documents must be carefully designed, drafted, reviewed and issued, and must agree, as appropriate, with the relevant parts of the Product Specification File (investigational products) and of the manufacturing and marketing authorisation dossiers. Making working copies from masters must not be able to introduce errors. Instruction documents must be approved, signed and dated by suitably authorised people and have a defined effective date; every document must have unambiguous content and be uniquely identifiable. Instruction documents should be orderly and easy to check, with style and language suited to their use; SOPs, work instructions and methods specifically must use an imperative, mandatory style.
system_implications: Batch record instances are generated programmatically from the approved master (no copy/retype). Master recipe workflow: author -> reviewer(s) -> approver with e-signatures, unique document ID + version, and an effective-from date after which it becomes executable. Mandatory regulatory cross-reference on each master (MA dossier section / variation number; PSF reference for investigational products) confirmed at approval - 4.2 expects compliance with the dossiers, so this should not be optional. Instructions rendered as numbered imperative steps. Verifier: unique identification applies to every controlled document and template, not only instructions (4.3). The imperative-style rule targets SOPs, work instructions and methods (4.4); step text should in any case be orderly and easy to check.
verification_test: Confirm the batch record content equals the master content (hash/field comparison) for a generated batch. A master with approval but future effective date cannot be instantiated before that date. Unapproved draft cannot be instantiated.
notes: MINOR correction: the paraphrase omitted the manufacturing authorisation dossier, limited 'unambiguous / uniquely identifiable' to instruction documents (4.3 applies it to all documents), and extended the imperative-style rule to all instructions (4.4 limits it to SOPs, work instructions and methods). Implications: the MA cross-check should be mandatory, not optional.

clause: Ch.4 4.5 (periodic review only); superseded-version control rests on 4.3 (effective date) and 4.20/4.21 (records based on currently approved instructions)
requirement: Documents in the quality management system must be reviewed regularly and kept current (4.5). Superseded instructions must not be usable for new batches; in the 2011 text this follows from 4.3 (a defined effective date) and 4.20/4.21 (records based on the currently approved instructions), not from 4.5.
system_implications: Masters carry a periodic review due date with alerts; upon approval of a new version the prior version is automatically retired for new batches. Defined rule for batches in progress when a master changes (continue on old version with justification or migrate under change control) and the record shows which version governed each step. Printed forms or labels from superseded versions are invalidated (version/ID printed on every output). Verifier: keep superseded-version blocking - it is required by 4.3 (defined effective date), 4.20/4.21 (records based on the currently approved instructions) and Annex 11 §10, even though the 2011 wording of 4.5 does not mention it.
verification_test: Approve v2 of a master; attempt to start a new batch on v1 -> blocked. Check in-flight batch behaviour follows the configured rule and is audit-trailed. Overdue periodic review is flagged on a dashboard.
notes: MODERATE (source) correction: the 'prevent inadvertent use of superseded documents' sentence is not in the 2011 text of 4.5; it matches the pre-2011 Chapter 4 wording. The eBMR should still implement it because 4.3, 4.20/4.21 and Annex 11 §10 lead to the same outcome. Implications unchanged.

requirement: Controlled documents should not be handwritten, but documents that call for data entry must leave enough room for the entries; any handwritten entry must be clear, legible and indelible.
system_implications: Every data point in the master has a defined, typed entry field (unit, precision, allowed range or list) so free-text is the exception. Where paper remains (hybrid printouts, emergency paper fallback forms), the printed form is generated from the approved master with enough space for each entry, carries a unique form ID, and is later reconciled into the electronic record. No handwritten master instructions. Verifier: typed fields are the electronic analogue of 'sufficient space' (design). Counting issued fallback forms and reconciling their return is data-integrity good practice (EMA GMP Q&A on data integrity; PIC/S PI 041), not stated in 4.6/4.7 - keep.
verification_test: Master editor refuses a data-entry step without a field definition. Printed fallback form shows batch ID, form ID/page x of y and dedicated fields for every entry; issued fallback forms are counted and all returned forms reconciled.
notes: No change.

requirement: Records must be made or completed as each action is taken, and in a manner that keeps every significant manufacturing activity traceable.
system_implications: Timestamps come from a synchronised server clock, never from a user-editable field. Steps are signed at completion; late entries are allowed only via a 'late entry' path that records actual time of activity, time of entry and a mandatory reason, and are flagged for review. Batch-level genealogy links materials, equipment, rooms, people and steps. Verifier: server-clock time stamps and the late-entry path are design means (supported by Annex 11 §12.4); 4.8 itself sets the contemporaneous-recording and traceability outcome.
verification_test: Attempt to backdate a timestamp -> not possible. Enter a step 2 h after its planned window via late-entry path: record shows both times, reason and a review flag that appears in the exception report.
notes: No change.

clause: Ch.4 4.9 (mandatory reason for GMP-relevant electronic data comes from Annex 11 §9)
requirement: Any alteration to an entry must be signed and dated and must leave the original information readable; where appropriate the reason must also be recorded.
system_implications: Corrections never overwrite: the system keeps original value, new value, who, when (server time) and a mandatory reason (pick-list plus free text) in a secure audit trail. Corrections to GMP-relevant data after step sign-off require re-signature and, for critical data (weights, IPC results, CPPs, yields), a second-person or QA approval. Correction history is shown inline in the batch record view and in the exception report. Verifier: 4.9 asks for a reason only 'where appropriate'; making it mandatory for GMP-relevant electronic data is justified by Annex 11 §9. Second-person/QA approval of corrections to critical data is good practice beyond both texts.
verification_test: Correct a weighed quantity after signing: original remains visible, reason required, correction appears in the audit trail and exception report, and step is re-signed. Attempt a correction without reason -> blocked. Direct DB update is detectable (audit trail/hash check).
notes: No change to the requirement.

requirement: It must be clearly defined which record belongs to each manufacturing activity and where that record is kept, and secure controls - validated where appropriate - must protect record integrity for the entire retention period.
system_implications: Record-type register inside the system (or linked SOP) mapping each activity to its record and storage location (eBMR DB, archive, attached external systems such as SCADA/historian, LIMS, weighing). Integrity controls: role-based write access, audit trail, backup/restore tested, checksums on archived records, readable-format migration plan. Archive/export produces complete human-readable batch record with metadata and audit trail. Verifier: the listed integrity controls are design means that also serve Annex 11 §7.1, §4.8 and §17.
verification_test: Restore a batch record from backup/archive and compare against checksum; record opens with all data, signatures and audit trail intact. Register lists location of every record type referenced by the master.
notes: No change.

requirement: Batch documentation must be kept for one year after the batch expires or at least five years after QP certification of the batch, whichever is longer. For investigational medicinal products it must be kept at least five years after the last clinical trial using the batch is completed or formally discontinued. Legislation for particular product types (e.g., ATMPs) may require longer periods for some documents.
system_implications: Retention engine computes a retention-until date per batch = max(expiry + 1 year, QP certification date + 5 years), stored with the record and recomputed if expiry is extended/changed; IMP batches use a separate rule tied to trial end dates entered by QA; configurable overrides for longer national or product-type rules. Purge/delete of batch records is impossible before that date and requires QA-approved, audit-trailed disposition afterwards. Retention applies to the full record including audit trails, attachments and linked data (e.g. historian extracts). Verifier (gap): 4.11 is keyed to expiry and QP certification, so define a QA rule for batches never certified (rejected, destroyed or abandoned) and identify validation or stability batches whose records also fall under 4.12.
verification_test: Batch with 24-month shelf life certified 2026-01-10: retention date = 2031-01-10 (5 y after certification exceeds expiry+1 y). Batch with 60-month shelf life: expiry + 1 y governs. Attempt deletion before retention date -> refused and logged.
notes: No change to the requirement. Implications: added handling for batches that are never certified (not addressed by 4.11).

requirement: Retention of other documentation depends on the business activity it supports. Critical documentation, including raw data (e.g., validation or stability) that supports information in the marketing authorisation, must be kept while the authorisation remains in force. Some of it may be retired once superseded by a complete new data set, with a documented justification that respects batch-record retention; for example, process validation raw data must be kept for no less time than the records of all batches whose release relied on that validation.
system_implications: Masters, master versions, recipe change history, and any validation-linked configuration (e.g. the validated state that justifies review-by-exception) are retained at least as long as any batch record that relied on them. Link each batch to the master version and validation references so retention of those objects is automatically extended while dependent batches are retained. Verifier: keeping master versions as long as dependent batch records is an inference from 4.10/4.12 (a batch record cannot be interpreted without its governing instructions) - sound design, not an explicit rule. Also mark batch records that are critical documentation supporting the MA (e.g., process validation or stability batches) so they are kept while the MA is in force.
verification_test: Attempt to archive-delete a master version still referenced by a batch within retention -> blocked with a dependency message.
notes: No change to the requirement.

requirement: Written release and rejection procedures must exist for materials and products, in particular for QP certification of finished product for sale. The QP must have access to every record, and a system must be in place to highlight special observations and any change to critical data.
system_implications: QP/QA review workspace that exposes the complete batch record plus linked deviations, change controls, lab results and audit trails. Automatic flags for special observations (comments, events, deviations) and for any post-entry change to data classified as critical, so the reviewer sees them without searching. Release status workflow: quarantine -> production approved -> QA reviewed -> QP certified / rejected, each with e-signature. Verifier: only the QP certification step must be an e-signature (Annex 11 §15); e-signing the other workflow states, and blocking certification until each flag is acknowledged, are good practice. Rejection must be supported for materials and intermediates as well as finished batches.
verification_test: Change a critical data point after completion and add an operator comment: both surface as flags in the QP review screen; QP certification is blocked until each flag is acknowledged.
notes: No change.

requirement: Major or critical production and analytical equipment, and rooms where product is processed, need logbooks that record in time order, as appropriate, each use of the area or equipment/method and any calibration, maintenance, cleaning or repair, with dates and the identity of the people who did it.
system_implications: Electronic equipment and room logbooks that are automatically populated from batch execution (usage start/stop with batch and product ID, cleaning events) and from maintenance/calibration modules; entries are chronological and immutable (corrections per EU4-13). Batch step checks equipment/room status from the logbook (last product, clean status, calibration due). Injectables: also autoclave/SIP cycles, filter integrity tests, isolator/RABS decontamination. Tablets: compression machine tooling (punch/die sets) usage. Verifier: filter integrity results belong in the batch record (4.20(f)) rather than the logbook; logbook-driven status checks at batch steps go beyond 4.31 but support 4.18(c) and 4.20(e). 4.31 also covers major/critical analytical equipment, usually handled in LIMS rather than the eBMR.
verification_test: Run two batches on the same granulator/filling line; logbook shows both usages and the intervening cleaning in chronological order with performer IDs; attempt to insert a back-dated logbook entry without the late-entry path fails.
notes: No change.

requirement: (Draft, not yet binding) Firms must run a data governance system inside the PQS that manages integrity of all GMP data in any format across its whole lifecycle, with controls scaled to risk and supported by suitable expertise and defined ownership.
system_implications: eBMR ships with a data-governance configuration layer: data inventory of every record type and field with an assigned data owner/system owner; documented data flows to/from integrated systems (scales, MES/SCADA, historian, LIMS, ERP, serialization); role model with segregation of duties; periodic data-integrity review reports (user access, audit-trail review status, failed log-ins, configuration changes).
verification_test: Export the data inventory and verify every master field has an owner and criticality; generate the periodic DI review report for a test period and confirm it lists access changes, config changes and open audit-trail reviews.

requirement: (Draft) Controls must cover each lifecycle stage: creation/recording; processing of raw data into reported (derived) data such that the processing can be reconstructed; review/verification; decisions based on the data; retention, archiving and retrieval; and controlled retirement or destruction.
system_implications: Store raw captured values (e.g. individual balance readings, each IPC tablet weight, each fill-weight check, sensor readings) alongside derived results (means, RSD, yields, reconciliation %) together with the formula/version used, so any derived number can be recalculated. Review step status per record. Archive and retrieve functions with readability checks. End-of-retention destruction only via QA-approved workflow with a destruction certificate.
verification_test: For a completed batch, recompute yield and IPC averages from stored raw values and compare with the reported derived values; change of a formula version is traceable to the batches it affected; destruction without approval is blocked.

requirement: (Draft) Controls are to be based on two assessments: how critical the data is (its influence on decisions and product quality) and how exposed it is (opportunity for change or deletion and the likelihood that this would be detected).
system_implications: Each master data field carries a criticality attribute (e.g. critical / major / minor) and each capture method a risk attribute (automatic interface vs. manual entry vs. transcription from paper). Rules engine derives controls from the pair: second-person verification, mandatory reason codes, correction approval level, audit-trail review sampling, exception-report inclusion. Manual entry of critical data is flagged and, where an interface exists, disallowed by default.
verification_test: Configure a critical field captured manually: system enforces witness verification and puts every entry in the exception report; the same field captured via validated interface does not require witnessing but every manual override is flagged.

requirement: (Draft) All GMP records, paper or electronic, are expected to meet the extended data integrity attributes: attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original, accurate, complete, consistent, enduring, available and traceable.
system_implications: Map each attribute to a feature: attributable = unique user IDs, no shared accounts, device/instrument ID on captured data; legible = human-readable rendering of every record incl. audit trail; contemporaneous = server time stamps and late-entry flag; original = first-capture value retained, interfaces store source files; accurate = validated calculations, range checks; complete = batch cannot close with open steps, all repeats/aborted attempts kept; consistent = sequence enforcement and time-order checks; enduring/available = archive and retrieval across retention; traceable = end-to-end audit trail and genealogy.
verification_test: Trace matrix from each ALCOA++ attribute to at least one validated test case; e.g. a repeated IPC measurement keeps both values (complete) and shows who/when (attributable/contemporaneous).

clause: draft metadata/audit trail provisions and glossary
requirement: (Draft) Records include the metadata and audit trail needed to reconstruct their history (who did what, when and why), whatever the medium; raw data (first capture) is defined and must be kept together with the derived data and the steps that produced it.
system_implications: Audit trail is always on, cannot be disabled or edited by any role, and records create/modify/delete/sign events with user, server time, old value, new value and reason. Metadata (units, instrument ID, method/formula version, recipe version, time zone) stored with each value and exported with the record. Audit-trail review of GMP-critical entries is a defined step in batch record review before release, with reviewer signature.
verification_test: Attempt to deactivate audit trail as admin -> impossible. Modify a critical value and confirm full audit entry. QA review cannot be completed while the audit-trail review task for the batch is open.

requirement: (Draft) Hybrid paper/electronic arrangements are acknowledged but must be clearly defined, with the interfaces and data flows between formats validated and risk-controlled; commentators report that printing electronic records to sign them by hand, and parallel paper-plus-electronic signatures, are treated as higher risk and to be avoided where possible.
system_implications: Design for fully electronic execution and signature; no built-in 'print to sign' path for GMP steps. Where paper is unavoidable (e.g. supplier CoA, thermal printouts, downtime forms), the system defines which is the original, captures a verified scan with metadata, links it to the step, and requires reconciliation of issued vs. returned paper forms. Business-continuity (downtime) procedure with controlled paper forms generated from the master and later data re-entry with second-person check.
verification_test: Search configuration for any step whose signature is paper-only -> none. Simulate downtime: printed forms bear unique IDs, are reconciled, and re-entered data are flagged as transcribed and verified.

clause: draft section on signatures in GMP documentation
requirement: (Draft) The purpose and control of signatures are spelled out: each signature must make clear who signed and what the signature means (e.g. performed, checked, reviewed, approved); a company signature policy is expected; electronic signatures are fully recognised but must be binding, traceable and stay permanently linked to the signed record for its lifetime.
system_implications: Signature manifestation on screen and in every rendered/exported record: full printed name, user ID, date-time with time zone, and signature meaning chosen from a controlled list configured per step. Signing requires re-authentication (e.g. ID + password or equivalent) at each signing event. Signature is cryptographically or logically bound to the exact record content/version; any later change invalidates or requires re-signing. Signature policy configured in system: which roles may sign which meanings, and a rule that performer and verifier must be different users.
verification_test: Sign a step: rendered record shows name, date-time, meaning. Attempt verifier signature with the same user as performer -> refused. Edit data after signing -> signature marked invalid / re-sign required. Copy/paste of a signature to another record is impossible.

clause: draft retention/copies provisions and glossary (true, certified, verified copy)
requirement: (Draft) Where the storage medium will not last for the retention period, verified true copies must be made; copies used in place of originals must preserve content and meaning (including metadata) and the verification must be documented; backup, restore and archiving must keep records readable and accessible for the full retention time.
system_implications: True-copy function: scans/exports carry source ID, checksum, capture metadata and a verifier e-signature confirming completeness and legibility; for electronic-to-electronic copies, include audit trail and metadata. Typical eBMR uses: thermal balance/pH/checkweigher printouts (fade), paper chart recorder output (e.g. autoclave/lyophiliser charts for injectables), label specimens. Archive format and migration plan preserve readability; periodic restore tests.
verification_test: Scan a thermal printout via the true-copy function: result carries checksum, verifier signature and link to step; alteration of the file breaks checksum validation. Annual restore test of an archived batch record opens with metadata and audit trail.

requirement: Yield checks and quantity reconciliations are to be performed as needed to show there are no discrepancies beyond acceptable limits; any significant departure from the expected yield must be recorded and investigated.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: the master defines yield/reconciliation checkpoints wherever the process needs them (5.8 says 'as necessary'), each with a theoretical basis, formula and acceptable limits; the system calculates the result from captured quantities (inputs, outputs, samples, rejects, waste, residues) and records it; a result outside the limit (i.e. a significant yield deviation) is recorded and investigated through a linked deviation. DESIGN CHOICES (not mandated by 5.8/5.44): separate alert and action limits; a hard block on moving to the next step until the deviation is opened/approved; holding batch disposition until the investigation closes (the release hold reflects Annex 16 certification expectations, not Ch.5). Examples - tablets: granule yield after drying/milling, tablet count vs theoretical, coating weight gain; injectables: compounded volume vs theoretical, filled units, lyophilised vials, visual-inspection rejects.
verification_test: Enter quantities that produce a yield below the action limit: system forces deviation creation before the next step and flags the batch; a yield inside limits proceeds without deviation. Recalculation from raw quantities matches the displayed yield.
notes: Clause numbers and paraphrase are correct. Implications re-labelled: Ch.5 only requires checks where necessary, a record, and investigation of significant yield deviations; blocking progression and holding disposition are design choices (the release hold is Annex 16-derived).

requirement: Before a processing operation starts, it must be confirmed that the area and equipment are clean and hold no materials, products, residues or paperwork unrelated to the operation about to begin.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: a clearance step before each processing operation starts; the system verifies electronically what it can (previous batch closed out in the room/equipment log, equipment status 'clean', no materials of other orders allocated to the room) and captures signed confirmation of the physical checks (no foreign materials, products, residues or documents). DESIGN CHOICES beyond 5.40: a formal checklist for processing clearance (Ch.5 mandates a checklist only for packaging line clearance, 5.50); an independent second-person verifier signature; repeating clearance after interruptions; clean-hold-time expiry checks (clean hold times come from cleaning validation under Annex 15, not from 5.40).
verification_test: Attempt to start granulation/compounding while the room logbook shows the prior batch not cleared or equipment clean-hold expired -> blocked. After signed clearance (and verifier signature if configured), the step unlocks and both signatures appear in the batch record.
notes: Clause and paraphrase correct. The original implication/test implied a checklist and two signatures; 5.40 requires neither, so both are marked as design choices, as is the clean-hold-time check (Annex 15).

requirement: Different products may only be handled in the same room at the same time, or back-to-back, if this has been shown to create no risk of mix-up or cross-contamination.
system_implications: Room/area occupancy control: the system tracks which batch/product occupies each room and refuses to start a second product in an occupied room unless the room is configured as segregated for concurrent work with a documented risk-assessment reference (the basis for 'no risk' should come from the 5.20 QRM). Consecutive use by a different product requires completed cleaning and clearance before the room returns to 'available'. DESIGN CHOICE: requiring QA approval of the concurrent-use configuration.
verification_test: Start batch A (product X) in room R; attempt to start batch B (product Y) in room R -> blocked with message. After batch A closes and cleaning + clearance are recorded, batch B can start.
notes: Clause and paraphrase correct ('shown' is an interpretive but reasonable reading: absence of risk needs a documented basis). Implications are within scope; only the QA-approval step is flagged as a design choice.

requirement: During processing, every material, bulk container, major equipment item and, where appropriate, room must carry a label or other identification showing the product or material, strength where relevant, batch number and, where applicable, the production stage. Labels must be unambiguous, easy to read and follow the company's standard layout; colours signalling status (such as quarantine, approved, rejected or cleaned) are an optional extra aid.
system_implications: REQUIRED minimum (5.12): product/material, strength where applicable, batch number, stage where applicable; identification may be a physical label OR another means such as an electronic status display, because 5.12 allows items to be 'otherwise identified'. 5.13: label templates are the company's agreed format (keep them under change control), clear and unambiguous; colour coding of status is optional ('often helpful'). DESIGN CHOICES: system-generated labels from batch data with a barcode/2D code; extra fields (container n of N, gross/tare/net, status, date/time, user); room/equipment status displays ('In use - product/batch/stage', 'Cleaned', 'To be cleaned'); scan-based identity checks at each step; forced relabel/reprint on status change with audit trail.
verification_test: Weigh a material into a container: label shows all required fields and a scannable code. Scan a container labelled for a different batch or stage at the next step -> rejected. Equipment status screen changes from 'In use' to 'To be cleaned' at batch end.
notes: Minor correction. Clause numbers correct (5.13 verified as the label-format/colour clause). Wording changed from 'recommended' to 'optional': the text only says colour coding is often helpful. Implications re-labelled: barcodes, scanning and extra label fields are design choices, and non-label identification is permitted by 5.12.

requirement: Deviating from instructions or procedures is to be kept to a minimum; when a deviation does happen, a competent person must give written approval, with Quality Control involved when relevant.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: recipe enforcement keeps departures to a minimum (sequence, limits, material identity); any departure (parameter outside range, skipped step, alternative equipment) is possible only through an in-line deviation record (description, impact) approved by the e-signature of a person designated as competent for that deviation class - an Annex 11/Ch.4-compliant e-signature satisfies 'approved in writing'; QC involvement is routed for deviation classes configured as quality-relevant. The deviation ID is linked to the step and appears in the batch record. DESIGN CHOICES beyond 5.15: routing to QA (the text names QC); forbidding operator self-approval (segregation of duties); blocking batch release while linked deviations are open (that hold follows Annex 16 certification prerequisites, not 5.15).
verification_test: Try to skip a mandatory step -> blocked unless a deviation is raised and approved by an authorised role. Operator cannot self-approve. Release blocked with an open deviation.
notes: Clause and paraphrase correct. Implications re-labelled: 5.15 only requires written approval by a competent person with QC involvement when appropriate; no-self-approval and the release block are design choices / Annex 16-derived.

requirement: Dispensing of starting materials is restricted to designated staff working to a written procedure, so that the right material in the right quantity ends up in clean, correctly labelled containers. An independent second check of each dispensed item and its quantity is required and must be documented. Everything dispensed for one batch is kept as a group and visibly labelled as belonging to that batch.
system_implications: Dispensing module: only users designated as dispensers (designation evidenced e.g. by role plus current training - the training interlock is a design choice) can dispense, following the procedure embedded in the step; material lot scanned and checked against the BOM, released status and retest/expiry (these status checks implement 5.34); weight/volume captured from a balance/meter with tolerance check against target (balance calibration/checks come from Ch.3, not Ch.5); container label printed automatically. The independent check (5.38) is recorded either as a second-person e-signature by a different user or as a validated automated check (barcode + balance interface) - 5.38 requires independence and a record but does not specify a second person. Dispensed items grouped into a batch kit with a conspicuous kit label and a completeness check before issue. Product-specific: WFI, pH adjusters and filter/stopper components (injectables); potency-adjusted API with compensating excipient (tablets).
verification_test: Log in without dispenser qualification -> refused. Scan wrong lot or a quarantined/expired lot -> refused. Weight outside tolerance cannot be confirmed. Verifier cannot be the dispenser. Kit cannot be issued with a missing component.
notes: Clauses and paraphrase correct. Implications re-labelled: training interlock, daily balance checks and potency adjustment are design/other-source items; a validated system check is a defensible alternative to a second person because the text does not mandate one.

requirement: Contamination of a starting material or product by another material or product must be prevented. The risk of accidental cross-contamination (airborne release such as dust or vapour, biological material, residues left on equipment, operators' clothing) must be assessed, bearing in mind that injectables and long-term therapies are the most sensitive although all products are at risk. Control relies on premises/equipment design (Ch.3) supported by process design and technical/organisational measures, including effective and reproducible cleaning. A QRM process that includes a potency and toxicological evaluation of the products (and considers facility/equipment design, personnel and material flows, microbiological controls, API properties, process, cleaning and analytical capability) decides whether and how far premises, equipment or product-contact parts must be dedicated, or whether a segregated self-contained area is justified, and how extensive the technical and organisational measures must be; Ch.5 gives these measures as examples, not a mandatory set. The measures and their effectiveness must be reviewed periodically under set procedures. Making non-medicinal products in medicinal areas/equipment should normally be avoided and is only acceptable where justified and controlled; technical poisons such as pesticides and herbicides must not be made or stored in medicinal manufacturing/storage areas (unless used to make medicines).
system_implications: Product master carries the QRM outputs: HBEL/PDE-based cleaning limits (the HBEL approach is the EMA guideline tied to this chapter's implementation dates), dedication flags for facility/area/equipment and for specific product-contact parts (e.g. tablet punches/dies, filters, filling needles, hoses, maintenance tools), allowed rooms/equipment, campaign rules, required cleaning procedure and whether cleaning verification is required. Execution enforces them: only permitted rooms/equipment/parts selectable; a changeover matrix sets the cleaning level; single-use assemblies (injectables) cannot be reused; where the QRM requires post-campaign cleaning verification, the result must be recorded before the equipment is released to another product. Any non-medicinal product is flagged so it cannot be scheduled on medicinal equipment without a recorded justification. A periodic review report (cleaning failures, changeovers, spills/events, EM excursions) supports the 5.22 review. CORRECTIONS vs original: cleaning verification is NOT required at every changeover by Ch.5 - 5.21 presents it as a detectability measure to consider for higher-risk products after a campaign; campaign-length limits are a design choice.
verification_test: Assign a highly potent product to non-dedicated equipment not in its allowed list -> blocked. Attempt to start product B on equipment after product A with only a minor clean when the matrix requires full clean + verification -> blocked. Campaign exceeding configured maximum batches -> blocked or deviation required.
notes: Clause range right but paraphrase understated: it omitted the potency part of the evaluation, the 5.18 risk-assessment content (sources; injectables/long-term products most sensitive), that the 5.21 measures are QRM-selected examples, the 'set procedures' for periodic review, the 'where justified' allowance for non-medicinal products and the absolute ban on technical poisons. The implication overstated cleaning verification as universal.

requirement: Packaging programmes must be planned to minimise risks of cross-contamination, mix-up or substitution; different products are not packaged close to each other unless physically segregated. The product name and batch number being packed must be displayed at every packaging station or line.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: line/room model with segregation attributes so that the scheduler/execution refuses to run a different product on an adjacent line that is not physically segregated; each packaging station or line (every station where a line has several, e.g. blister machine, cartoner, labeller, case packer) shows at least the product name and batch number of the active order. DESIGN CHOICES: using an electronic HMI/screen rather than a physical line board (either satisfies 5.51); adding strength, pack and status; clearing the display only after order close and line clearance.
verification_test: Start product X on line 1; attempt product Y on non-segregated line 2 in the same room -> blocked. Line display shows current product/batch and reverts to 'awaiting clearance' at order close.
notes: Both clause numbers verified as correct (they had been flagged uncertain). Implication adjusted: the text requires only name and batch number at each station or line; an electronic display and the extra fields are design choices.

requirement: Before packaging starts, the work area, packaging lines, printers and other equipment must be verified clean and free of any product, material or document from earlier work that is not needed now; this line clearance follows an appropriate checklist.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: packaging order has a mandatory first step 'line clearance' performed against a master-defined, line-specific checklist (e.g. feeder hoppers, reject bins, printer ribbons/plates, vision-system recipe, floor/under-machine areas, documents removed). DESIGN CHOICES (not mandated by 5.50, though a common inspector expectation for mix-up risk): each item individually confirmed; performer plus independent verifier signatures by two different users; an electronic check that the previous order on the line is closed and reconciled and that no components of another order remain allocated to the line; blocking any packaging step, printer job or line start until clearance is signed.
verification_test: Attempt to start the first packaging step with clearance unsigned or only single-signed (when dual is configured) -> blocked. Same user signing as performer and verifier -> refused. Previous order on the line not closed -> clearance cannot be completed.
notes: Clause and paraphrase correct. The original implication already marked the dual signature as a design choice; the previous-order/reconciliation interlock is now also marked as a design choice.

requirement: On arrival at the packaging area, every product and packaging component must be checked to confirm the right quantity, the right identity and agreement with the packaging instructions.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: receipt-at-line step in which each bulk container and packaging-component lot is checked for quantity, identity (item code, artwork/version) and conformity with the packaging instructions/BOM, with the result recorded; received quantities posted to the order's reconciliation ledger. The released-status and expiry check supports 5.5 (quarantine until released for use) rather than 5.52. DESIGN CHOICES: scan-based checking and a hard block of the step on any mismatch.
verification_test: Scan a carton of the wrong artwork version or a leaflet for another market -> rejected. Scan a quarantined component lot -> rejected. Received quantity feeds reconciliation.
notes: Clause and paraphrase correct. Implication kept; the status check is attributed to 5.5 and blocking is marked as a design choice.

requirement: Containers must be clean when they are filled - the text sets the condition, not an in-house washing step, so supplier-cleaned ready-to-use containers can qualify - and care must be taken to avoid and remove foreign matter such as glass or metal particles. Filling and sealing should normally be followed by labelling as soon as possible; where that is not the case, procedures must prevent mix-ups and wrong labels.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: the cleanliness basis of each container/component lot is established before filling, and foreign-matter controls are applied (recorded where the master defines them as checks). Unlabelled filled units (e.g. vials held for inspection before labelling) are managed under a procedure that prevents mix-ups: tracked as 'bright stock' with unique tray/container IDs, location, count and hold start; a labelling order can only consume bright stock of the matching batch, verified by scan. SOURCED ELSEWHERE: for injectables, washing/depyrogenation/sterilisation records and their hold-time limits (and blocking filling when they expire) implement Annex 1, not Ch.5.
