NOT MANDATED: a container-washing step for tablet bottles - supplier-clean bottles with any air-rinse/inversion step defined by the master are acceptable. DESIGN CHOICE: configurable maximum filling-to-labelling interval with an alert (the text only says 'as quickly as possible' normally).
verification_test: Attempt to label bright-stock trays from batch A under order for batch B -> rejected. Bright stock exceeding maximum unlabelled hold time raises an exception. Filling step blocked if container depyrogenation/sterile hold time has expired (injectables).
notes: Clauses correct. Wording corrected from 'must be cleaned before filling' to 'must be clean' - the text states a condition, which matters for RTU vials and supplier-clean bottles. Depyrogenation/sterile hold-time controls re-attributed to Annex 1; the filling-to-labelling time limit is a design choice.

requirement: Printed packaging materials need particular care: they are stored securely so that unauthorised people cannot get to them, and cut labels and other loose printed items are kept and moved in separate closed containers to avoid mix-ups. Issue of packaging materials of any kind (not only printed ones) is limited to authorised staff working to an approved, documented procedure. Each incoming lot or delivery of primary or printed packaging is given its own reference number or identifying mark. Outdated or obsolete primary or printed packaging material must be destroyed and the disposal recorded.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: access-controlled storage locations for printed materials; the packaging-material issue transaction (all packaging materials) restricted to an authorised role and executed per the approved procedure; each delivery/batch of printed or primary material carries its own internal reference, and each issued unit (reel, carton bundle, sealed box of cut labels) is scanned by that reference and linked to the order, with the closed-container ID recorded for cut labels; outdated or obsolete stock is destroyed with a record (quantity, method, date, performer). The obsolescence logic must cover BOTH superseded artwork versions AND outdated primary/printed material past its expiry or retest date (e.g. stoppers, vials, blister foil, labels) - the original covered only artwork changes. DESIGN CHOICES: automatic blocking/routing of such stock to a destruction task, and a witness signature (5.48 requires only destruction plus a record).
verification_test: Non-authorised user attempts to issue labels -> refused. Issue of a lot whose artwork version is obsolete -> blocked. Destruction task for obsolete stock requires quantities, method, date and signatures and closes the lot.
notes: Clauses correct. Scope corrected: the issue-control sentence of 5.46 applies to all packaging materials, not only printed ones; 5.48 covers outdated (expired) primary packaging as well as obsolete artwork. Witnessed destruction re-labelled as a design choice.

requirement: Correct execution of every printing operation (e.g. batch code, expiry date), whether done separately or during packaging, must be checked and recorded, and any hand printing re-checked at regular intervals. Extra care is required with cut labels and with off-line overprinting; roll-fed labels are normally preferred over cut labels to help avoid mix-ups.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: every printing/coding operation (in-line or off-line) is checked and the check recorded; hand printing has a recurring re-check at a configured interval with overdue alerting; cut-label use and off-line overprinting are flagged in the master as operations needing additional controls. DESIGN CHOICES: variable print data sent electronically from the batch record to printers/coders (no manual keying); expiry calculated from a master shelf-life rule; start-of-run and periodic verification with specimen images; 100% vision or dual verification as the extra control for cut labels/off-line overprint; invalidating a print job when batch data change after set-up; blocking production mode until the start-up print check is recorded.
verification_test: Batch data change after print setup -> printer job invalidated until re-verified. Start-up print check missing -> line cannot go to production mode. Hand-print re-check overdue -> alarm and exception entry.
notes: Clauses and paraphrase correct (the roll-feed preference in 5.56 is advisory). Implications re-labelled: most mechanisms are design choices supporting the required check-and-record.

requirement: The correct operation of electronic code readers, label counters and comparable devices must be checked. Printed or embossed information on packs must be clear and must not easily fade or rub off.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: documented checks that code readers, label counters and similar devices work correctly; printed/embossed information on packaging materials is distinct and resistant to fading or erasure - a property controlled through the packaging-material specification and print-quality checks. DESIGN CHOICES: challenge tests with deliberate wrong-code/missing-label/unreadable-code/missing-leaflet pieces at start-up, after interventions/stoppages and at end of run; blocking production mode on a missing or failed challenge; counting challenge pieces out and back in; 2D-code grading and rub-resistance tests recorded as IPCs.
verification_test: Skip the start-up challenge -> line cannot run in production mode. Record a failed challenge -> line stopped and deviation required. Challenge pieces not all returned at end -> reconciliation exception.
notes: Clauses and paraphrase correct. Ch.5 sets no challenge frequency and no blocking rule; these are re-labelled as design choices.

requirement: During packaging, on-line checks must at least confirm that finished packs look right and are complete, that the correct product and components are being used and any overprint is right, and that line monitoring devices are working. Units taken off the line as samples must never be put back.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: the packaging master's IPC plan contains, as a minimum, the 5.59 check categories (pack appearance, completeness, correct product/materials, correct overprint, line-monitor function) at a defined frequency with pass/fail and sample counts; samples withdrawn are recorded by quantity and purpose and deducted in reconciliation, and the system offers no transaction to return sampled units to the line. DESIGN CHOICES: alerts for missed IPCs. BEYOND the 5.59 minimum (product-specific or Annex 1): container-closure checks such as crimp/seal and vial label placement (injectables); blister seal integrity/leak tests and count per bottle (tablets).
verification_test: IPC not recorded within its interval -> alert and exception report entry. Attempt to add sampled units back to good output -> not possible. Reconciliation shows sample quantities as a separate line.
notes: Clause and paraphrase correct. Product-specific checks are kept but flagged as going beyond the 5.59 minimum.

requirement: If product is caught up in an unusual event (e.g. jam, spill, dropped units, suspected mix-up), it may re-enter the process only after it has been specially inspected, the event investigated, and authorised staff have approved; this must be documented in detail.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: a 'set-aside/unusual event' transaction in which affected units are counted and held in a set-aside bucket linked to an event record (what happened, time, quantity, location); reintroduction requires an inspection result, an investigation reference and approval by an authorised role, all recorded in detail; quantities flow into reconciliation. DESIGN CHOICES: forbidding the operator who raised the event from approving it; defaulting non-reintroduced units to reject.
verification_test: Record a jam with 40 units set aside; attempt to add them back to good output without approval -> blocked. With inspection + approval, reintroduced quantity appears in the record and reconciliation with the event ID.
notes: Clause and paraphrase correct. Only the segregation-of-duties rule and the default-to-reject route are re-labelled as design choices.

requirement: Any significant or unusual discrepancy found when reconciling bulk quantity and printed packaging materials against units produced must be investigated and satisfactorily explained before the batch is released.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: end-of-order reconciliation of bulk product and printed packaging materials against units produced (issued = used + destroyed + returned + samples + rejects + set-aside), with master-defined limits that define a 'significant' discrepancy; an out-of-limit result requires a linked investigation, and release/certification is blocked until it is satisfactorily accounted for. DESIGN CHOICES: zero tolerance for batch-coded printed items; blocking order close as well as release; requiring QA as the approver of the investigation. Examples - tablets: bulk tablets by weight/count vs packs; injectables: filled/inspected units vs labelled units vs cartons.
verification_test: Enter counts leaving 12 labels unaccounted with a zero-tolerance limit -> order close blocked, deviation required; QP certification blocked until deviation closed. Counts within limits -> order closes normally.
notes: Clause and paraphrase correct; the release block is required by the text, the order-close block and QA approver are design choices.

requirement: When packaging is finished, any unused packaging material already coded with the batch must be destroyed and the destruction recorded; returning uncoded printed materials to stock must follow a documented procedure.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: order close-out distinguishes batch-coded from uncoded leftovers (based on whether in-line/off-line coding occurred); coded leftovers go to a destruction record (quantity, method, date, performer) and can never be returned to stock; uncoded printed leftovers can be returned only through a return-to-stock transaction that embodies the documented procedure (count, container relabelling, update of the component lot quantity). DESIGN CHOICES: a witness signature on destruction; QA/stores acceptance and a count-verification signature on returns.
verification_test: Attempt to return batch-coded cartons to stock -> no transaction available. Uncoded label return requires counted quantity, verification signature and updates stock. Destruction quantities appear in the reconciliation.
notes: Clause and paraphrase correct; witness and acceptance signatures re-labelled as design choices.

requirement: Necessary in-process and environmental controls must be performed and recorded, and intermediate and bulk products must be held under appropriate conditions.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: IPCs and environmental controls defined as necessary in the master (frequency, sample size, limits) are performed and recorded (automatic capture from balances, hardness/thickness testers, checkweighers, fill-weight systems, pH/conductivity meters where possible); intermediate/bulk holds record container, location and storage condition. DESIGN CHOICES: alerts for missed IPCs; linking room environmental data (temperature/RH, particle counts, pressures) by time window; pulling excursions into the exception report and blocking QA review completion until assessed. SOURCED ELSEWHERE: maximum hold times for intermediates/bulk come from process validation/hold-time studies and the MA dossier, grade A/B viable and non-viable monitoring and pre-filtration bioburden limits come from Annex 1 - Ch.5 only requires 'appropriate conditions' and that necessary controls are done and recorded.
verification_test: Miss a scheduled IPC -> alert and exception. Inject an EM excursion during the filling window -> appears in batch exception report and blocks QA review completion until assessed. Bulk hold exceeding validated time -> blocked or deviation required.
notes: Clauses and paraphrase correct. Implications re-attributed: hold-time limits come from validation studies/the MA and aseptic EM requirements from Annex 1, and the review block is a design choice.

requirement: Rejected materials and products must be clearly marked as rejected and segregated in restricted-access storage. Their fate (return to supplier, reprocessing where appropriate, or destruction) must be approved and documented by authorised people.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: 'Rejected' is a hard system status that blocks every consumption, issue, packaging and shipping transaction and is shown on the label; rejected stock must be physically moved to a restricted, separate location (unlike quarantine under 5.5, Ch.5 offers no purely administrative alternative for rejected goods, so the electronic status complements but does not replace physical segregation); the disposition (return to supplier / reprocess / destroy) is approved by an authorised role and the executed action and quantities are recorded. In-process rejects (e.g. checkweigher rejects, vials rejected at visual inspection) are counted into identified reject containers and follow the same path.
verification_test: Try to dispense or package a rejected lot -> blocked. Attempt to move rejected stock to a normal location -> blocked. Disposition without authorised approval -> blocked; completed disposition visible in lot history.
notes: Clause and paraphrase correct. Implication clarified that physical segregation in a restricted area is required and cannot be satisfied by system status alone.

requirement: Reprocessing of rejected product is to be exceptional: allowed only when final quality is unaffected, specifications are met, and it follows a defined, authorised procedure after risk evaluation; a record of the reprocessing must be kept.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: reprocessing can only be executed from a pre-approved reprocessing procedure/master linked to the product (never ad hoc), launched after a documented risk evaluation; the reprocessing record is linked to the original batch genealogy and flagged for release review; conformity with specifications is confirmed before release. Also capture the QC decision on additional testing required by 5.69 for reprocessed batches (see EU5-22). SOURCED ELSEWHERE: restrictions on reprocessing sterile products (e.g. re-filtration only if validated and registered) come from the marketing authorisation and Annex 1, not Ch.5 - the per-product ability to disable reprocessing masters is a design choice. DESIGN CHOICE: launching reprocessing from an approved deviation/change record.
verification_test: Attempt to start reprocessing without an approved reprocessing procedure and approved risk assessment -> blocked. Completed reprocessing appears in the original batch genealogy and QP review flags.
notes: Clause and paraphrase correct. Sterile-product reprocessing limits re-attributed to MA/Annex 1; the 5.69 QC testing decision is added for reprocessed batches, which the original implications only covered for recovered material.

requirement: Adding all or part of earlier batches that meet quality requirements into a later batch of that same product, at a predefined manufacturing stage, needs prior authorisation, must follow a defined procedure after assessing risks (including any effect on shelf life), and must be recorded. QC must decide whether reprocessed product, or product containing recovered material, needs extra testing.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: recovered-material addition is a specific step type available only where the master defines it (defined stage); the source batch must be the same product and of conforming quality; authorisation is recorded before the addition; the procedure's risk evaluation (including shelf-life effect) is referenced; genealogy records source batch IDs and quantities; a QC decision on additional testing is a mandatory field before release for BOTH recovered-material batches and reprocessed batches (5.69 covers both). DESIGN CHOICES: a maximum proportion and batch-age limits in the master; calculating the receiving batch expiry from the oldest contributing batch (one way of implementing the shelf-life evaluation).
verification_test: Try to add material from a different product or a non-conforming batch -> blocked. Add eligible recovered material: pre-authorisation required, genealogy and expiry calculation updated, QC decision field mandatory before release.
notes: Clauses and paraphrase correct. Implication extended so the 5.69 QC decision also applies to reprocessed batches; age/proportion limits and the expiry rule re-labelled as design choices.

requirement: Market returns that have been outside the manufacturer's control default to destruction unless their quality is not in doubt. Resale, relabelling or use in a later batch is allowed only after QC has critically assessed them under a written procedure, considering the product type, any special storage needs, its condition and history, and how long it has been out. If quality is doubtful the goods must not be reissued or reused (though basic chemical recovery of the active substance may be possible). All actions must be recorded.
system_implications: Returned-goods receipt creates a quarantined 'returned' lot linked to the original batch; disposition requires a QC assessment record (nature of product, storage requirements and history - e.g. cold chain for injectables - condition, time since issue) and QC e-signature; default disposition is destroy. Returned units cannot be relabelled, resold or used as recovered material unless the assessment permits it; if doubt is recorded only destruction (or a chemical-recovery route) is available. The resulting action is recorded against the original batch history.
verification_test: Try to repackage returned units without a QC assessment -> blocked. Assessment 'doubt' -> only destruction (or chemical recovery route) available.
notes: Clause and paraphrase correct; implications are within scope and kept (lightly reworded).

requirement: Incoming materials and finished products must be quarantined, physically or administratively, as soon as they are received or produced, and stay so until released for use or distribution. Finished products remain in quarantine, under conditions set by the manufacturer, until final release; the evaluation of product and documentation needed before release is governed by Ch.6. After release they are held as usable stock, again under manufacturer-set storage conditions. (QP certification is required by Directive 2001/83/EC Art. 51 and Annex 16, not by Ch.5.)
system_implications: Every produced lot is created in 'Quarantine' at the moment its output is posted (5.5 'immediately'); the change to 'Released' is only possible through the release transaction after record review is complete (steps signed, deviations closed, reconciliation passed, lab results approved) - these prerequisites come from Ch.6 and Annex 16, and the QP-certification step is an Annex 16 requirement. Interfaces to ERP/WMS must respect status (no allocation or shipment of quarantined stock). Administrative (electronic) quarantine is acceptable under 5.5 provided the system enforces it. Storage-condition attributes of the finished product apply both before and after release.
verification_test: Attempt to ship or allocate a quarantined finished lot via ERP interface -> rejected. QP certification button disabled while any release prerequisite is open. Status history shows who released and when.
notes: Clauses correct. Paraphrase corrected: QP certification had been attributed to Ch.5 but comes from Art. 51 of Directive 2001/83/EC and Annex 16; added the 'immediately after receipt or processing' timing of 5.5 and the post-release storage-condition requirement of 5.65.

requirement: Throughout every processing stage, products and materials must be protected against microbial and other contamination. When dry materials and products are handled, special precautions must stop dust from being generated and spreading, above all for highly active (potent) or sensitising materials.
system_implications: Ch.5 states the protection objective only; the mechanisms are design choices or come from other texts. Tablets (design choices consistent with 5.11/5.21): the master can require dust-control prerequisites before open-handling steps (local extraction/containment on, pressure cascade OK, contained transfer connected) as signed checks or interface signals; potent-API weighing only in designated booths. Injectables (SOURCED FROM Annex 1, not Ch.5): aseptic prerequisites before exposure steps (grade A airflow/particle status, sterile equipment within hold time, gowning qualification valid, interventions logged) and bioburden/time limits for non-sterile bulk solution before sterile filtration - keep them but trace them to Annex 1.
verification_test: Attempt to start an open-powder step while the containment/extraction check is not recorded -> blocked (tablets). Attempt to start filling with sterile-hold expired on filling parts or with an active grade A alarm -> blocked (injectables). Bulk solution time from compounding start to filtration exceeding limit -> deviation required.
notes: Clauses correct. Wording corrected: the text refers to 'highly active' (i.e. potent) materials, not 'highly hazardous' ones. Injectable aseptic controls in the implication re-attributed to Annex 1.

requirement: Checks must confirm that pipelines and other equipment that transfer product from one area to another are correctly connected.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: transfer steps (e.g. bulk solution from compounding vessel to filling line via transfer panel/hoses; vacuum/pneumatic powder transfer to a tablet press hopper) include a connection check before transfer, recorded in the batch record (recording follows from 5.2). DESIGN CHOICES: scanning source vessel, panel/hose/port and destination IDs, or reading panel proximity sensors, and comparing them with the master route; blocking the transfer on mismatch; a second-person verifier signature (5.14 requires a check, not two people).
verification_test: Scan a hose connected to the wrong destination vessel -> transfer blocked. Correct route scan -> transfer enabled and recorded.
notes: Clause and paraphrase correct. The verifier signature and interlocks re-labelled as design choices.

requirement: Starting materials in the storage area must be suitably labelled with at least the designated material name (plus the internal code where applicable) and the batch number assigned at receipt, and, where relevant, the lot's QC status (for instance quarantine, under test, released or rejected) and its expiry or retest date; when a fully computerised storage system is used, this information need not all be legible on the label. Procedures or measures must make sure every container holds what it is supposed to hold, and bulk containers that have been sampled must be identified as such. Only starting materials released by QC and still within their retest period may be used.
system_implications: The eBMR relies on (or provides) a validated inventory status as the master for material status; at dispensing and at charging, each container scan checks identity (item code), released status, retest/expiry date and, where Annex 8 requires it, container-level identity-test status (5.35 requires at least identity testing of each batch per Annex 8). The sampling transaction sets a 'sampled' flag on the container, shown on its label/record and at dispensing (5.33, see Ch.6). If labels carry only a barcode, the system is the authoritative source for the omitted data and must be validated for that purpose (Annex 11).
verification_test: Scan a container whose lot is 'on test', rejected, past retest date, or whose container identity test is pending -> blocked at dispensing and at charging. Released, in-date container -> accepted.
notes: Clauses correct. Paraphrase understated: it omitted the internal code reference, that status and expiry/retest are required only 'where appropriate', and the 5.33 requirement to identify sampled bulk containers; all added, with the matching sampled-container flag in the implications.

requirement: Production must be carried out and overseen by competent staff, and every handling activity for materials and products, from goods receipt through processing and packaging to distribution, must follow written procedures or instructions and be recorded where necessary.
system_implications: REQUIRED by the text: each master step is executed according to, and links to, the governing procedure/instruction version; handling activities that need a record are captured in the batch record; performer and supervisor/verifier roles are distinct permissions so that competent people perform and supervise. DESIGN CHOICE (one way to evidence competence; training requirements themselves sit in Ch.2): each step declares the required qualification per procedure version and the system checks the user's current training status (LMS interface or internal records) before allowing them to perform or verify the step.
verification_test: User trained on SOP v3 attempts a step now requiring SOP v4 training -> refused. Qualified user can perform; verifier role cannot be assigned to an untrained user.
notes: Clauses and paraphrase correct. The training-status interlock is re-labelled as a design choice: 5.1 requires competent people but prescribes no mechanism.

requirement: Validation studies must be run according to defined procedures, with results and conclusions recorded. When a new formula or preparation method is introduced, it must be demonstrated fit for routine production: run as defined with the specified materials and equipment, the process must reliably deliver product of the required quality. Significant changes to the process (including equipment or material changes) that may affect product quality or reproducibility must be validated; critical processes must be validated (5.42); and processes and procedures must undergo periodic critical re-validation to confirm they still achieve the intended results.
system_implications: REQUIRED support: master recipes record the validation basis of the process; process-impacting master changes (CPP ranges, equipment class, materials/suppliers, batch size, sequence) cannot be approved without a linked change-control and validation reference. DESIGN CHOICES: classifying every master change as editorial vs process-impacting; a master comparison (diff) report. SOURCED ELSEWHERE: flagging batches made under a master still in validation (PPQ/concurrent batches) and conditioning their release on the validation outcome follows Annex 15, not Ch.5. Periodic re-validation is a QMS activity; the eBMR can support it with batch-data trend reports.
verification_test: Attempt to approve a master revision with a changed CPP range and no change-control/validation link -> blocked. Diff report lists changed fields. PPQ-flagged batch cannot be certified without validation outcome entry.
notes: Clause set extended with 5.42 (critical processes validated), which no original line cited. Paraphrase corrected: the text requires periodic critical re-validation of processes and procedures (not merely 'reassessment'), recording of conclusions as well as results, and consistent quality using the specified materials and equipment. PPQ release control re-attributed to Annex 15.

requirement: The manufacturer must promptly tell the marketing authorisation holder about manufacturing constraints that could cause an abnormal restriction of supply, so the MAH can notify the competent authorities.
system_implications: Organisational duty; no eBMR function is mandated. Optional support (design choice): batch/campaign rejection, prolonged line holds or major deviations can carry a 'potential supply impact' attribute that creates a notification task to the supply/QA contact for the MAH, with timestamped acknowledgement.
verification_test: Reject a batch flagged 'supply impact' -> notification task created with due date and audit trail of acknowledgement.
notes: Clause and paraphrase correct (5.71 is the 2015 addition on supply restrictions; the MAH's reporting duty stems from Directive 2001/83/EC, Articles 23a and 81). eBMR support is optional.

clause: Ch.4 4.3; 4.9; 4.13; 4.20(c),(f),(h),(i); 4.21(c),(g),(i); 4.31; e-signature properties Annex 11 §14, QP certification §15
requirement: Chapter 4 signature/identification points: instruction documents approved, signed and dated by authorised persons (4.3); specifications authorised and dated (4.13); alterations signed and dated (4.9); processing and packaging records identify who performed each significant step and, where appropriate, who checked it (4.20(c), 4.21(c)), and who performed in-process controls (4.20(f)); departures from instructions carry signed authorisation (4.20(h), 4.21(g)); the responsible person approves the completed processing or packaging record (4.20(i), 4.21(i)); logbooks identify who carried out each operation (4.31). Annex 11 §14, now checked, lets these be electronic signatures that carry the weight of handwritten ones inside the company, stay permanently linked to the record and show date and time; §15 requires QP certification by e-signature.
system_implications: Signature catalogue built into the product with one configurable signature type per point: master approval, correction, step performed, step verified, deviation authorisation, production/packaging record approval, QA review, QP certification. Each type defines the allowed roles, whether the signer must differ from earlier signers on the same object, and whether re-authentication is needed. Every signature event is recorded in the audit trail and shown in the rendered record. Verifier: add signature types for IPC performer (4.20(f)), specification approval if specifications are held in the system (4.13) and logbook entries (4.31). Every e-signature must carry date and time and be permanently bound to its record (Annex 11 §14). Signature 'meaning' and re-authentication at each signing come from 21 CFR Part 11 (11.50, 11.200), not the 2011 EU texts - keep for dual-market use.
verification_test: For each signature type, test: correct role accepted, wrong role refused, the same person refused where independence is required, and the signature (name, date-time, meaning) appears in the rendered batch record and audit trail.
notes: MINOR correction: added missed identification points (IPC performer 4.20(f), specification authorisation 4.13, logbook identity 4.31) and replaced the 'Annex 11 not re-checked' caveat with the verified §14/§15 content.

clause: Ch.4 Principle and preamble 'Required GMP documentation' (Records definition); see also 4.28 (distribution records to support recall)
requirement: 'Written' means recorded or documented on any medium from which data can be rendered human-readable. Records provide evidence of actions taken and, for manufactured batches, a history of each batch including its distribution (4.28 adds that distribution records must allow recall of any batch). Controls must keep documents accurate, intact, available and legible.
system_implications: Every electronic batch record, including its metadata, attachments and audit trail, can be rendered on demand as a complete human-readable report (screen and PDF/print) for inspectors and the QP, for the whole retention period. The batch genealogy can be linked to distribution data held in ERP, so the history of a batch can be traced forward to customers for recall.
verification_test: Render an archived batch record: every step, value, signature, comment, deviation link and audit-trail entry is present and legible. From a finished batch ID, a forward trace returns its distribution records.
notes: No change; clause refined (the records definition sits in the 'Required GMP documentation' preamble; 4.28 is the specific distribution-record clause). The researcher's verified=false can now be treated as verified. The raw-data sentence of the same preamble is not covered by any line - added as EUA-NEW-01.

requirement: Annex 11 covers every computerised system used in GMP-regulated activities. The application must be validated and the IT infrastructure qualified. Replacing a manual operation with a computerised system must not reduce product quality, process control or quality assurance, and must not raise the overall risk of the process.
system_implications: Every control that exists in the paper BMR (line clearance sign-off, second-person checks, yield reconciliation, label reconciliation, in-process checks) needs an equivalent electronic control in the eBMR, or a documented risk-based justification that overall process risk does not rise (the Principle judges the overall outcome rather than demanding control-by-control equivalence; e.g., Ch.4 4.21(h) lets robust electronic controls replace reconciliation data). The vendor/customer must be able to deliver validation evidence for the configured application (recipes, workflows, calculations, interfaces) and qualification evidence for servers, database, network and any cloud tenancy.
verification_test: Inspect a paper-to-electronic control mapping matrix: each paper control maps to a named system control and at least one executed test case. Confirm approved infrastructure qualification records and application validation summary report exist for the release under test.
notes: No change to the requirement. Implications: 'equal or stronger control per paper control' overstates the Principle; reframed as an equivalent control or a risk-justified alternative.

requirement: Risk management must be applied across the system's whole life cycle, weighing patient safety, data integrity and product quality; how far validation and data-integrity controls go must be decided on a justified, documented risk assessment of the system.
system_implications: The eBMR should let the regulated user tag each data field / step with a criticality class (e.g., critical process parameter, GMP-relevant, informational) and drive controls from that tag: second-person verification, mandatory reason-for-change, audit-trail review flags, and exception reporting. The risk assessment behind the classification must be stored/linked as a controlled document. Injectables will typically classify more steps as critical (aseptic interventions, sterilisation, filtration, environmental monitoring excursions) than tablets. Verifier: criticality tagging is a design means, not required by §1, but it is a practical way to evidence the risk basis that §1, §6 and §9 call for.
verification_test: Pick a sample of recipe steps; confirm each has a criticality classification traceable to an approved risk assessment and that the behaviour (e.g., witness required) changes when the classification changes, under change control.
notes: No change.

requirement: A current inventory listing every relevant computerised system and the GMP functions it performs must be available. For critical systems there must also be a current description covering the physical and logical set-up, how data flow, the interfaces to other systems or processes, hardware and software prerequisites, and the security measures.
system_implications: The regulated user is accountable for the inventory and description; the eBMR vendor should supply (and keep current per release) an architecture/system description: modules, database, integration points (ERP/material management, LIMS, weighing scales, SCADA/PLC, historian, label printers, QMS for deviations), data flow diagrams, and security design. The system should be able to export its own configuration inventory (interfaces enabled, versions) to help keep the description current. Verifier: the site inventory must also list the connected systems themselves (scales, PLC/SCADA, LIMS, printers, vision systems), each with its GMP function.
verification_test: Compare the documented interface list with the interfaces actually configured in the production instance; any undocumented interface is a failure. Confirm the description is version-controlled and was updated at the last change.
notes: No change to the requirement. Implications: the obligation sits with the regulated user (vendor documentation supports it); connected systems added to the inventory.

requirement: When data are moved into a different format or a different system, the validation must verify that neither their values nor their meaning change during that migration.
system_implications: Upgrades, database migrations, archive exports and legacy-record imports must include automated reconciliation: record counts, checksums/hashes per record, field-level comparison of values and units, and preservation of audit trail, signatures and metadata. Signature manifestations and audit-trail links must survive migration and remain bound to the same records. Verifier: §4.8 requires the checks, not that they be automated (automation is a design choice). Preserving signature linkage follows from §14 (permanently linked).
verification_test: Run a migration on a validation copy; compare source vs target record counts and hashes; spot-check that audit trails, e-signature meaning/date/time, units and precision are unchanged; confirm the migration report is approved before go-live.
notes: No change.

requirement: Critical data keyed in by hand need an additional accuracy check, either by a second person or by a validated electronic check; risk management must address how critical the data are and what wrong or mistaken entries could cause.
system_implications: For fields classified critical (e.g., dispensed weight typed manually, lot number of an API, compression force set-point, fill volume/weight, sterilisation cycle parameters, filter integrity test result), the eBMR must either (a) capture the value directly from the instrument/scale/PLC or verify it by barcode scan against the expected item, or (b) force an independent second-user verification with its own authentication before the step can be completed. The verifier must be a different user from the performer (system-enforced), and both identities, timestamps and the verified value are stored. Verifier: option (a) removes the manual entry rather than checking it - acceptable and usually preferable, but the interface then falls under §5 and must be validated (§4).
verification_test: Configure a critical manual field; attempt to complete the step without verification (must block); attempt verification by the same user (must be rejected); verify by a second user and check the audit record holds both identities and times. Test that a barcode mismatch blocks progression.
notes: No change.

requirement: Data must be protected against damage by both physical and electronic means; stored data must be verified as accessible, readable and accurate; and access to the data must be assured throughout the retention period.
system_implications: Database and file storage must sit on protected, redundant infrastructure; the system should provide integrity checking (e.g., record-level hashes or database consistency checks) and a retrievability check that proves old batch records can still be opened and rendered with their audit trail and signatures. Retention rules per record type (EU batch documentation: at least one year beyond expiry or five years after QP certification, whichever is longer, per EU GMP Chapter 4) must be configurable and must block premature deletion.
verification_test: Restore/open a batch record older than the current software version and confirm full rendering incl. audit trail and signatures; attempt to delete a record inside its retention period (must be blocked); review the output of the periodic integrity/readability check.
notes: No change (the retention rule quoted in the implications is correctly attributed to Ch.4 4.11).

requirement: All relevant data must be backed up regularly, and backups must be shown to be complete, accurate and restorable - first during validation and then through periodic monitoring.
system_implications: Backups must cover the database, attachments, configuration (recipes/master batch records, user/role definitions) and audit trails as a consistent set. Restore procedures must be documented and exercised; the system should log backup job success/failure and alert on failure. Point-in-time recovery objectives should be set by risk (an injectable line running continuous aseptic filling needs a tight recovery point so in-progress batch data are not lost). Verifier: backup alerts and recovery-point objectives are design choices set by risk (§1, §16).
verification_test: Perform a restore of a production backup into an isolated environment; compare record counts/hashes and open a sample of batch records with audit trails; confirm backup failure raises an alert; confirm restore test records exist at the defined frequency.
notes: No change.

requirement: The system must be able to produce clear paper copies of data it stores electronically, and for records that support batch release it must be able to print a version indicating whether any value was changed since first entry.
system_implications: The eBMR needs a controlled print/export of the executed batch record (human-readable, complete, paginated, with unique record ID, version and 'page x of y') in which every value that was modified after first entry is visibly flagged, ideally with original value, new value, who, when and why, or a cross-reference to the audit trail entry. The rendered copy must also show signatures with name, date/time and meaning. Verifier: §8.2 requires the ability to generate a printout that indicates changed data; showing signer name and meaning reflects 21 CFR 11.50 (Annex 11 §14 itself requires date/time and permanent linkage); pagination and record ID are good practice.
verification_test: Enter a value, correct it with a reason, then generate the batch release printout/PDF: the corrected field must be flagged and the original value and change details must be visible or referenced. Confirm unchanged fields are not flagged and that the print is complete (no truncated fields).
notes: No change.

requirement: Where the system exchanges data electronically with other systems, suitable built-in checks must ensure the data are entered and processed correctly and securely, so as to reduce risk.
system_implications: Every interface (ERP/material status, LIMS results, balances, PLC/SCADA, historian, label printing, QMS deviations) must validate what it receives: message schema and completeness, identity matching (material code, lot, batch ID), unit and range checks, duplicate/sequence detection, acknowledgement and retry, and authenticated/encrypted transport. Failed or rejected transfers must raise a visible alert and must never silently drop or default a value into the batch record. Verifier: authenticated/encrypted transport is security good practice (supports §12) rather than a §5 requirement.
verification_test: Inject malformed, out-of-range, duplicate and wrong-batch messages at each interface; confirm rejection, alerting and logging. Interrupt the connection mid-transfer and confirm no partial or duplicated values land in the batch record.
notes: No change (the line's 'corruption or loss' wording is a harmless gloss on 'risks').

requirement: Based on a risk assessment, building into the system an automatically generated audit trail of every GMP-relevant change or deletion should be considered. When GMP-relevant data are changed or deleted, the reason must be documented. Audit trails must be retrievable, convertible into a form people can generally understand, and reviewed at regular intervals. (For an eBMR holding batch-release data the risk assessment will in practice conclude that an audit trail is needed.)
system_implications: Every create/modify/delete of GMP data in the eBMR (step results, parameters, material entries, comments, status changes, signatures, voids) must write an append-only, system-generated entry holding user ID and full name, date/time with time zone, record/field identity, old value, new value and a mandatory reason (reason list plus free text). Ordinary users and administrators must not be able to edit, delete or switch off the trail; the trail must be viewable and exportable in plain language (not only raw database codes), filterable by batch, and flagged for review. Verifier: the 2011 §9 makes the audit trail risk-based (consideration should be given); for an eBMR the risk assessment should conclude it is required, and EMA GMP Q&A on data integrity expects it. Blocking administrators from editing or disabling the trail, full-name and time-zone capture, and logging record creation go beyond the 2011 text (EMA Q&A, PIC/S PI 041, 2025 draft revision of Annex 11) - still implement. Keeping the old value is also required by Ch.4 4.9.
verification_test: Change and delete sample GMP values with each role; confirm entries appear with old/new value, reason, user and timestamp; confirm the save is blocked without a reason; attempt to edit/delete audit entries and to disable auditing via UI, API and admin console (all must fail or, for privileged DB access, be detectable via integrity hashes).
notes: MODERATE correction: 2011 §9 says an audit trail should be CONSIDERED on the basis of risk; the line stated it as an unconditional 'the system should generate'. The reason-for-change and the availability, intelligibility and regular-review parts are firm. The eBMR should still implement a full, always-on audit trail (EMA Q&A expectation).

requirement: Any change to a computerised system, configuration included, may be made only in a controlled way that follows a defined procedure.
system_implications: Master batch records/recipes, workflows, calculations, limits, role definitions and interface settings must be version-controlled objects with draft-review-approve-effective states, e-signed approvals, and an audit trail of configuration changes. Only one effective version per product and batch size (processing) or per product, pack size and type (packaging) may be usable for new batches; in-flight batches must stay bound to the version they started on unless an approved change says otherwise. Software releases must go through a test environment before production. Verifier: master batch records are also GMP instruction documents, so their approval and versioning derive from Ch.4 4.3/4.5 and their change-control records from Ch.4 4.29, in addition to §10. Testing releases in a test environment first is good practice (§4.7 refers to test environments).
verification_test: Edit a master recipe: confirm it cannot be used in production until approved; confirm running batches keep their original version; confirm configuration audit trail shows who changed what; confirm production configuration cannot be changed directly without the controlled path.
notes: No change to the requirement. Implications: the 'one effective version' rule scoped per product and batch size / pack size and type.

requirement: Computerised systems must be evaluated periodically to confirm they are still in a validated state and GMP-compliant; where relevant the review considers the system's current functions, its deviation, incident and problem history, the upgrades made, how it has performed and how reliable and secure it has been, and its validation status.
system_implications: The eBMR should make periodic review easy by providing reports for the review period: configuration and software changes, incident/error logs, interface failures, user-access changes and privileged activity, backup/restore results, performance/uptime, open validation gaps. System-generated reports are preferable for reliability, but §11 does not require the evidence to be system-generated.
verification_test: Generate the periodic-review report pack for a defined period and cross-check a sample of entries against the underlying logs; confirm the pack covers all listed topics.
notes: No change to the requirement. Implications: system-generated evidence relabelled as a preference.

requirement: Physical and/or logical controls must limit system access to authorised persons (examples include physical keys or badges, individual passwords, biometrics and locking away hardware and storage); how strong the controls are depends on how critical the system is; and granting, changing and withdrawing access rights must be recorded.
system_implications: Individual named accounts with role-based permissions (operator, verifier/witness, supervisor, QA reviewer, QP, master-data author, administrator); user administration workflow that logs every grant/change/revocation with requester, approver, date and reason; history of who held which role on any past date must be queryable. Shop-floor terminals in cleanrooms (injectables, Grade A/B gowned operators) need an authentication method usable with gloves (badge/RFID + PIN or biometrics) without resorting to shared logins. Verifier: §12.3 requires access changes to be recorded; requester/approver/reason fields and point-in-time role history are good practice. Individual named accounts are implied by §12.4 (identity of the operator) and explicit in EMA GMP Q&A / PIC/S PI 041.
verification_test: Create, modify and disable a user; confirm each action is logged with approver; query role membership as of a past date; confirm a disabled user cannot log in or sign; confirm there is no generic/shared account with write access.
notes: No change.

requirement: Systems managing data and documents must capture who entered, changed, confirmed or deleted each item of data, and when (date and time).
system_implications: Each recorded value and each confirmation (e.g., 'performed', 'verified', 'checked') must carry the authenticated user identity and a trusted server timestamp (not a client-device clock the operator can change). Timestamps should be synchronised to a reliable time source and stored with time-zone information so multi-site data line up. Verifier: deletions must be attributed too (§12.4 covers deleting); the time source and time-zone storage are design means.
verification_test: Change a terminal clock and record a step: the stored timestamp must still come from the synchronised server source. Confirm every entry, verification and deletion in a test batch shows user identity and date/time.
notes: No change.

requirement: Every incident, including but not limited to system failures and data errors, must be reported and evaluated; for critical incidents the root cause must be determined and must drive corrective and preventive action.
system_implications: The eBMR must log technical and functional incidents (interface failures, lost connections, crashes during a step, failed signatures, time-sync failures, printing failures) in a way that links them to affected batches, so an incident can be raised in the QMS and its batch impact assessed before release. Batches touched by an open incident should be flagged on the release/QP view. Verifier: batch linkage and QP-view flags go beyond §13 but support Ch.4 4.27 (a system to indicate special observations). §13 also requires root-cause analysis feeding CAPA for critical incidents - the incident record should hold a criticality rating and a CAPA link.
verification_test: Simulate an interface outage during a weighing step; confirm an incident/event record is created, linked to the batch, and shown as open on the batch review/QP screen until closed.
notes: No change to the requirement. Implications: added root cause and CAPA linkage.

requirement: Electronic records may be signed electronically. Such signatures are expected to carry, within the company, the same weight as handwritten ones, to stay permanently tied to the record they sign, and to show the date and time they were applied.
system_implications: Signing must require the signer's own credentials at the moment of signing; the signature object (user ID, printed full name, date/time with zone, meaning such as performed/verified/reviewed/approved/certified) must be stored bound to the exact record version (e.g., via record hash), must display on screen and on every rendered copy, and cannot be copied, moved or re-used on another record. A company policy/attestation that users accept e-signatures as equivalent to handwritten ones should be captured in the system (acknowledgement at account activation). Verifier: printed name, signature meaning and credential entry at each signing reflect 21 CFR Part 11 (11.50, 11.200); Annex 11 §14 asks for equal effect to handwritten signatures inside the company, permanent linkage and date/time - keep the Part 11 elements for dual-market use. Equal effect inside the company is primarily a company policy; user acknowledgement is one way to evidence it.
verification_test: Sign a step, then inspect storage: signature references the record version/hash; try to transplant a signature to another record via API/DB manipulation (must be rejected or detected); confirm signature manifestation appears on screen and on the printout with name, date/time and meaning.
notes: No change.

requirement: If a computerised system records batch certification and release, it must let only Qualified Persons certify batch release, must clearly identify and record who released or certified each batch, and this must be done by electronic signature.
system_implications: A distinct 'QP certification' permission, granted only to persons named as QP on the manufacturing/import authorisation (with an approval workflow and a register of QP accounts). Certification is an e-signature with the meaning 'certified by QP' and the QP's identity; release status changes (quarantine to certified/released) must be possible only through this action and must feed downstream systems (ERP/warehouse) to lift quarantine. Other users, including admins and QA reviewers without QP status, must not be able to certify. Verifier: feeding ERP/warehouse status from the certification is a design choice beyond §15.
verification_test: Attempt certification with QA reviewer, supervisor and admin accounts (must fail); certify with a QP account and confirm the record shows QP name, date/time, meaning; confirm ERP stock status changes only after certification.
notes: No change.

requirement: Where computerised systems support critical processes, provisions such as a manual or alternative system must keep those processes going if the system breaks down; how quickly the fallback must be available is set by risk and by the system and process concerned; and the arrangements must be adequately documented and tested.
system_implications: Provide a validated downtime mode: controlled pre-printed/printable emergency batch record sheets generated from the current master record (uniquely numbered, reconciled), local buffering on the shop floor for short network outages with guaranteed ordered re-sync, and a controlled back-entry procedure after recovery where late-entered data are flagged as transcribed from paper, second-person verified, and linked to the scanned original. Injectables: an aseptic filling run cannot simply stop, so fallback must be immediate and pre-staged; tablets may tolerate a planned pause at defined hold points. Verifier: §16 requires the arrangements to be documented and tested; calling it a 'validated' mode goes further (reasonable for injectables). Back-entry of transcribed data is manual entry of critical data, so Annex 11 §6 accuracy checks apply.
verification_test: Execute a downtime drill: cut the network mid-batch, continue on the fallback, restore, back-enter data; confirm back-entered values are flagged, verified, linked to scanned originals and time-stamped with both the original execution time and the entry time.
notes: No change.

requirement: Data may be archived; archived data must be verified as accessible, readable and intact, and when relevant changes to the system (e.g., hardware or programs) are planned, the ability to retrieve the archived data must be ensured and tested.
system_implications: Archive function that moves completed, released batch records (with full audit trail, signatures, attachments and metadata) into read-only storage, with fixity checks (hashes) run periodically and a restore/re-render capability that still works after application upgrades. Upgrade validation must include retrieval tests of archived records from earlier versions. Verifier: §17 sets no frequency for the checks; periodic fixity checking is a design choice. Archiving must also cover rejected and non-released batch records, not only released ones.
verification_test: Archive a batch, run fixity check, then upgrade the application in a test environment and retrieve/render the archived record; confirm content, audit trail and signatures are intact and hashes match.
notes: No change to the requirement. Implications: archiving scope extended to non-released batches.

requirement: Process owner, system owner, QPs, IT and other relevant staff must cooperate closely, and all personnel need appropriate qualifications, access level and defined responsibilities (§2). Formal agreements stating the third party's responsibilities are required whenever a third party is involved in supplying, setting up, integrating, validating, maintaining (including by remote access), changing or hosting/retaining the system, or in processing data; internal IT departments are to be treated the same way (§3.1). Supplier competence and reliability are key selection factors and the need for an audit is decided by risk (§3.2). Quality-system and audit information on software and system suppliers or developers must be made available to inspectors on request (§3.4).
system_implications: Roles for process owner and system owner should be configurable in the system and shown on validation/periodic review outputs. For a SaaS or vendor-hosted eBMR: a quality/technical agreement covering data ownership, backup, change notification, incident reporting, audit-trail retention, access for inspections and exit/data return; the vendor should support customer audits and provide release notes and validation packages. Verifier: agreements are also needed with internal IT or group shared-service IT running the infrastructure or application (§3.1 treats IT departments like third parties), and with validation contractors, remote-maintenance providers and archive/retention providers. Showing owner roles in the application is a design choice.
verification_test: Check the quality agreement covers the listed topics; confirm the vendor audit report is on file with a risk-based rationale; confirm the system shows named process and system owners.
notes: MINOR correction: the line narrowed the agreement requirement to parties that 'supply or run' the system; §3.1 also covers integration, validation, remote maintenance, modification, retention and data processing, and treats internal IT departments like third parties.

requirement: User requirements must describe the functions the system needs, rest on a documented risk assessment and GMP-impact analysis, and stay traceable through the life cycle. Validation must evidence appropriate test methods and scenarios, paying special attention to limits on process parameters, limits on data values and how errors are handled; automated test tools and test environments need documented assessments of their adequacy.
system_implications: Maintain a URS-to-test traceability matrix for the system (§4.4); verifying each configured product/recipe is good practice beyond §4.4. The eBMR must enforce configured limits (warning vs action/reject limits for weights, in-process results, CPPs) and must handle errors deterministically (e.g., instrument disconnect, invalid barcode, double submission) - all of which must be tested, including boundary values. If automated/regression testing tools are used, keep an assessment of their fitness.
verification_test: Boundary tests on each critical limit (just inside, on, just outside); negative tests for error paths; review traceability matrix completeness; confirm the test-tool assessment exists.
notes: No change to the requirement. Implications: per-recipe traceability relabelled as beyond the clause.

requirement: The draft widens and hardens the audit trail rule: wherever users can create, modify or delete GMP data, the system must automatically log each such manual interaction, now including the creation of data and not only changes/deletions. Each entry should identify who acted (with role), what changed (previous and new value), when (with time zone where relevant) and why (the system should prompt for the reason). The audit trail is to be configured and switched on from installation and should not be possible to turn off, edit or delete; commentators note the draft still tolerates such functions being reachable only by administrators independent of GMP work.
system_implications: No configuration switch that disables auditing of GMP data in production; the audit log is append-only and tamper-evident (e.g., hash chaining); entries include creation events; each entry holds user ID, full name, role at the time, old value, new value, UTC timestamp plus local zone, and a prompted reason (controlled list plus free text). Any privileged maintenance that could affect audit data must itself be logged and restricted to admins with no GMP role. Keep data audit trails distinct from technical/system event logs so reviewers see GMP-relevant entries clearly.
verification_test: Create, modify and delete values as operator/supervisor/QA: confirm entries for all three event types with role, old/new, zone-aware time and reason; search the admin console and API for any disable/purge function; attempt direct DB edit and confirm tamper detection flags the chain break.

requirement: Per secondary analyses of the draft: audit trail review must be governed by a written procedure, performed by someone independent of the business process being reviewed, documented, and may be done as part of batch record review; discrepancies found must be investigated, resolved and escalated per a defined route; review frequency is risk-based, and QPs must be given access to the relevant audit trail entries.
system_implications: Build audit-trail review into the batch review workflow: a batch-scoped audit trail view that highlights GMP-critical changes (value changes after first entry, deletions, voids, late entries, re-opened steps, signature failures) with a 'reviewed' e-signature by a reviewer who did not execute the batch (system-enforced), a way to raise/link a deviation from any entry, and blocking of batch disposition while review is incomplete or discrepancies are open. Grant QP role read access to the complete audit trail. Provide validated exception reports so review focuses on meaningful events rather than every log line.
verification_test: Execute a batch with changes; attempt batch review sign-off by a user who executed steps (must be blocked); confirm the exception report lists all post-entry changes; confirm open discrepancy blocks disposition; confirm QP account can open the full audit trail for the batch.

requirement: According to published analyses, the draft no longer carries a stand-alone clause on QP batch certification by electronic signature (that topic is left to Annex 16); instead it requires that QPs can access audit trail entries. Until the draft is final, the 2011 clause 15 still applies.
system_implications: Keep the QP-only e-signature certification (A11-17) - it remains required today and remains good practice under Annex 16 - and additionally ensure the QP certification screen gives one-click access to the batch audit trail and review outcome. Do not design on the assumption that the QP e-signature control can be dropped.
verification_test: Confirm QP-only certification still enforced (see A11-17) and that the QP certification screen links to the full batch audit trail and audit-trail review record.

requirement: Per secondary analyses, the draft expects: the signer to re-authenticate when signing; the meaning of the signature (e.g., review, approval) to be clear to the signer at the time of signing; the displayed/printed signature to show the signer's name, role, meaning, and date/time with time zone where applicable; and, for hybrid set-ups where a handwritten signature relates to an electronic record, measures that give high confidence that any later change to the electronic record invalidates the signature. It also references use of external (trust service) e-signature providers.
system_implications: At signing: fresh credential entry (password/PIN, biometric or badge+PIN) even within an active session; the dialog states the meaning explicitly ('I verify the dispensed quantity of lot X'). Store meaning, role, UTC time and zone. Bind the signature to a hash of the signed content; if the content changes after signing, the system must automatically mark the signature invalid/superseded and require re-signing, and show the record as unsigned in the meantime. Avoid hybrid wet-ink signing on printouts of eBMR data; if unavoidable, link scanned signed pages to the electronic record version hash.
verification_test: Sign a record, then change a value: the prior signature must show as invalidated and the step must require re-signature. Confirm the signing dialog requires credential re-entry and shows meaning; inspect manifestation for name, role, meaning, date/time and zone on screen and PDF.

clause: 12 (Audit trails - timing of review relative to release)
requirement: Secondary summaries of the draft report that review of audit trails should be targeted and risk-based (not line-by-line), done by persons not involved in the reviewed activity, and completed before batch release unless a later review is justified; audit-trail review outcomes that bear directly on product release should be available to the QP when certifying.
system_implications: Batch disposition/QP certification must be blocked until the batch-scoped audit trail review is signed off (or a documented, approved justification for deferral exists). The QP certification screen must display the audit-trail review status, reviewer, date, findings and any linked deviations. Review scope rules (which event types, which data classes) should be configurable per product/process risk and version-controlled.
verification_test: Try to certify a batch with no audit-trail review record (must be blocked); record a justified deferral and confirm it requires QA approval and appears on the QP view; confirm reviewer independence is enforced.

requirement: The draft replaces the short 2011 security clause with a detailed identity and access management section. Reported expectations: unique personal accounts (shared accounts tolerated only for read-only use, never for creating or changing data); least privilege (no more rights than the job needs); segregation of duties so that people doing GMP work do not also hold administrator privileges; multi-factor authentication for remote access to critical systems; automatic lock-out after repeated failed log-ins; and controlled, timely handling and review of access rights.
system_implications: Enforce one identity per person (SSO/IdP integration allowed), no shared write-capable accounts, role catalogue with least-privilege defaults, hard separation between GMP roles and system-administration roles (system prevents a user holding both), MFA for any remote or vendor access, lock after a configurable number of failed attempts, idle-session lock on shop-floor clients, prompt deprovisioning on leaver events from HR/IdP, and a periodic access-recertification report listing each user, role, last login and approver.
verification_test: Try assigning an administrator role to a user holding operator/QA/QP roles (must be refused); exceed the failed-login threshold (account locks, event logged); connect remotely without second factor (refused); run access recertification report and confirm it lists all accounts with roles and last activity.

requirement: Alarms were not covered in 2011; the draft adds a dedicated section. Reported expectations: GMP-relevant alarms and their acknowledgements are logged automatically with full details; alarm handling and verification are documented (for example in the batch record) with a log that cannot be erased or deactivated; alarm logs are reviewed periodically for handling and trends. Alarm/event logs are distinct from the audit trail of manual data changes.
system_implications: The eBMR (or the connected SCADA/EMS feeding it) must bring GMP alarms occurring during a batch (e.g., out-of-limit temperature/humidity, pressure cascade loss, particle count excursions, compression force out of range, checkweigher rejects, sterilisation/depyrogenation cycle faults) into the batch context: time raised, time acknowledged, who acknowledged, comment/action, and link to deviation where required. Alarm limits are controlled configuration. Provide an alarm log per batch and trending across batches. Injectables: aseptic-area alarms (differential pressure, particle monitoring, isolator/RABS glove breach, filter integrity failures) will dominate and must be visible to reviewers and the QP.
verification_test: Generate a simulated out-of-limit event during a batch: confirm it appears in the batch alarm log with raise/ack times, acknowledger identity and comment; confirm acknowledgement without comment is prevented for GMP-critical alarms; confirm the log cannot be deleted; run the alarm trend report.

requirement: Reported to cover four themes: verification of input (plausibility checks for manually entered critical data, plus second-person or validated electronic verification); data transfer (preference for validated electronic interfaces over manual transcription, with manual transfer treated as an exception needing extra control); controlled and validated data migration; and risk-based encryption of critical data in storage and in transit.
system_implications: Field-level plausibility rules (type, range, format, expected lot/material match, unit consistency); direct capture from balances, PLCs, checkweighers, LIMS and environmental monitoring instead of manual typing wherever feasible; when manual transcription is unavoidable, force double verification and mark the value as manually transcribed; encryption at rest (database, backups, archives) and in transit (TLS for all clients and interfaces); validated migration tooling with reconciliation reports.
verification_test: Enter implausible values (wrong unit, out-of-range, wrong lot) and confirm rejection/warning; confirm interface-captured values are marked as such and cannot be overwritten without audit; confirm manually transcribed values require verification; confirm TLS on all endpoints and encryption of database files/backups.

requirement: Cyber/IT security becomes an explicit GMP expectation. Reported content: firewalls and network segmentation, timely patching, protection against malware, restrictions on removable media, disaster recovery with defined recovery time and recovery point objectives, isolation of unsupported/unpatched platforms, multi-factor authentication for remote access to critical systems, and (reported as draft 15.19) regular penetration testing of critical systems that are exposed to the internet.
system_implications: Vendor and customer must evidence a security baseline for the eBMR stack: supported OS/DB versions with patch SLAs, hardened shop-floor clients (kiosk mode, USB storage disabled), network zoning between OT (line PLCs) and IT, malware protection on servers/clients, documented RTO/RPO per module (a stricter RPO for the execution module during aseptic filling than for reporting), DR runbooks tested, and periodic penetration tests for internet-facing/SaaS deployments with remediation tracking.
verification_test: Review last penetration test report and remediation closure; attempt to mount USB storage on a shop-floor client (blocked); check patch levels against vendor support matrix; run a DR exercise and compare achieved recovery time/point to targets.

requirement: The draft expands both topics: backups must be kept physically and logically separate from the primary data and restore capability must be tested regularly; archiving receives its own, more detailed section than in 2011 (retention, protection and retrievability of archived records).
system_implications: Backups written to a separate site/account (immutable or write-once storage preferred so ransomware or an admin cannot alter them), encrypted, with scheduled restore tests whose results are recorded; archives read-only with fixity checks and retrieval tests across software versions (see A11-07, A11-19).
verification_test: Confirm backup target is on separate infrastructure/credentials; attempt deletion of a backup with production admin credentials (should fail if immutable); review restore-test log for the defined frequency; retrieve an archived record.

requirement: Periodic review grows from one sentence in 2011 to a section of about twelve sub-clauses. Secondary summaries mention review of system documentation, maintenance, service agreements, adequacy of backup, disaster recovery and archiving arrangements, data integrity status, changes in regulatory requirements, training effectiveness, and ongoing confirmation of validated status (a one-off qualification is not enough).
system_implications: Provide a periodic review dashboard/report pack generated from system data for a chosen period: changes and releases, open validation gaps, incidents and interface failures, user and privileged-access changes, audit-trail review completion rates, backup/restore and DR test results, supplier SLA performance, alarm statistics, training status of active users. Store the approved periodic review report and its actions in or linked to the system.
verification_test: Generate the pack for a test period and trace a sample of each metric to underlying records; confirm the pack covers each topic listed in the site's periodic review SOP mapped to draft section 14.

requirement: The regulated company stays fully responsible for GMP compliance even when a vendor, cloud/SaaS provider or internal IT runs the system. Suppliers and service providers must be qualified (audit as needed) and covered by written agreements/contracts that fix responsibilities, including data ownership and access, security, communication of security issues, support during inspections, and an exit strategy; complete validation documentation must be accessible for cloud services.
system_implications: For a SaaS eBMR: contractual right to audit, inspection support, notification of security incidents and planned changes, data residency and ownership, return/export of all records with audit trails and signatures in a readable format on exit, and access to the provider's qualification and validation evidence. The product should support a full, validated export of the customer's data set to make the exit clause workable.
verification_test: Review the contract/quality agreement against the listed elements; perform a trial full export of a test tenant and re-open batch records with audit trails and signatures in the export viewer.

requirement: If AI/ML is used in a critical GMP function, the draft limits it to static, deterministic models and expects a precisely defined intended use, predefined performance/acceptance metrics, representative test data kept independent of training data, explainability and confidence information for outputs, change control, and ongoing performance monitoring; generative AI/LLMs only for non-critical tasks with a human in the loop.
system_implications: Keep AI out of GMP decision paths in the eBMR (e.g., no AI auto-approval of steps, deviations or release) unless the model is static, validated and governed as above. Any AI helper (e.g., drafting deviation text, summarising a batch for the reviewer, visual inspection of tablets or vials) must be flagged as such, its output must be reviewed and signed by a human, and the model version and confidence must be recorded with the output. Injectables: AI-based automated visual inspection of filled units would be a critical application needing full Annex 22-style validation.
verification_test: Inventory all AI/ML features; confirm none can change GMP data or status without human e-signature; for any critical-use model, confirm locked version, documented test set independence, acceptance metrics and monitoring records.

source: EU GMP Chapter 4 Documentation - draft revision (July 2025)
clause: Data governance and data lifecycle (reported as 4.12 onward)
requirement: The draft requires a data governance system, integrated in the PQS and applying whatever the format (paper, electronic, hybrid), covering the whole data lifecycle - reported as creation, processing, verification, decision-making, retention and controlled destruction - and treating metadata and audit trails as part of the record, with defined ownership.
system_implications: Model each eBMR data element with its lifecycle state (captured, verified, reviewed, used for decision/released, archived, eligible for destruction) and keep metadata (units, instrument ID, method/recipe version, user, time, context) inseparable from the value. Destruction at end of retention must be an authorised, recorded act.
verification_test: Trace one critical value from capture through verification, review, QP decision and archive, confirming metadata and audit trail travel with it; confirm destruction requires authorisation and leaves a destruction record.

source: EU GMP Chapter 4 Documentation - draft revision (July 2025)
requirement: Per secondary summaries, the draft gives hybrid (paper plus electronic) systems specific attention: they must be clearly defined, validated and risk-controlled, with procedures for the hand-offs between manual and computerised parts; the draft also expressly recognises electronic signatures in GMP documentation.
system_implications: Minimise hybrid steps in the eBMR; where they remain (downtime sheets, external lab certificates, instrument printouts), the system must record the linkage (scan, unique ID, who attached, when), verify completeness (all issued sheets returned) and prevent the paper and electronic versions from diverging. Electronic signatures should be the default signing method everywhere in the batch record.
verification_test: Run a hybrid scenario (downtime sheet); confirm issuance log, return reconciliation, scan attachment with audit trail and second-person verification of transcribed values.

source: EMA GMP Q&A on data integrity (Aug 2016)
clause: Q&A on assessing data risk / data lifecycle
requirement: Data risk should be judged by how exposed the data are to accidental or intentional amendment, deletion or re-creation; controls that stop unauthorised actions or make them more visible/detectable reduce risk. The assessment should focus on the business process (production, QC) and factors such as complexity, consistency, degree of automation vs human input, and subjectivity of outcomes, at every lifecycle stage. Holding data in temporary memory before it is saved is flagged as a risk because changes there are often not audit-trailed; removing or shortening such temporary storage lowers the risk.
