They normally cover: product name; dosage form, strength and (where relevant) method of application; pack size by count, weight or volume; a complete list of packaging materials for a standard batch with quantities, sizes, types and each material's specification code; where appropriate a specimen of the printed packaging material showing where batch number and expiry date go; special precautions including line-clearance checks of the area and equipment before and after packaging; a description of the operation, subsidiary operations and equipment; and in-process controls with sampling instructions and acceptance limits.
system_implications: Master packaging record (MPR) is a separate approved object per product x pack size x pack type, linked to the MBR; it stores a packaging bill of materials with spec codes and an image of each approved artwork with the coding positions marked; line-clearance checklists before and after; IPC definitions with sampling plan and limits.
verification_test: Create two pack sizes for one product and confirm each needs its own approved MPR; confirm a packaging order cannot start unless the MPR has artwork specimens attached for every printed component.
notes: confirmed in official text (matches WHO 15.23 and EU 4.19).

requirement: A batch processing record is kept for every batch, built from the currently approved documents, prepared so as to avoid errors (copying or validated computer programs are recommended; transcription from approved documents is to be avoided). Before processing, a recorded check confirms that equipment and workstation are free of previous products, documents and materials and that equipment is clean and suitable. During processing each item is recorded when the action is taken, and on completion the record is dated and signed by the person responsible for processing. Items: product name; batch number; dates and times of starting significant intermediate stages and of completing production; name of the person responsible for each stage; initials of operators of significant steps and, where appropriate, of checkers (e.g., weighing); batch or analytical control number and actual quantity of each starting material weighed, including any recovered or reprocessed material added; relevant operations, events and major equipment; permitted hold time for intermediate and in-process material; IPCs with performer initials and results; yields at pertinent stages with explanations of significant deviations from expected yield; notes on special problems with signed authorisation for any departure from the master formula.
system_implications: This is the core eBMR content model. Generate the batch record electronically from the approved MBR (no re-typing); capture timestamps at stage start and batch completion; person-responsible per stage plus performer and verifier identities per step; lot/AR number and actual weight per material including recovered material flag; equipment IDs; hold-time start/stop with limit check; IPC results with performer; stage yields with mandatory comment when outside limits; deviation notes with authorisation signature; final signature of the person responsible for processing.
verification_test: Execute a batch end-to-end and confirm the rendered record contains every listed item; enter an out-of-limit stage yield and confirm a comment and deviation link are forced; exceed a hold time and confirm the system blocks or raises a deviation; confirm the completed record carries the dated signature of the processing-responsible person.
notes: confirmed in official text. Mostly equal to WHO/EU 4.20 and FDA 211.188; the hold-time item and the 'person responsible for each stage' are explicit Indian additions.

requirement: A batch packaging record is kept for each batch or part-batch packed, based on the approved packaging instructions and prepared to avoid errors (copying or validated computer programs recommended). Before packaging, a recorded check confirms equipment and workstation are clear of previous products, documents and materials and are clean and suitable. Each item is recorded when the action happens, with date and responsible person identified by signature or electronic password: product name, batch number and bulk quantity to be packed, finished-product batch number, planned and actual quantity and the reconciliation; date and time of packaging operations; name of the responsible person; initials of operators of significant steps; identity and conformity checks against the instructions including IPC results; details of operations, equipment and lines, plus instructions or records for unpacked product returned to store; where possible, samples of printed packaging materials used, including specimens showing print approval and periodic checks of batch number, expiry date and overprinting; notes on special problems and deviations with written authorisation; and quantities and reference numbers of all printed materials and bulk issued, used, destroyed or returned, and product obtained, allowing a proper reconciliation.
system_implications: Separate eBPR per packaging batch or part-batch linked to the bulk batch; electronic identification of the signer is expressly acceptable ('electronic password'); scanned or photographed specimens of printed materials (carton, label, foil) with the coded batch/expiry/MRP overprint captured at start and at intervals; component issue/use/destroy/return ledger with automatic reconciliation.
verification_test: Run a packaging order with two part-batches and confirm two linked packaging records; attach coding specimens at start, mid-run and end; enter issue/used/destroyed/returned quantities that do not balance and confirm the record cannot close without an investigation reference.
notes: confirmed in official text (matches WHO 15.26 and EU 4.21 closely; 'signature or electronic password' wording is WHO's).

requirement: An SOP must define the batch (lot) numbering system so each intermediate, bulk and finished batch has its own number; processing and packaging numbering must be related; numbers must never be reused, including for reprocessing; each allocation must be recorded at once (e.g., in a logbook) with at least the allocation date, product identity and batch size.
system_implications: Configurable batch-number generator with a global uniqueness constraint per site (never recycled, even after cancellation), a rule linking bulk and packaging batch numbers, and an allocation register storing date, product and batch size.
verification_test: Cancel a batch and confirm its number is never reissued; attempt manual entry of an existing number and confirm rejection; export the allocation register and confirm the three required fields.
notes: confirmed in official text

clause: Part I, 18.2.2 (deviations) and 18.5.12 (batch record review and failure investigation)
requirement: Departures from instructions or procedures should be avoided; where they happen they must follow an approved procedure and be authorised in writing by a designated person, with QC involvement where appropriate. Production records must be reviewed as part of batch-release approval before going to the authorised person. Any divergence or specification failure must be investigated thoroughly, extended where needed to other batches and products, and written up with conclusion and follow-up.
system_implications: Deviation workflow: capture at point of occurrence, authorisation e-signature by a designated role (optionally with QC co-approval), impact assessment that can list other affected batches/products, conclusion and follow-up actions; production review step as a mandatory state before AP review.
verification_test: Raise a deviation and confirm it needs designated-person approval before the step can continue; confirm the batch cannot move to AP review until production review is signed; add linked batches to an investigation and confirm they are flagged.
notes: confirmed in official text

requirement: Yield checks and reconciliation of quantities must be done as needed to show no discrepancy outside acceptable limits. Any significant deviation from expected yield must be recorded and investigated. Any significant or unusual discrepancy found when reconciling bulk, printed packaging materials and units produced must be investigated, explained and recorded before release.
system_implications: Automatic yield calculation at each stage against MBR limits; automatic reconciliation of printed components and bulk; out-of-limit results open a deviation that blocks release until closed.
verification_test: Enter a stage yield below the lower limit and a carton reconciliation with a 2% unexplained loss (above configured limit); confirm deviations open automatically and release is blocked.
notes: confirmed in official text

requirement: Throughout processing, materials, bulk containers, major equipment and, where appropriate, rooms and packaging lines must show the product, strength and batch number, and the stage where applicable; recording the previous product can help. Before any processing or packaging, the area, lines, printers and equipment must be checked clean and free of earlier products, materials, labels and documents; packaging line clearance follows a procedure and checklist and is recorded. Needed in-process and environmental controls must be done and recorded. Each packaging station or line must display the product name and batch number.
system_implications: Room/line/equipment status model (in use by product X batch Y, cleaned, to be cleaned) with printable or on-screen status labels; electronic line-clearance checklist as a gating step before and after each operation, recording the previous product; environmental readings captured into the batch record.
verification_test: Try to start compression or packaging on a line whose status is 'to be cleaned' and confirm it is blocked; complete line clearance and confirm the checklist, signer, time and previous product appear in the batch record.
notes: confirmed in official text

requirement: Labelling should follow filling and sealing quickly, or controls must prevent mix-ups. Any printing of codes or expiry dates, on-line or separate, must be checked and recorded, and hand printing re-checked at intervals. Extra care is needed with cut labels, off-line overprinting and hand packing; electronic code readers, label counters and similar devices must be checked for correct operation, and manual labelling needs more frequent checks. Printed or embossed information must be distinct and fade-resistant. On-line checks must at least cover pack appearance, completeness, correct product and materials, correct overprint and working line monitors; samples taken off the line are not returned. Product from an unusual event goes back only after inspection, investigation and approval, with a detailed record. After packaging, unused batch-coded materials are destroyed with a record; uncoded printed materials go back to stock only after documented checks.
system_implications: Packaging IPC schedule with configurable frequency (tighter for manual labelling); challenge-test records for vision systems, barcode/2D-code readers and counters at start, intervals and end; coding verification entries; 'unusual event' sub-workflow; destruction record for coded leftovers; controlled return-to-stock for uncoded items.
verification_test: Configure a start-of-run camera/reader challenge and confirm packaging cannot begin until it passes; record a reader failure mid-run and confirm product since the last good challenge is placed on hold; close the order with coded cartons outstanding and confirm a destruction entry is required.
notes: confirmed in official text

clause: Part I, 14.14, 14.16-14.20 (dispensing and use of starting materials)
requirement: Only starting materials released by QC and within shelf life may be used. There must be means of confirming the identity of the contents of every container, and sampled bulk containers must be identified. Dispensing is done only by designated persons under a written procedure, into clean, properly labelled containers, with accurate weighing or measuring. Each dispensed material and its weight or volume must be independently checked and recorded. Materials dispensed for a batch are kept together and clearly labelled as such.
system_implications: Dispensing module: container-level barcode identity check; hard block on status other than 'released' and on expired or past-retest lots; role check for designated dispensers; second-person verification or validated balance interface for every weighing; dispensed-kit labels linking to the batch.
verification_test: Scan a quarantined lot, an expired lot and a lot past retest date and confirm all are refused; weigh without a verifier and confirm the step cannot be signed unless the balance is a validated interface configured as the independent check.
notes: confirmed in official text (FDA 211.101(c)-(d) has an equivalent second-person or automated check).

requirement: Reworking or recovering rejected product must be exceptional, allowed only if final quality is unaffected and specifications are met, and done under a defined, authorised procedure after risk evaluation; a record is kept and the reworked batch gets a new batch number. Adding all or part of earlier conforming batches into a batch of the same product at a defined stage must be authorised in advance, follow a defined procedure after risk evaluation (including shelf-life impact) and be recorded. QC must consider extra testing of any finished product that was reprocessed, reworked or contains recovered product.
system_implications: Rework is modelled as a new batch with a new number and parent-child genealogy to the rejected batch(es), a rework MBR or approved protocol, and a risk assessment reference; recovered-material additions are pre-authorised steps that record source batch numbers and quantities and feed the shelf-life/expiry assignment logic; QC flag for additional testing.
verification_test: Rework a rejected batch and confirm the system forces a new batch number, links genealogy to the parent, and requires an approved rework procedure and risk assessment; add recovered material without pre-authorisation and confirm the step is blocked.
notes: confirmed in official text. The mandatory new batch number for a reworked batch comes from WHO; neither 21 CFR 211.115 nor EU Chapter 5 (5.62-5.64) requires a new number, so this is the stricter rule for Indian products.

clause: Part I, 14.15 (release of non-API raw materials without batch testing)
requirement: QC may release raw materials other than APIs for manufacturing without specific batch testing, but only on the basis of vendor approval and statistical analysis of earlier test results for that material.
system_implications: Material status engine must support a 'released on vendor history' route for non-API excipients with the statistical justification stored. Because FDA 211.84(d) requires at least an identity test per lot and EU Chapter 5 expects identity testing of every batch/container, a per-market rule must force an identity test for lots destined for FDA/EU-market batches, and the dispensing check must block such lots from those batches.
verification_test: Release an excipient lot without testing under the vendor-history rule, then try to dispense it into a batch whose target markets include the US or EU; confirm the system blocks it until an identity result exists.
notes: confirmed in official text. This is a relaxation compared with FDA/EU, so the stricter foreign rule must win for exported products.

clause: Part I, 14.13 (labelling of starting materials) and 14.10-14.12, 14.23-14.25 (receipt and packaging materials)
requirement: Stored starting-material labels must show at least the designated name and internal code, the supplier's batch number and the manufacturer's own control or batch number, the status (quarantine, on test, released, rejected, returned or recalled) and, where appropriate, an expiry or retest date; with fully validated computerised storage systems, not all of this needs to be human-readable on the label. Each batch within a delivery is treated separately for sampling, testing and release. Each delivery or batch of printed or primary packaging material gets its own reference number, and packaging materials are checked on delivery to the packaging area for quantity, identity and conformity with the instructions.
system_implications: If the eBMR or its warehouse module is validated, labels may carry only a barcode or 2D code plus minimal text, with status held in the system; the system is then the authority for material status, so status changes must be audit-trailed and e-signed.
verification_test: Print a barcode-only label for a released lot, scan it at dispensing and confirm name, lot, status and retest date are shown from the system; change status to rejected and confirm the next scan blocks use.
notes: confirmed in official text

clause: Part I, 17.3.1 (labels of finished drugs, reference standards and containers)
requirement: Every finished drug must be labelled with at least: drug name; active ingredients (with INNs) and amount of each, plus net contents; the manufacturer's batch number; expiry date and date of manufacture in uncoded form; any special storage or handling conditions; directions for use, warnings and precautions; and the name and address of the manufacturer or the company or person placing it on the market. Labels on containers, equipment or premises must be clear, unambiguous and in the company's format, optionally colour-coded for status.
system_implications: The packaging record must capture and verify, per pack level, the printed batch number, date of manufacture and expiry date in plain (uncoded) form. Date of manufacture is mandatory on Indian labels (WHO only requires expiry), so artwork templates for India need a Mfg. date field that is optional for EU/US-only packs.
verification_test: Load an India artwork template lacking a manufacturing-date field and confirm MPR approval fails; confirm coding verification in the eBPR checks both manufacturing and expiry dates against batch data.
notes: confirmed in official text. Adding 'date of manufacture' to the WHO list is an Indian change; Rule 96 of the Drugs Rules separately requires it on the label.

clause: Part II (sterile products), 4.1-4.6 and Table 1 (clean-area grades and particle limits)
requirement: Sterile manufacture uses four grades (A-D) classified to ISO standards. Table 1 sets maximum particles per cubic metre, at rest and in operation, for sizes of 0.5 and 5.0 micrometres. Grade A: 3,520 and 20 in both states. Grade B: 3,520 and 29 at rest; 352,000 and 2,900 in operation. Grade C: 352,000 and 2,900 at rest; 3,520,000 and 29,000 in operation. Grade D: 3,520,000 and 29,000 at rest; not defined in operation. Grade A unidirectional air must run at about 0.36-0.54 m/s (guidance) measured 15-30 cm below the terminal filter, never below 0.36 m/s at working level, shown by airflow visualisation. Classification is kept separate from routine monitoring.
system_implications: Room and zone master data carry a grade and the limit table; EM results imported into the batch record are checked against grade limits. Because EU Annex 1 (2022) uses different values (e.g., 5.0 micrometre limits at Grade A 'not specified' but trended; Grade C/D 2,930/29,300), the limit table must be market-configurable, and for EU-market batches the EU 2022 values and rules apply.
verification_test: Load Indian and EU limit sets; import a Grade B in-operation 5.0 micrometre count of 3,000/m3 and confirm it exceeds the Indian limit (2,900) and is evaluated under the EU set (2,930) for an EU batch; confirm grade A velocity readings below 0.36 m/s are flagged.
notes: confirmed in official text (table values reassembled from scattered cells; they match the WHO TRS 961 Annex 6 / pre-2022 EU Annex 1 table). The minimum working-level velocity sentence appears to be an Indian addition.

clause: Part II, 4.7-4.10 and Table 3 (environmental monitoring; microbial limits)
requirement: Clean rooms must be monitored in operation at risk-based locations. Grade A needs particle monitoring for the whole of critical processing, including equipment assembly (with stated exceptions), capturing interventions and transient events and alarming on alert-limit excursions; Grade B uses a similar system at lower frequency. Recovery ('clean-up') after operations of about 15-20 minutes to the at-rest limits. Microbial monitoring (settle plates, active air, contact plates, swabs, glove prints) must be frequent during aseptic work, and monitoring results must be considered when reviewing batch documentation for release. Recommended in-operation microbial limits (average values): Grade A under 1 CFU for air per m3, 4-hour settle plate, contact plate and 5-finger glove print; Grade B 10, 5, 5, 5; Grade C 100, 50, 25; Grade D 200, 100, 50. Alert and action limits must be set; exceeding action limits or an adverse alert trend triggers investigation and CAPA per SOP.
system_implications: The injectables batch record must pull or link EM data (non-viable continuous Grade A counts, viable results by location and session) for the batch's processing window and show excursions to the reviewer; release must be blocked until EM results for the filling window are complete and reviewed. Limits must be configurable per market because EU Annex 1 (2022) requires 'no growth' at Grade A, where any growth needs investigation.
verification_test: Record a Grade A settle plate of 1 CFU during a fill: under the Indian table it breaches '<1' and under the EU set it breaches 'no growth'; confirm both raise an excursion linked to the batch and that release is blocked until the investigation is closed. Confirm release is blocked while any viable plate from the filling window is still incubating.
notes: confirmed in official text; table cells reassembled from scattered lines. EU 2022 Annex 1 is stricter on Grade A viable results and on contamination control strategy.

clause: Part II, 5.3-5.7 (process simulation / media fills) and 4.11 (hold times and fill duration)
requirement: Aseptic processing must be validated by media fills: three consecutive successful runs initially, repeated at defined intervals and after significant HVAC, equipment or process changes, simulating routine steps, normal and worst-case interventions and each shift and shift change. Container numbers must allow valid evaluation and, for small batches, at least equal the batch size. Target is zero growth; acceptance: under 5,000 units no contaminated unit; 5,000-10,000 units one contaminated unit means investigation and possible repeat, two means revalidation after investigation; over 10,000 units one means investigation, two means revalidation. Intermittent contamination at any size must be investigated, and gross failures must consider impact on batches made since the last good media fill. Media fills are also used to set processing hold times and the maximum fill duration.
system_implications: The eBMR must record, per aseptic batch, which line and qualified media-fill envelope it ran within (fill duration, hold times, interventions performed, operators and shifts), and block or flag batches whose duration, interventions or personnel fall outside the last successful media fill. A media-fill failure must be able to query all batches since the last passing run. Acceptance must be market-configurable: EU Annex 1 (2022) treats any contaminated unit as a failed simulation.
verification_test: Run a batch with fill duration longer than the qualified maximum and confirm a deviation; record an intervention type not simulated in the media fill and confirm it is flagged; mark a media fill failed and confirm the system lists all batches filled on that line since the previous successful run.
notes: confirmed in official text. Indian acceptance matches FDA 2004 aseptic guidance and WHO 2011, but is less strict than EU Annex 1 (2022); requalification frequency is only 'defined intervals' (EU and FDA expect about every six months per line/shift).

clause: Part II, 5.12-5.17 (processing time limits, bioburden, endotoxins) and 2.4
requirement: The processing stage of cleaned components, bulk containers and equipment must be identified. The intervals from washing/drying to sterilisation and from sterilisation to use must be as short as possible and within validated time limits. The time from starting solution preparation to sterilisation or sterile filtration must be as short as possible, with a maximum permitted time set for each product. Purge or blanket gases must pass a sterilising filter. Bioburden must be tested before sterilisation on every batch for both aseptic and terminally sterilised products (scheduled intervals allowed only for overkill cycles; each batch as an IPC for parametric release), against working limits; endotoxins monitored where appropriate. WFI, relevant intermediates and finished injectables must be monitored for endotoxins by a validated pharmacopoeial method; for LVPs, water or intermediate monitoring is always required.
system_implications: Timers in the injectables MBR: wash-to-sterilise, sterilise-to-use and preparation-start-to-filtration, each with product-specific maximums and hard alarms; a mandatory pre-sterilisation bioburden sample step per batch with result entry and limit check; endotoxin test steps; component/equipment status identification by processing stage.
verification_test: Let the preparation-to-filtration timer exceed the product maximum and confirm a deviation is forced; try to close the batch without a bioburden result and confirm it is blocked; for an LVP product confirm an endotoxin step on water or intermediate cannot be removed from the MBR.
notes: confirmed in official text (WHO 2011-derived; EU 2022 and FDA have equivalent expectations).

requirement: All sterilisation processes must be validated, with effectiveness in every part of each load type shown by physical measurements and, where appropriate, biological indicators, and re-verified at least once a year and after significant equipment changes. Validated loading patterns are required. Every carrier (basket, tray) must be labelled with material name, batch number and sterilised/not-sterilised status. A sterilisation record must exist for every run and be approved as part of batch release. Heat cycles are recorded on suitably accurate equipment with the probe at the validated coolest point, preferably checked against an independent second probe; temperature and pressure both monitored; control instruments independent of monitoring; automated control/monitoring validated; system and cycle faults registered by the system and seen by the operator; vacuum-phase chambers leak-tested regularly. For EO, each cycle records time, pressure, temperature, humidity and gas concentration with a continuous pressure/temperature chart and biological indicators; radiation dose is measured by dosimeters; these records form part of the batch record. Cooling fluids contacting product must be sterile.
system_implications: Steriliser/autoclave/depyrogenation tunnel integration: import each cycle report (cycle ID, load pattern ID, recorder trace, min/max temperature at coolest probe, pressure, F0 where used, alarms) into the batch record; mandatory reviewer sign-off of each cycle before batch release; validated load pattern chosen from a list; annual requalification date checked before the steriliser can be selected; carrier labels printed with batch and status.
verification_test: Select a steriliser whose annual requalification has lapsed and confirm it is blocked; import a cycle report with an alarm and confirm the batch cannot be released until the cycle is reviewed and the alarm dispositioned; confirm the release checklist lists every sterilisation cycle used by the batch.
notes: confirmed in official text. 'At least annually' revalidation matches EU Annex 1 expectations; FDA also expects periodic requalification.

clause: Part II, 6.11.2 (aseptic processing and sterile filtration)
requirement: Aseptic processing must control environment, personnel, critical surfaces, container/closure sterilisation and transfer, the maximum holding time of product before filling, and the sterilising filter. Solutions that cannot be terminally sterilised may be filtered through a 0.22 micrometre (or equivalent) sterile filter into sterilised containers; filtration alone is not enough when terminal sterilisation is possible. A second (redundant) filtration just before filling may be advisable; the final filter should be as close to the fill point as possible; filters must not shed fibres (asbestos filters banned). Filter integrity must be checked before use and confirmed immediately after use (bubble point, diffusion or pressure hold); filtration time for a known volume and the pressure difference are set during validation, with significant routine differences noted and investigated, and the results go into the batch record. Critical vent filters are confirmed after use. The same filter may not be used for more than one working day unless validated.
system_implications: Filtration step template: filter ID/lot, pre-use and post-use integrity results (with instrument printout or data import), filtration start/stop time and differential pressure compared with validated ranges, vent filter post-use test, filter-use duration check against 'one working day'. Hold-time timer from end of compounding to end of filling.
verification_test: Enter a failing post-use integrity result and confirm the batch is put on hold and a deviation opens; reuse a filter ID on a second day without a validated extended-use flag and confirm it is blocked; enter a filtration time outside the validated range and confirm the system requires an investigation note.
notes: confirmed in official text. EU Annex 1 (2022) additionally requires pre-use post-sterilisation integrity testing (PUPSIT) unless justified by risk assessment; apply that for EU-market products.

clause: Part II, 2.1-2.3 (sterility testing and release) and 4.8
requirement: The sterility test is only the last of a series of controls and must be validated for the product using pharmacopoeial methods. Sterility samples must represent the whole batch and include the riskiest parts: for aseptic fills, containers from the start and end of the batch and after any significant interruption; for heat-sterilised products, the potentially coolest part of the load. Batch processing records, and for aseptic processing the environmental records, must be examined together with sterility results. Parametric release, where authorised, needs special attention to validation and monitoring of the whole process.
system_implications: The batch record must mark sterility sample pull points (start, end, after each significant interruption, coolest load position) and record which units were pulled; the release review screen must present processing record, EM data and sterility result together; a parametric-release mode only if the product licence permits it.
verification_test: Log a significant interruption during filling and confirm the system adds a mandatory sterility sample pull after restart; confirm release review cannot be signed unless the sterility result, EM summary and processing record have each been opened and acknowledged.
notes: confirmed in official text

clause: Part II, 10.3-10.8 (finishing: capping, vacuum-sealed containers, inspection) and Part I 11.5.1
requirement: Cap crimping generates particles and needs a separate station with extraction; if capping is done outside the aseptic core, vials must stay under Grade A air until crimped; vials with missing or displaced stoppers are rejected before capping, and human intervention at capping must avoid direct contact. Vacuum-sealed containers must be tested for maintained vacuum after a set period. Every filled parenteral container must be inspected individually for extraneous contamination or defects; visual inspection needs controlled lighting and background, inspectors must pass regular eyesight checks (with their own corrective lenses) and get frequent breaks; automated inspection must be validated and its performance checked at intervals; results must be recorded. Staff doing visual inspection must also have periodic eye checks under Part I.
system_implications: 100% inspection step recording inspector identity, booth/lighting check, start/stop times (break enforcement), quantities inspected and rejects by defect category; inspector qualification (eye test and inspection qualification) checked against personnel records before sign-on; automated inspection machine challenge-set results at intervals; stopper-presence reject counts before capping; vacuum-hold test results for vacuum-sealed packs.
verification_test: Assign an inspector whose eyesight check has expired and confirm sign-on is refused; run manual inspection beyond the configured continuous-inspection time and confirm a break prompt/hold; skip an interval challenge on the automated inspection machine and confirm the lot is flagged.
notes: confirmed in official text; equivalent to EU Annex 1 (2022) 8.30-8.33 and FDA expectations. Part II clauses 10.1-10.2 (closure integrity of fusion-sealed and other containers) were not found in the extracted text.

clause: Part VIII (oral solid dosage forms), 3.3-3.8 (compression in-process controls)
requirement: Calibrated weighing equipment must be at hand for in-process tablet weight checks, with procedures able to catch out-of-limit tablets. At the start of each compression run, and for multi-station or multi-point machines at fixed intervals, enough individual tablets must be examined so that each station/point is checked for pharmacopoeial parameters (appearance, weight variation, disintegration, hardness, friability, thickness), with results recorded in the batch documentation. During compression, samples must be taken at intervals of no more than thirty minutes against the in-process specification, with periodic checks of the same parameters plus contamination by lubricating oil. Tablets must be de-dusted (preferably automatically) and checked for foreign matter and defects, collected in clean labelled containers, and rejected or discarded tablets must be kept in identified containers with their quantity recorded in the BMR.
system_implications: Compression step template with: start-of-run per-station/per-punch checks; an IPC timer that forces a sample entry at most every 30 minutes (configurable downward, never upward for India-market products); parameter set configurable per pharmacopoeia (IP/BP/USP limits for weight variation, DT, friability, hardness and thickness as in-house limits); balance calibration status check; reject/discard tablet quantities recorded and included in yield reconciliation; lubricant-oil contamination check field.
verification_test: Run compression for 45 minutes without an IPC entry and confirm the system raises a missed-IPC alarm/deviation at 30 minutes; for a 16-station press confirm the start-of-run check cannot be signed until each station has a result; confirm rejected tablet quantity feeds the yield calculation.
notes: confirmed in official text. The fixed maximum 30-minute IPC interval and the named parameter list are Indian specifics; FDA 211.110 and EU Chapter 5 leave frequency to the firm.

requirement: Critical operating parameters such as time and temperature for every mixing, blending and drying step must be set in the master formula, monitored during processing and recorded in the batch record. Unless closed, mixing, sifting and blending equipment needs dust extraction or a dedicated area. Sieve residues must be examined periodically for foreign material. Fluid-bed drier filter bags must be washed between products, and product-dedicated for certain highly potent or sensitising products; inlet air must be filtered. Granulation and coating solutions must be made, stored and used so as to limit contamination and microbial growth. All dry ingredients are sifted before use (normally in dedicated areas) unless input quality is assured. A metal detector is recommended, wooden equipment is to be avoided, and screens, sieves, punches and dies must be checked for wear or breakage before and after each use.
system_implications: MBR step types for sifting, dry mixing, granulation, drying (FBD/tray), blending and lubrication with typed CPP fields (time, temperature, impeller/chopper speed, inlet/outlet air temperature, LOD) and limits; FBD filter-bag ID and product-dedication check; sieve integrity check before and after use with sieve ID and mesh; punch and die inspection record before and after each use; metal-detector challenge records; solution preparation time and hold-time limits.
verification_test: Enter a drying outlet temperature outside the MBR range and confirm a deviation prompt; try to use an FBD bag registered to another product and confirm it is blocked unless a washing record exists (or blocked outright for a dedicated-bag product); confirm the sieve integrity check is required both before and after sifting.
notes: confirmed in official text. Before-and-after-use checks of sieves, punches and dies and the explicit FBD-bag rule are more prescriptive than FDA or EU texts.

clause: Part VIII, 4 (coating), 5 (capsule filling), 6 (printing of tablets and capsules)
requirement: Air supplied to coating pans for drying must be filtered and of suitable quality, with exhaust and temperature/humidity control in the area. Coating solutions and suspensions are made fresh and used so as to minimise microbial growth, and their preparation and use are documented. Empty capsule shells count as a drug component and must be stored away from excess heat and moisture. Printing on tablets or capsules needs special care against mix-ups, with segregation if different products or batches are printed at the same time, edible-grade colours and suitable inks; printed tablets or capsules must be approved by QC before release for packaging or sale.
system_implications: Coating step template recording solution preparation time, use-by time, spray rate, inlet/exhaust temperatures and room temperature/RH; capsule shells handled as a component lot with storage-condition checks; a QC approval gate between tablet/capsule printing and packaging.
verification_test: Try to use coating suspension past its configured use-by time and confirm it is blocked; confirm a packaging order for a printed tablet cannot start until a QC approval of the printed bulk is recorded.
notes: confirmed in official text. The QC approval gate after printing is an explicit Indian requirement not found in FDA/EU text.

requirement: Automatic counting, strip and blister machines must be cleared of every 'rogue' tablet, capsule or foil before a new packaging operation, and an independent, recorded check of the equipment is required before a new batch is handled. Uncoated tablets are packed on equipment designed to limit cross-contamination, in an isolated area for potent or beta-lactam tablets. Strips leaving the machine are inspected for misprints, cut foil, missing tablets and poor sealing. Strip and blister pocket integrity must be checked periodically by a vacuum (leak) test, with records.
system_implications: Line-clearance for blister/strip lines needs a second, independent verifier signature (different user from the performer); packaging IPC template with defect categories (misprint, foil cut, empty pocket, seal) and a periodic leak-test step with frequency, sample size and pass/fail; product attributes 'uncoated', 'potent', 'beta-lactam' drive line/area eligibility.
verification_test: Attempt to sign both 'performed' and 'verified' for blister line clearance with the same user and confirm refusal; skip the scheduled leak test and confirm the packaging record flags a missed IPC; try to schedule a beta-lactam product on a non-isolated line and confirm it is blocked.
notes: confirmed in official text. The independent recorded equipment check and periodic vacuum leak testing of blisters are explicit Indian rules; FDA/EU cover them only generally.

clause: Part VIII, 1.5, 1.14, 1.17, 1.25, 1.27-1.28 (pressure cascades, temperature and humidity)
requirement: Where rooms are designed with pressure differentials, these must be monitored regularly and any deviation reported at once to Production and QA. Pressure-differential limits of adjacent rooms must not overlap. Pressure control and monitoring devices must be calibrated and qualified, compliance verified regularly and recorded, and alarms set from risk analysis. Room pressure indicators must show normal range and alert/action limits at the point of reading. Where relevant, temperature and relative humidity must be controlled, monitored and recorded, with alert and action limits.
system_implications: Tablets eBMR steps carry room ID and capture differential pressure, temperature and RH at start (and during long steps), manually or from the BMS/EMS, compared with room-specific alert/action limits; excursions notify Production and QA and link to the batch as a deviation; product-specific humidity limits for moisture-sensitive products.
verification_test: Enter a differential pressure below the action limit at a compression start and confirm the step is blocked or a deviation is opened and QA/Production are notified; confirm RH captured during granulation is printed in the batch record.
notes: confirmed in official text (drawn from WHO HVAC guidance for non-sterile products); FDA/EU expect similar control but without this detail.

clause: Part I, 17.3.10.5, 17.3.10.16-17.3.10.17 (equipment SOPs and logs) and 18.4.3, 18.4.9 (equipment failure, calibration)
requirement: Each instrument and piece of equipment needs SOPs (use, calibration, cleaning, maintenance) kept close to it. Records must be kept for major and critical equipment of validations, calibrations, maintenance, cleaning and repairs with dates and who did them, and use of major/critical equipment and of processing areas must be logged in chronological order. There must be a means of signalling equipment or utility failures; defective equipment is withdrawn until fixed; equipment is cleaned promptly after use and stored clean and dry. Measuring, weighing, recording and control instruments are serviced and calibrated at set intervals with records, checked daily or before use for analytical tests, and labelled with the calibration date and next due date.
system_implications: Electronic equipment and room logbooks populated automatically from batch execution (who, what product/batch, start/end, cleaning, maintenance), chronological and non-editable except via audited corrections; equipment status (qualified, calibrated, cleaned, out of service) checked before any step can use it; daily balance verification records; calibration due-date blocking.
verification_test: Use a balance whose calibration is past due and confirm the weighing step is blocked; mark a blender 'out of service' and confirm no batch can select it; export the equipment log for a granulator and confirm entries are chronological and include batch numbers and users.
notes: confirmed in official text (FDA 211.67/211.68/211.182 and EU 3.x/4.31-4.32 are equivalent).

clause: Part I, 18.4.4 (time limits after cleaning) and 18.4.5, 18.2.8
requirement: Time limits for storing process materials and cleaned equipment before use must be stated and based on data. Containers for filling must be cleaned before filling, with attention to glass fragments and metal particles. In-process controls done in production areas must not harm the product or another product.
system_implications: Clean-hold-time (and dirty-hold-time where defined) per equipment class, validated and stored in master data; the system computes 'clean status valid until' and blocks use after expiry, forcing re-cleaning; process-material hold times as in SM-11/SM-13.
verification_test: Clean a tablet press, wait past its validated clean-hold time (simulated clock) and confirm the next batch cannot use it until it is re-cleaned.
notes: confirmed in official text

requirement: A formal change-control system must assess all changes that could affect production and control. Written procedures cover identifying, documenting, reviewing and approving changes to raw materials, specifications, analytical methods, facilities, support systems, equipment (including computer hardware), processing steps, labelling and packaging materials and computer software. Proposals are drafted, reviewed and approved by the relevant units and by the quality units. Impact on product quality is evaluated, and changes may be classified (e.g., minor/major) to decide testing and validation. All affected documents must be revised when the change is implemented. The first batch made or tested after the change must be evaluated, and effects of critical changes on retest or expiry dates assessed (possibly with accelerated or ongoing stability).
system_implications: Every MBR/MPR version, equipment or software configuration change references an approved change record; the system flags the 'first batch after change' for mandatory post-change evaluation by QA and can route it to stability; eBMR software and configuration changes themselves follow change control (see SM-10).
verification_test: Approve an MBR revision under change record CC-1 and confirm the first batch executed on it is flagged 'post-change evaluation required' and cannot be released until that evaluation is signed.
notes: confirmed in official text. The explicit first-batch evaluation (from ICH Q7) is not written into 21 CFR 211 or EU Chapter 1 for finished products, though EU 1.4(xii)/ICH Q10 expect post-implementation evaluation.

clause: Part I, section 10 (self-inspection, quality audits, suppliers), 10.1-10.8
requirement: Self-inspections must be routine and at least once a year (frequency stated in the procedure), done by an objective team of GMP-knowledgeable staff (internal or external), and may also be triggered by recalls, repeated rejections or announced inspections. A report must cover results, evaluation and conclusions and recommended corrective actions, with management follow-up; the self-inspection checklist covers documentation, production and IPCs, QC, sanitation, validation, complaints, recalls, labels control and results of previous self-inspections. Suppliers are approved by QC together with other departments after evaluation, audited where needed, and listed as approved.
system_implications: The eBMR should provide an audit mode for self-inspection (read-only access to records, sampling of batches, export of deviations/CAPA status) and link CAPA from self-inspection findings; approved-supplier list is master data used by dispensing (SM-20).
verification_test: Create a self-inspection finding referencing three batch records and confirm the linked CAPA and batch references are traceable both ways; confirm an auditor role can view but not modify batch records.
notes: confirmed in official text. A fixed minimum of one self-inspection per year is stricter than 21 CFR 211 (no self-inspection clause) and EU Chapter 9 (no fixed frequency).

clause: Part I, sections 6 (complaints and adverse reactions) and 7 (product recalls)
requirement: Complaints about possible defects are recorded in full, investigated (normally with the QC head), and all decisions and measures recorded and cross-referenced to the batch records; other batches, including any containing reprocessed material from the defective batch, must be considered; complaint records are reviewed for trends; the licensing authority is told when action is contemplated for serious quality problems. A pharmacovigilance system must collect and forward ADR reports to the licensing authorities. Recalls: written SOP able to reach every distribution level down to retail quickly (print and electronic media may be used); the authorised person runs recalls; distribution records with wholesaler and direct-customer details must be readily available; recalled stock is segregated securely; the licensing authority is informed of any intended recall; progress is recorded and a final report reconciles delivered and recovered quantities; recall arrangements are tested periodically.
system_implications: Batch genealogy must answer 'which batches share this material lot or contain reprocessed/recovered material from batch X' in seconds; complaint and recall records link to batch IDs; distribution data (customer, quantity, date) per batch available for recall reconciliation.
verification_test: Given a defective API lot, list all finished batches using it, including batches containing recovered material from affected batches; generate a recall reconciliation for one batch showing distributed vs returned quantities.
notes: confirmed in official text

requirement: Staff must be qualified and trained, with written job descriptions, an organisation chart, no gaps or unexplained overlaps in GMP responsibilities, and deputies only if suitably qualified. Training follows a written programme for everyone entering production or QC areas, including maintenance and cleaning staff; there is job-specific training for new recruits, continuing training with periodic assessment of effectiveness, specific training for clean areas and hazardous materials, and training records (including evidence of qualification for consultants and contract staff). Health checks are required before and during employment, with periodic eye checks for visual inspectors; sick staff with lesions are excluded from handling products; untrained visitors are kept out or supervised.
system_implications: User qualification matrix: each MBR step type requires a training record (and, for inspectors, a current eye test); the system refuses sign-on or step execution by untrained users and records training status at the time of signature; visitor/contractor accounts are read-only or supervised.
verification_test: Assign a compression step to a user without the compression training record and confirm it is refused; let an operator's training expire mid-campaign and confirm new steps are blocked while earlier signatures remain valid.
notes: confirmed in official text

clause: Part I, section 9 (production under loan licence or contract, contract analysis), 9.1-9.5
requirement: Production under a loan licence or contract must follow the product licence and a written contract that sets each party's responsibilities (including release, sampling and testing) and states how the authorised person releases each batch. Only a holder of a valid manufacturing licence may manufacture under contract; subcontracting needs the contract giver's prior approval. The loan licensee or contract giver must review records and results, confirm GMP and licence compliance and release by the authorised person, and must hold or have access to manufacturing, analytical and distribution records and reference samples, including any needed for complaints or suspected fraud.
system_implications: Multi-party batch model: a batch can belong to a loan licensee (the brand owner's licence) while made on the facility's premises; batch records must carry both parties' licence numbers and allow controlled, read-only sharing with the loan licensee/contract giver; release workflow configurable to show which party's authorised person releases.
verification_test: Create a loan-licence batch and confirm the record shows the loan licence number and the host manufacturing licence number, and that a contract-giver reviewer can view but not edit the completed record.
notes: confirmed in official text. 'Loan licence' is an Indian legal construct (Drugs Rules Forms 25A/28A) without an exact FDA/EU equivalent; EU Chapter 7 covers outsourced activities.

clause: Part I, section 5 (qualification and validation), 5.1-5.12; Appendix I (site master file) item on computerised-system validation
requirement: Each company must identify the qualification and validation needed to show critical aspects are controlled, in a validation master plan covering DQ, IQ, OQ, PQ and process validation, per approved protocols, with written reports; any change that may affect quality must be qualified or validated; validation is ongoing with periodic review, and processes are set on validation results. Particular attention goes to analytical methods, automated systems and cleaning procedures. The site master file must describe qualification and calibration, including recording systems and arrangements for computerised-system validation.
system_implications: The eBMR (an automated system) must be included in the customer's VMP; vendor should supply validation deliverables and support periodic review; the site master file section on computerised systems will describe the eBMR, so the vendor should provide a short, accurate system description.
verification_test: Check the validation package contains URS, risk assessment, IQ/OQ scripts, traceability matrix and a periodic-review template; check a site-master-file text snippet describing the eBMR is available.
notes: confirmed in official text

requirement: Classified areas are to be qualified and routinely monitored with most weight on in-operation (dynamic) data taken near exposed materials. Recommended limits per class: ISO 5 / Class 100 = 3,520 particles >=0.5 um per m3, active air action 1 cfu/m3, settle plate action 1 cfu per 4 h; ISO 6 = 35,200, 7, 3; ISO 7 = 352,000, 10, 5; ISO 8 = 3,520,000, 100, 50. Firms may set alternative microbial action levels with justification; settle plates are optional; ISO 5 is roughly EU Grade A.
system_implications: Room/zone master data must hold the FDA class, ISO class and EU grade, plus configurable particle and viable limits that default to the Table 1 values (with a separate EU profile). Each MBR step names the minimum class required. The eBMR resolves which room/zone each step ran in, so EM data for that zone and time window can be attached to the batch.
verification_test: Load default limits and check the four classes against Table 1. Configure an EU profile and check that both profiles can coexist. Run a step that needs ISO 5 in a zone classed ISO 7 and confirm the system blocks it.

requirement: Clean-area control parameters rest on qualification data, and the routine monitoring program should confirm on an ongoing basis that each area still meets its class while operations are running.
system_implications: The eBMR checks the room's qualification/classification status (current, expired, or suspended) at line clearance and at each aseptic step start. It blocks the step or forces a deviation when the status is not current. The status and due date in effect at execution time are stored in the batch record.
verification_test: Set the filling room's qualification to expired and attempt line clearance: it must be blocked or deviation-gated. Then check that the batch record shows the qualification status as it stood at execution time.

requirement: In the ISO 5 critical zone, non-viable particles (>=0.5 um) should stay at or below 3,520 per m3. Counts are taken during filling/closing at representative high-risk points, generally within about one foot of the work site and inside the airflow, with a justified probe orientation. Monitoring should happen in every production shift, preferably with a remote (continuous) counting system. For powder operations, sampling may be adapted to separate product particles from extrinsic contamination.
system_implications: The eBMR imports or links continuous particle counter data for each ISO 5 point used by the batch, covering the whole fill/close window. It plots the data on the batch timeline alongside interventions, compares it with limits, and flags any shift the batch spans that has no particle data. Excursions during the batch window become review items that need an assessment.
verification_test: Simulate a fill spanning two shifts with counter data for only one shift: the review must flag missing data. Inject a count above 3,520/m3 during the fill: the review must show an excursion needing assessment before QA can sign.

requirement: HEPA air in the critical zone should flow fast enough to sweep particles away and keep airflow unidirectional. Each line needs a justified velocity range (commonly 0.45 m/s +/-20%). In-situ smoke/airflow studies under dynamic conditions, including the effect of interventions, should be documented with conclusions. Periodic velocity readings should be taken close to the filter (roughly 15 cm / 6 in below its face) and at a fixed height over the work surface, then compared with the range established in the airflow studies. Filters showing non-uniform velocity should be replaced.
system_implications: Line/equipment master data holds the justified velocity range, date and reference of the last airflow visualisation study, and last velocity check with its due date. The eBMR pre-use check confirms these are current for the line used. The intervention catalogue should note whether each intervention type was assessed in airflow studies. Batch review shows any unassessed intervention.
verification_test: Set the velocity check past its due date and start a fill: the step must be blocked or deviation-gated. Record an intervention type not flagged as airflow-assessed: the review must highlight it.

requirement: Viable air samples from the critical ISO 5 zone should normally show no growth. Any contamination found there should get proper investigative attention.
system_implications: Any viable recovery (>0 cfu) from an ISO 5 sample taken during a batch window automatically opens a linked deviation/investigation and places a disposition hold on every batch whose aseptic window overlaps the sample time. QA release is blocked until the investigation is closed with a documented batch-impact decision.
verification_test: Enter a 1 cfu result on an ISO 5 active air sample taken during a fill. Confirm a deviation is auto-created and linked to the batch, and that the release e-signature is blocked until closure.

requirement: Support areas are classed by what happens in them. The room right next to the aseptic line should be at least ISO 7 when in operation (ISO 6, or the whole room at ISO 5, is also acceptable). ISO 8 suits less critical work such as washing equipment. Support areas should keep bioburden low on items that will be sterilised later.
system_implications: The MBR assigns a minimum room class to each step: component dispensing, compounding, equipment washing, container/closure preparation, filling, and so on. At step start the eBMR checks the room actually used against that class, and records the room ID and class in the batch record.
verification_test: Start a compounding step marked 'ISO 7 minimum' in an ISO 8 room: it must be blocked. Start an equipment-wash step in an ISO 8 room: it must be allowed.

requirement: Cleaner rooms should hold a clear positive pressure over adjacent less clean rooms: about 10-15 Pa between different classes with doors closed, and at least about 12.5 Pa at all times between the aseptic room and any unclassified neighbour. Door-open time should be tightly controlled. If the differential falls below its minimum, the aseptic room's environmental quality should be restored and confirmed before work continues.
system_implications: Room-pair master data holds the dP limits. For every room pair used during the batch, the eBMR links or imports BMS/EMS pressure-differential data for the whole execution window and shows minimum values against limits. Any low-dP period needs a documented restoration and confirmation (for example extra EM or a clean-up) before further aseptic steps can be signed. The event and its impact assessment stay attached to the batch. Door-held-open alarms from interlocks or the BMS are captured in the same batch alarm register (see ASEP-08), and their duration is compared with the configured maximum door-open time.
verification_test: Replay a BMS trace with an 8 Pa dip lasting 5 minutes during filling. Confirm the batch shows the excursion, that the next aseptic step needs a restoration record, and that release is blocked until the impact assessment is signed.

requirement: Differential pressures between cleanrooms should be monitored continuously through each shift and recorded often. Every alarm should be documented and every out-of-limit condition investigated. The monitoring system should use alarms to catch a developing low-pressure trend early, so conditions can be restored before action levels are reached.
system_implications: The eBMR pulls all EMS/BMS alarms (dP, particle, temperature/RH) for the batch's rooms and window into an alarm register in the batch record. Each alarm needs an acknowledgement and an assessment of whether it affects the batch. Alarms that breach limits must be linked to a deviation. QA cannot release while any alarm in the window is unassessed. Gaps in the data feed are treated as alarms.
verification_test: Create three alarms in a batch window, assess two and leave one open. Release must be blocked. Cut the data feed for 30 minutes: the gap must appear as an item that needs assessment.

requirement: Compressed gases used in cleanrooms (air, nitrogen, CO2 for purging or overlay) should be suitably pure, for example oil-free. After filtration they should be at least as clean, microbiologically and in particles, as the room air they enter. Sterile membrane filters are advised on autoclave air lines, lyophiliser vacuum breaks, and tanks holding sterilised material. Sterilised holding tanks and their contents should be kept under positive pressure or sealed, with safeguards against back-flow of non-sterile air or liquid.
system_implications: For every product-contact or sterile-boundary gas use (nitrogen overlay, lyo vacuum break, tank blanketing), the eBMR records the gas system ID, the point-of-use filter ID, and whether the gas quality test is current. For sterilised holding tanks it records that positive pressure was kept (or the seal status) from sterilisation to end of use. A loss of pressure is recorded as a deviation.
verification_test: Record a nitrogen overlay whose gas quality test is expired: the step must be blocked or deviation-gated. Record a tank pressure drop to zero during a hold: a deviation must be required.

requirement: Gas and vent filters should stay dry (hydrophobic media, heated where appropriate). Filters that form a sterile boundary or supply sterile gas that can affect product should be integrity tested at installation, periodically afterwards (for example at end of use), and after any event that could damage them. Integrity-test failures should be investigated, and filters replaced at defined intervals.
system_implications: The eBMR keeps a vent/gas filter register (filter ID, part/lot, installation date, service-life limit, integrity test history) linked to the equipment used by each batch. It blocks use of a filter past its replacement interval. A failed integrity test automatically links to every batch processed since the filter's last passing test and opens a deviation.
verification_test: Mark a tank vent filter as failing its end-of-use test. The system must list every batch processed since the last pass and open a deviation linked to each. A filter past its change interval must block equipment release.

requirement: HEPA filters should be leak tested in place at installation and then at set intervals (about twice a year for the aseptic processing room). This includes filters in depyrogenation tunnels and ovens. Extra tests are appropriate after poor air results or renovation, or during a media fill or sterility failure investigation. A single probe reading of about 0.01% of the upstream challenge means a significant leak: repair or replace, then retest. Scans should be fully documented, and the manufacturer stays responsible for the specifications and acceptance criteria used by contractors.
system_implications: Equipment/room master data holds HEPA leak-test status and due date for each filling room, ISO 5 unit, depyrogenation tunnel/oven and isolator. The eBMR checks all of them are current at line clearance, stores the status seen, and blocks or deviation-gates expired items. Sterility-positive and media-fill-failure investigation templates include a HEPA retest task.
verification_test: Expire the depyrogenation tunnel HEPA certification and start a vial washing/depyrogenation step: it must be blocked. Open a sterility-positive investigation and confirm a HEPA leak retest task is generated.

requirement: Personnel and material flows should avoid unnecessary activity. The number of people in the aseptic room should be kept to a minimum. Entries to and exits from the room, and especially the critical zone, should be limited, as should transfers into the critical zone of a cleanroom or isolator. Movement next to the critical zone should be restricted.
system_implications: The eBMR records who was present in the aseptic room during the batch, from access-control integration or manual sign-in/out, with entry and exit times. It computes the peak headcount and compares it with the maximum qualified in the latest media fill for that line. It also counts transfers into the critical zone. Exceeding the qualified headcount triggers a deviation.
verification_test: The media fill qualified 4 people. Record 5 people present at once during filling: the system must raise a deviation and show the peak on the batch timeline. The personnel roster must be printable in the batch report.

requirement: Every aseptic intervention or line stoppage adds contamination risk, so equipment and processes should keep interventions few and simple. Examples: in-line weight checks instead of manual ones, sterilise-in-place of pre-assembled connections instead of aseptic connections, automation or robotics.
system_implications: Each line's MBR carries a catalogue of permitted interventions (inherent and corrective), each with an ID, description, and the media fill in which it was qualified. The eBMR records every stoppage and intervention against that catalogue. An intervention not in the catalogue cannot be logged as routine: it must go through a deviation path.
verification_test: Try to log an intervention type that is not in the line's catalogue: the system must force a deviation. Log a catalogued intervention: the system must record the catalogue ID and link to its qualifying media fill.

requirement: In lyophilisation, partially stoppered sterile product should only move through critical (ISO 5) conditions. The path from filler to lyophiliser, and the transport and loading steps, should give ISO 5 protection, for example with qualified transfer equipment.
system_implications: For freeze-dried products the eBMR has a transfer/loading step that records the transfer device ID and its qualification status, confirms ISO 5 protection, and timestamps the first tray out of the filler, the last tray loaded, and chamber closure. It computes and enforces the maximum exposure of partially stoppered vials. EM for the transfer path is linked to the batch.
verification_test: Record loading with an unqualified transfer cart: it must be blocked. Exceed the configured partial-stopper exposure limit: the system must require a deviation.

requirement: Materials, supplies, equipment and utensils moving from lower to higher classified areas should follow written procedures that protect room conditions. Items are disinfected by a defined method or, if used in the critical zone, sterilised by a suitable method. Double-door or integrated sterilisers, airlocks and interlocked doors support controlled transfer.
system_implications: The eBMR logs each item brought into the aseptic area for the batch. The log records the transfer route (pass-through steriliser with cycle ID, or airlock disinfection with agent, lot, contact time and operator) and whether the item is destined for the critical zone. It blocks an item from being used in an ISO 5 step unless it has a valid sterilisation record within its hold time.
verification_test: Try to use a tool in the filling zone that only has a disinfection record: the step must be blocked. Add an autoclave cycle record: the step must be allowed, and the cycle ID must appear in the batch report.

requirement: If stoppered but uncapped vials leave the aseptic zone or room, the product should be protected (for example with local air protection) until crimping is done. On-line detection of stoppers that are not properly seated adds assurance.
system_implications: The eBMR records the capping location and its protection status, the stopper-to-crimp time window (with a configured maximum), and counts of units rejected by the seating-detection system. These counts feed into unit reconciliation. Exceeding the time limit or losing local protection triggers a deviation.
verification_test: Record a 3-hour stopper-to-crimp gap against a 2-hour limit: a deviation must be required. Check that the reconciliation includes stopper-height rejects.

requirement: Deviation or change control should cover abnormal states caused by shutdowns of air handling or other utilities, and the effect of construction work on facility control. Written procedures should say how a facility is brought back to operating conditions after a shutdown.
system_implications: At line clearance the eBMR checks for open utility/HVAC shutdown, construction, or change-control events affecting the batch's rooms. If one is open, it requires the documented return-to-service evidence (cleaning/disinfection, EM confirmation, and requalification if needed) before aseptic steps can start. Utility interruptions during execution are linked to the batch for review.
verification_test: Log an HVAC shutdown for the filling room without a return-to-service record: line clearance must fail. Close the return-to-service record: clearance must succeed and reference that record.

requirement: Before anyone may enter the aseptic manufacturing area they should be trained in aseptic technique, cleanroom behaviour, microbiology, hygiene, gowning, the patient-safety risk of non-sterile product, and the area's specific SOPs. They should then take part in ongoing periodic training.
system_implications: At each e-signature on an aseptic-area step, the eBMR checks the LMS (training management system) for current training on the aseptic curriculum and on the SOPs linked to that step. If training is missing or expired, the signature is refused, and the batch record stores a snapshot of the training status at the moment of signing.
verification_test: Let one SOP training for a user expire, then have that user try to sign a filling step: the signature must be rejected with a reason. Check that the batch report shows the training status at signing for each signer.

requirement: Only people who are qualified and correctly gowned should be allowed into the aseptic area. Gowns should be sterile and non-shedding and cover skin and hair. Gowning qualification should include microbial surface sampling at several justified gown sites (for example glove fingers, mask, forearm, chest). Requalification should be periodic: yearly is usually enough for automated operations with little personnel involvement and good environmental data, and more often after adverse findings.
system_implications: A personnel qualification register holds gowning qualification status and expiry, the date of the person's last media fill, and any restriction flags. The eBMR refuses aseptic-area sign-in and step signatures from anyone whose gowning qualification is expired, missing or suspended. Each person's qualification snapshot is stored in the batch roster.
verification_test: Set an operator's gowning qualification to expired: aseptic sign-in must be refused. Suspend an operator after a failing glove print: that operator must be blocked from aseptic steps on every open batch.

requirement: Supervisors should routinely watch each operator during real operations to check they follow procedures. The quality unit should regularly oversee adherence to SOPs and aseptic technique on the floor.
system_implications: The eBMR provides a structured observation record for aseptic behaviour during the batch: observer, role (supervisor or QA), time, operator observed, checklist result, and any findings. Findings can open a deviation linked to the batch. The batch review summary shows whether QA oversight took place.
verification_test: Record a QA observation that finds an operator leaning over open vials. Confirm a deviation can be raised from it, that it is linked to the batch, and that it appears in the review summary.

requirement: Sterilised materials should only be handled with sterile instruments. Between uses, instruments are kept under ISO 5 in sterilised containers and replaced as needed. Gloves should be sanitised or changed often. Any torn or defective gown part should be changed at once. Operators should never touch sterile product, containers, closures or critical surfaces with their gown or gloves.
system_implications: The eBMR offers quick-log event types for glove sanitisation or change, gown change, gown breach or damage, and instrument replacement, each timestamped against the operator and batch. A gown breach event needs an immediate-change record and an assessment of units exposed during the breach period, which may require segregating or rejecting units.
verification_test: Log a torn glove during filling. The system must require a change record plus an impact assessment, which feeds the deviation and the review summary.

requirement: Written procedures should define when personnel must be retrained, requalified, or moved to other areas.
system_implications: When a person has a personnel-monitoring excursion, a gown breach, or an observation finding, rule-driven triggers set their status to retrain, requalify, or restricted. The eBMR enforces that status at sign-in and at signature, until an authorised QA user clears it with a reference to the completed action.
verification_test: Create a glove-print action-level result. The operator's status must become 'requalification required', and aseptic signatures must be blocked until QA clears it with the requalification record ID.

requirement: People who take aseptic samples or run microbiology tests should meet the same training, aseptic-technique and qualification principles as manufacturing staff. Otherwise the laboratory data, and so the state of control, cannot be trusted.
system_implications: EM, personnel-monitoring, bioburden and sterility sampling tasks generated by the eBMR record the sampler's identity, and the sampler must be qualified for aseptic sampling. Results that come back from the LIMS carry the analyst ID. The review checks that samplers and analysts were qualified on the sampling or test date.
verification_test: Assign an EM sampling task to a user without aseptic-sampler qualification: completion must be rejected. Check that the batch report lists the sampler and analyst for each result.

requirement: There should be an active personnel monitoring program. Each operator's gloves are surface-sampled every day or with each lot, plus other chosen gown sites at a set frequency. The quality unit should apply more thorough monitoring to people doing labour-intensive work that involves repeated or complex aseptic manipulations.
system_implications: For every person on the batch's aseptic roster, the eBMR creates the required glove (and, per configuration, gown) sampling tasks, triggered at exit from the critical zone or at end of session. It captures sample IDs, sites and times. Batch review stays blocked until results for every operator have come back from the LIMS and been assessed. Operators flagged as high-intervention get extra sampling tasks.
verification_test: On a batch with 4 aseptic operators, complete only 3 glove samples: the review must flag a missing sample. When results arrive for all 4, the block must clear only after assessment.

requirement: Gloves should not be sanitised just before sampling, because that can hide organisms that were present during the aseptic manipulation.
system_implications: The glove-sampling task records the sample time and the operator's last glove-sanitisation event. It requires the sampler to attest that no sanitisation happened right before sampling. The system warns if a sanitisation event falls within a configured minimum interval before the sample.
verification_test: Log a glove sanitisation 30 s before a glove print with a 5-minute rule: the system must warn and require a justification or re-sample.

requirement: If an operator exceeds set levels or shows an adverse trend, an investigation should start promptly. Follow-up can include more sampling, closer observation, retraining, gowning requalification, or reassignment outside the aseptic area.
system_implications: A personnel-monitoring result above alert or action level is automatically linked to every batch the operator worked on in that session, and at action level opens an investigation. The eBMR trends results per operator over time and applies the resulting status change (see ASEP-22). Batch release waits for the investigation's documented impact conclusion.
verification_test: Post an action-level glove result for operator X. The investigation must open and link to all batches X worked that day, and release of those batches must be blocked until closure.

requirement: For every component that could carry contamination (API, WFI, excipients), the microbial content (bioburden) and endotoxin level should be characterised and acceptance limits set. Written procedures and specifications should govern accepting or rejecting each lot of any component that may carry endotoxin, and lots that fail endotoxin limits should be rejected.
system_implications: Material master data carries flags and specification references for bioburden and endotoxin. At dispensing, the eBMR checks that the lot's QC disposition is Released and that the bioburden and endotoxin results are present and within limits. It blocks rejected, quarantined or untested lots. The lot numbers and test result references of the components used are written into the batch record.
verification_test: Issue an excipient lot whose endotoxin result is missing: dispensing must be blocked. Issue a lot with an endotoxin result over the limit: it must be blocked and show as rejected. Check that the batch report shows each component's endotoxin result.

requirement: Any lot of a component, container or closure that could carry microbial contamination objectionable for its use must pass microbiological testing before use. Components, containers and closures must always be handled and stored so as to prevent contamination.
system_implications: The material master includes a 'micro test before use' attribute. The eBMR will not let a lot flagged this way be consumed or staged until the LIMS micro result is released. Storage location and condition checks run when material is issued to the batch.
verification_test: Flag a stopper lot 'micro test required' and leave the result pending: issuing it to the filling order must be refused.

requirement: Each component is sterilised on its own, or components are combined and the mixture sterilised, and knowing the bioburden helps judge whether the sterilisation is adequate.
